audits.title: Follow-up Audit Report on New York City Public Schools’ Efforts to Maximize Medicaid Reimbursement Claims for Special Education Services
audits.plain_title: Schools left an estimated $431.6 million in Medicaid money unclaimed
audits.agency: Department of Education (New York City Public Schools)
audits.what_they_audited: A follow-up to a 2021 audit that found the school system was not seeking Medicaid reimbursement it was entitled to for special education services. Auditors checked whether New York City Public Schools carried out the 30 earlier recommendations and measured how much reimbursement went unclaimed in fiscal years 2023 through 2025.
audits.background: Federal law requires the school system to provide the special education services spelled out in each student's individualized education program, and Medicaid reimburses school districts for 10 types of covered services delivered to Medicaid-enrolled students, with the state and city splitting the money evenly. A claim fails if even one documentation requirement is not met.

findings.plain: Auditors estimate the city failed to claim about $431.6 million in Medicaid reimbursement for special education services in fiscal years 2023 through 2025.
findings.quote: the City failed to claim approximately $431.6 million in Medicaid revenue during Fiscal Years 2023, 2024, and 2025

findings.plain: The school system claimed reimbursement for only 54% of the documented occupational, physical and speech therapy sessions it provided to Medicaid-enrolled students, largely because it failed to collect required paperwork. That gap cost at least $273.4 million over the three years.
findings.quote: NYCPS only claimed reimbursement for 54% of all documented OT, PT, and ST services provided to Medicaid-enrolled pre-K to Grade 12 students

findings.plain: There is no record of 16.2% of the therapy services that students' education plans required. Either children missed services considered medically necessary or the services happened but were never documented, which would add up to $132.8 million more in lost reimbursement.
findings.quote: NYCPS lacks any record of providing 16.2% of all OT, PT, and ST services that were mandated for eligible students with IEPs

findings.plain: The school system still chooses not to seek reimbursement for seven of the 10 service types Medicaid covers, including psychological counseling, evaluations, special transportation and skilled nursing. Auditors conservatively put the added cost at $25.4 million.
findings.quote: It is still NYCPS’ policy not to claim for seven of the 10 service types for which Medicaid reimbursement is available

findings.plain: Of the 30 recommendations from the 2021 audit, the school system fully implemented three, partially implemented eight and did not act on the other 19.
findings.quote: NYCPS has fully implemented only three recommendations and partially implemented eight others, leaving a total of 19 that were not acted upon

findings.plain: Cooperation with the audit was poor. The school system took 52 business days on average to hand over requested information and denied auditors direct access to its record systems.
findings.quote: On average, it took NYCPS 52 business days to provide requested information or documentation

Do a cost-benefit analysis of expanding claiming to more of the covered services and develop a staged expansion plan.

Promptly give auditors the information and documents needed to complete legally authorized audits.

audits.title: Elder Abuse Services, Training, and Coordination
audits.plain_title: How the city monitors elder abuse services
audits.agency: New York City Department for the Aging
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department for the Aging effectively oversees the provision of elder abuse services. The audit covered April 2019 through April 2025.
audits.background: The Department for the Aging's Elder Justice Program contracts with six community-based providers, at a cost of about $12.6 million for 2023 through 2025, to serve and protect people age 60 and older who have been abused by someone in a trusting relationship. Program standards set deadlines for contacting, assessing and following up with clients, with faster action required in high-risk cases.

findings.plain: Providers did not always meet required timelines for contacting, assessing and following up with clients. In 17 of 41 sampled cases the referral described high-risk conditions such as physical violence or no access to food, and in none of them did case workers act within the required time frame.
findings.quote: For all 17 cases, the case workers did not act within the required time frame to provide crucial services to clients

findings.plain: In one case, a 68-year-old woman who said her foster son had struck her was not treated as high risk and was not contacted for 26 days, instead of within 24 hours as required for high-risk cases.
findings.quote: the provider did not designate this case as high risk and did not attempt to contact the client until 26 days later

findings.plain: The department did not ensure direct service staff got required training in detecting, reporting and counseling on elder abuse. Fifteen of 21 workers tested, or 71%, had not completed all required training, and some providers did not know the requirements existed.
findings.quote: Fifteen of the 21 workers tested (71%) did not complete all the required training.

findings.plain: The department did not enforce education and outreach requirements. It did not require providers to submit the annual outreach plans their contracts call for, and no provider submitted any during the audit period.
findings.quote: none of the providers submitted any annual plans to DFTA during the audit scope

findings.plain: Auditors also found broader oversight gaps, including a bill payer assistance program that was never evaluated, inconsistent performance metrics across records, unclear guidance to providers and unsupported expenses.
findings.quote: Significant deficiencies in DFTA’s oversight of the Elder Justice Program

numbers.label: Cost of elder abuse service contracts for 2023 through 2025
High-risk sampled cases where required deadlines were missed
Tested workers who had not completed all required training

recommendations: Strengthen oversight and monitoring of elder abuse cases so contracted providers deliver timely and appropriate services.
Take additional steps to make sure Elder Justice Program workers are properly trained.
Collect better documentation and step up monitoring to confirm providers hold the required number of educational presentations and outreach activities.
Enforce the requirement that providers submit annual plans and review those plans to see whether activities reach the intended people and communities with the right content.
For future programs, define what success looks like and set up monitoring and evaluation measures, including lessons learned, to guide decisions.

audits.title: CBC Recommends COGE Strengthen Proposed Charter Rainy Day Fund Language
audits.plain_title: Six changes proposed to the city's rainy day fund charter language
audits.agency: New York City Commission on Government Efficiency
audits.what_they_audited: A memo from the Citizens Budget Commission to the Commission on Government Efficiency (COGE) reviewing the commission's proposed New York City Charter amendment on the city's Rainy Day Fund, called the Revenue Stabilization Fund (RSF).
audits.background: The proposed amendment would set a target fund size of 12 percent of the prior year's tax revenue and would carry over the withdrawal rule that is currently in state law.

findings.plain: The proposed withdrawal rule would let half the fund be spent for any purpose, with the rest available under a mayor's own definition of a compelling fiscal need.
findings.quote: would allow 50 percent of the fund to be used for any reason

findings.plain: The target size in the proposal could be met with money held in other funds, including the Retiree Health Benefits Trust and the General and Capital Stabilization Reserves.
findings.quote: would allow the Retiree Health Benefits Trust (RHBT), General and Capital Stabilization Reserves, or other funds to be included, in effect, as rainy day reserves

findings.plain: Under the proposed language the city could write a policy that lets it skip deposits, for instance to fund a new or expanded program in a strong revenue year.
findings.quote: The proposed language would allow the City to draft a policy that permits it to forgo deposits

findings.plain: The report says a 12 percent target is too small measured against past recessions, and puts the amount needed to cover two years of recessionary tax revenue losses at 16 percent.
findings.quote: sets a target size of 12 percent of tax revenue in the preceding year, which is too small based on history

findings.plain: The proposal asks for consultation with the city comptroller but does not require the comptroller's assessment to be published.
findings.quote: The proposed language requires Comptroller consultation, which is beneficial but not sufficient.

findings.plain: The proposal would set the fund's operating rules through policy rather than local law.
findings.quote: The proposed amendment would set rules by policy.

recommendations: Allow withdrawals only during a recession defined by economic indicators or a severe emergency causing revenue losses or added spending above 1 percent of city funds, and cap the first-year withdrawal at two-thirds of the balance.
Apply the target fund size only to the Revenue Stabilization Fund, leaving out the Retiree Health Benefits Trust and the General and Capital Stabilization Reserves.
Require deposits based on revenue strength alone, using a trigger such as inflation or tax revenue growth above 3 percent.
Raise the target fund size to 16 percent of tax revenue, the amount the report says would cover two years of recessionary tax revenue losses.
Require the city comptroller to publish an opinion on whether the fund's implementation policy is reasonable and appropriate.
Set the fund's implementation rules and definitions in local law rather than in policy.

audits.title: The Remediation Action Plan
audits.plain_title: The Rikers remediation manager's first-year plan to fix the jails
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The first annual Remediation Action Plan from Nicholas Deml, the court-appointed remediation manager in Nunez v. City of New York, laying out his assessment of the city jail system and the specific reforms he will direct the Department of Correction to carry out from July 14, 2026 through June 30, 2027.
audits.background: The federal court held New York City in civil contempt of eighteen provisions of four court orders meant to stem violence and excessive force in the jails, and appointed a remediation manager with broad authority over department operations. The court ordered him to produce yearly work plans, each building on the last, with this first plan prioritizing safety-related areas.

findings.plain: The remediation manager found the department struggles to perform even the most basic correctional functions such as staffing posts and securing housing units, and spent more than $370 million on overtime in the past fiscal year even as jail infrastructure crumbles.
findings.quote: spent more than $370 million on overtime this past fiscal year

findings.plain: In his team's first days he observed a housing unit filled with smoke from fires set by people in custody while an officer shrugged, and reviewed a large-scale fight involving nearly 30 people that started when an officer left a pantry door unsecured and abandoned his post.
findings.quote: A large-scale fight ensued, involving nearly 30 individuals

findings.plain: Such incidents are not outliers: from January to May 2026 people in custody set 130 fires and engaged in 2,978 fights, and the report notes the court has found violence in the jails is now worse than when the consent judgment took effect in 2015.
findings.quote: fires and engaged in 2,978 fights

findings.plain: The department operates inside an unusually dense network of oversight bodies in which each institution holds authority over part of jail operations but none is responsible for the whole system.
findings.quote: The environment is chaotic.

findings.plain: The remediation manager concluded that after more than a decade without meaningful improvement, incremental reform has itself become a form of failure, and said he will use his full court-granted authority to force change.
findings.quote: The system has reached the point where incrementalism is

findings.plain: He found the department's investigative and disciplinary units were disconnected and dispersed, weakening accountability, and in May 2026 began consolidating them into a single division under a new senior deputy commissioner who reports directly to his team.

audits.title: New York City Housing Authority Monitorship: Monitors' Report (Eighth Report)
audits.plain_title: Mold repairs speed up while heat and elevators slip
audits.what_they_audited: The federal monitors' eighth quarterly report on whether the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) is meeting the housing conditions it promised under its 2019 agreement with the federal government, covering heat, elevators, pests and waste, mold and leaks, lead paint and inspections, plus organizational change and capital spending. It reports data for February 1, 2026 to April 30, 2026.
audits.background: On January 31, 2019 NYCHA agreed with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the City of New York to fix housing conditions, and a monitor was appointed to evaluate compliance. Neil Barofsky and Matthew Cipolla of Jenner & Block LLP began a five-year term as co-monitors on February 28, 2024.

findings.plain: Mold repairs got much faster. NYCHA met the agreement's mold timeframes 42% of the time in the first quarter of Year 8, up from 20% in the same period of Year 7, including removing mold within five business days 36% of the time compared with 16%. The monitors still call NYCHA substantially out of compliance with the 95% standard.
findings.quote: dramatically improved its response rates to mold

findings.plain: The mold that residents report is still overwhelmingly severe. In the first quarter of Year 8, 86% of verified mold complaints involved visible mold covering ten square feet or more, against an agreement limit of 15%.
findings.quote: 86% of verified mold complaints

findings.plain: Heat came back faster but went out more often. NYCHA restored heat after in-apartment heating failures in an average of 13 hours, down from 14.6 hours at the same point last season, yet the share of occupied apartments hit by more than three heating service interruptions rose from 28% to 36% and unplanned heating outages climbed from 358 to 472.
findings.quote: heat in an average of 13 hours, down from an average

findings.plain: Elevator service slipped even though NYCHA beat one target. It resolved 89% of unplanned elevator car outages within ten hours, above the 85% requirement, but the average length of an unplanned outage grew 27% from 4.9 hours to 6.2 hours.
findings.quote: from 4.9 hours during the ﬁrst quarter of last year to 6.2

findings.plain: Pest results were mixed. NYCHA answered 98% of rat complaints within two business days against a 90% target and cut its estimated mouse population by 23% and bed bugs by 11.5%, but its estimated rat population rose 46% from the same period last year.
findings.quote: NYCHA’s rat population estimate in the ﬁrst quarter of

findings.plain: Lead work stayed on schedule. NYCHA has finished X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) testing in about 94% of apartments presumed to have lead-based paint and has removed lead paint from 19,416 apartments, roughly 31.2% of those known to contain it, keeping it on track to abate half by 2029. Two children under six were reported with elevated blood lead levels in the quarter, down from 10 and 8 in the same period of the two prior years.
findings.quote: testing initiative. NYCHA has abated 19,416 apartments

findings.plain: The repair backlog remains enormous. NYCHA has roughly 62,000 open mold and leak work orders. Its Mold and Leak Restore and Renew program, which sends dedicated crews to the highest-need developments, has closed 1,981 work orders open for more than 100 days across four developments since August 2025, but a growing share of those closures involve no physical repair.
findings.quote: NYCHA has approximately 62,000 open mold and leak work

audits.title: 5 Ideas to Advance Economic Mobility in NYC
audits.plain_title: Five ideas for raising incomes and building wealth in the city
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, setting out five policy ideas for raising incomes and building wealth in the city. It accompanies the group's third annual NYC Economic Mobility Summit.
audits.background: The report says the Mamdani administration and City Council have taken steps on the cost of living, from expanding free childcare for two-year-olds to a housing plan and city-supported grocery stores, and it turns to the other side of the affordability question: raising incomes and building wealth.

findings.plain: Adult students are a large and growing share of the City University of New York, but they finish at lower rates. Among transfer students pursuing bachelor's degrees, 51.1 percent of those over 25 graduate within six years, compared with 65.3 percent of those under 25.
findings.quote: students over 25 graduate within six years at significantly lower rates than their younger peers: 51.1 percent, compared with 65.3 percent of transfer students under 25

findings.plain: Small businesses are closing faster than new ones open, and few have started using artificial intelligence tools. The report cites a net loss of 1,050 businesses citywide in the third quarter of 2025.
findings.quote: Business closures have outpaced openings in three of the last five quarters

findings.plain: Entry-level job postings in New York City have fallen sharply since 2022, with the steepest declines in occupations most exposed to generative artificial intelligence.
findings.quote: with occupations most exposed to generative AI facing the steepest declines

findings.plain: Homeownership gaps have widened. The number of Black homeowner households fell 14.7 percent between 2002 and 2023 even as the total number of owner-occupied units in the city rose 13 percent.
findings.quote: a 14.7 percent decline, even as the total number of owner-occupied units increased 13 percent

findings.plain: City homeownership programs are small relative to demand. HomeFirst had helped just over 3,000 households since 2004 as of December 2022, and Open Door had financed 451 units across 10 projects since 2017.
findings.quote: had helped just over 3,000 households secure homeownership since launching in 2004

findings.plain: CityFHEPS is the largest municipal housing voucher program in the country, but many voucher holders wait a long time or never find a unit. A state comptroller sample of 52 cases found an average of 292 days from the first shopping letter to shelter exit and that about 21 percent of households issued shopping letters received placements.
findings.quote: the average time from the first shopping letter to approval and shelter exit was 292 days, while only about 21 percent of households issued shopping letters ultimately received CityFHEPS placements

recommendations: Partner with the City University of New York to make it the nation's leading public university system for adult learners, by making flexible course formats the norm, piloting a CUNY Flex support model for part-time adult students, launching a CUNY Fresh Start initiative to clear small unpaid balances, scaling credit for prior learning and funding an NYC Adult Learners Network of community organizations.

Create a CUNY AI Small Business Corps that pays City University of New York students to help small businesses adopt artificial intelligence tools, prioritizing lower-income neighborhoods and commercial corridors with many immigrant- and minority-owned firms.

Launch an AI Workforce Preparation Fund and a citywide AI Workforce Task Force, with the fund supporting skills training, paid work experience, retraining for workers whose jobs are changing and rapid response for displaced workers, and the task force producing a citywide plan within six months.

Expand pathways to affordable homeownership, aiming to help 5,000 lower- and moderate-income households buy a first home and 5,000 current lower-income homeowners keep theirs by the end of 2028, by scaling Open Door, HomeFirst and HomeFix, backing community land trusts, adding homeownership tools to neighborhood plans and starting a multigenerational homeownership initiative.

Strengthen CityFHEPS navigation by carrying out the administrative reforms already proposed and expanding hands-on housing navigation, helping families consider higher-opportunity neighborhoods and connecting households to college, training, childcare and other supports.

Strengthen CityFHEPS navigation by carrying out the administrative reforms already proposed and expanding hands-on housing navigation, helping families consider higher-opportunity neighborhoods and connecting households to college, training, childcare and other supports.

audits.title: Thirtieth Report of the Independent Monitor: Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Stop and frisk compliance snapshot for summer 2025
audits.what_they_audited: A quarterly visual "compliance snapshot" updating the monitor's Twenty-Ninth Report on the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, covering the third quarter (July to September) of 2025.
audits.background: The report covers the third quarter of 2025 and in several slides compares it to the third quarter of 2024. It draws on the monitor team's audits of 100 stop reports per month and quarterly body-worn camera video audits, plus audits by the NYPD Quality Assurance Section, command self-inspections and first-line supervisor reviews; the quarter's sample includes 22 Community Response Team stops.

findings.plain: In the third quarter of 2025, the monitor's audits found 94% of reported stops, 81% of frisks and 74% of searches lawful, minimal improvement over the same quarter of 2024, with search compliance still far below acceptable levels.
findings.quote: compliance rates were 94% for stops, 81% for frisks, and...

findings.plain: Self-initiated stop compliance has improved over time, reaching a department-wide rate of 87% for the quarter, though frisks and searches during self-initiated stops were lawful only 68% and 66% of the time.
findings.quote: Self-initiated stop compliance rates have improved over time, with a Department-wide...

findings.plain: While assembling the data, the monitor discovered that the department's Quality Assurance Section never audited any stops by the Citywide Community Response Team from March 2023 to March 2026. The monitor requested and assessed a sample of 100 of those stops and included the results in the snapshot.
findings.quote: QAS never audited stops by this command

findings.plain: Supervisor review remained poor. The monitor found 6% of stops, 18% of frisks and 27% of searches unlawful, while reviewing supervisors flagged only 1% of stops, 4% of frisks and 7% of searches.
findings.quote: supervisors found that only 1% of stops, 4% of frisks, and 7% of searches

findings.plain: Officers failed to complete stop reports for 29% of stops identified in the monitor's audit (10 of 35), down from 47% in the third quarter of 2024, though the monitor said underreporting continues at an unacceptable rate and likely affects the accuracy of compliance figures.
findings.quote: For 29% of stops identified in the Monitor's audit for underreporting in the third

findings.plain: Officers recorded 96% of stops in their entirety on body-worn camera, up from 90% a year earlier.
findings.quote: for 96% of stops identified in the Monitor's audit

findings.plain: Housing Bureau compliance was low, especially for searches: 82% of stops, 75% of frisks and only 43% of searches were lawful, a sharp decline in search lawfulness from the previous quarter. Trespass arrest compliance was 96% on both the reason to approach and probable cause.
findings.quote: decline in the percentage of searches found lawful from the second quarter of 2025 to the third quarter of 2025.

audits.title: Suicide Prevention in City Jails: March 2026 Observation Aide Assessment
audits.plain_title: Suicide watch aides missing from about a third of special units
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: Staff of the New York City Board of Correction (BOC), the city's jail oversight board, ran two structured audits in March and early April 2026 of the New York City Department of Correction's (DOC) Observation Aide program, which uses trained people in custody to watch over units where individuals may be at risk of suicide. Auditors visited housing areas, reviewed logbooks and interviewed aides and correction officers.
audits.background: New York City Charter section 626(e) charges the Board with setting minimum standards for the care and supervision of people held by DOC, and city rules require DOC to run an Observation Aide program to monitor individuals at risk of suicide. Under DOC's directive, aides must tour designated housing areas every 10 minutes, and if no aide is assigned uniformed staff must tour every 15 minutes.

findings.plain: In the March baseline survey, 41 of the 62 housing units visited had an observation aide assigned and present. About one in three units had no aide at the time of inspection.
findings.quote: about one in three units lacked coverage

findings.plain: Officer paperwork was almost always incomplete. In only 4 of the 41 staffed units did the control room officer record the aide's name and identifying number in the logbook as DOC's directive requires.
findings.quote: only 4 (9.8%) had proper “A” post officer

findings.plain: Where no aide was assigned, the backup safeguard often did not happen. Only 7 of 21 unstaffed units met the 15-minute tour requirement, and staff in one restrictive housing area said they skipped the tours when nobody was on suicide watch.
findings.quote: if there is no suicide watch on the tier, we do not make

findings.plain: Aides frequently lacked the gear they need. Only 11 of the 41 staffed units had all required equipment, with flashlights, logbooks and working clocks the most common items missing, and some aides used tablets or televisions to time their rounds.
findings.quote: Only 11 of 41 staffed units (26.8%) had all required equipment.

findings.plain: The follow-up audit three weeks later found real gains. Aide coverage, aide logbook use and equipment availability all rose.
findings.quote: Observation aide coverage improved (66.1% to 82.8%)

findings.plain: Two measures stayed weak or got worse. Officer documentation moved only from 9.8 percent to 12.5 percent, and 15-minute tour compliance in units without an aide fell from 33.3 percent to 20 percent.
findings.quote: remained low (9.8% to 12.5%)

findings.plain: One unit was outside the program entirely. Officers do not let people housed in the Rose M. Singer Enhanced Supervision Housing (RESH) serve as observation aides, citing security risk, and staff there log tours every 30 minutes rather than the 15 minutes the policy requires when no aide is present.
findings.quote: allow individuals in RESH to participate in the Observation Aide program

audits.title: 2025 Annual Anti-Corruption Report
audits.plain_title: Half of city agencies have no internal audit plan
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) surveyed city agencies about their internal auditing capacity: who performs audits, whether agencies can hire and keep auditors, what kinds of audits they run, whether they have an audit plan and whether they buy outside audit services. The report covers October 1, 2024, through September 30, 2025, and draws on responses from 50 agencies.
audits.background: Mayoral Executive Order No. 105 makes the DOI commissioner the city's independent inspector general and requires this annual report. City Charter section 389(a) requires agency heads to maintain an internal control system that reduces the agency's vulnerability to fraud, waste, abuse, error, conflict of interest and corruption. Like DOI's other annual anti-corruption reports, this one summarizes what agencies report about themselves rather than DOI's own investigative findings.

findings.plain: Seventy percent of responding agencies have staff who perform internal audit functions, and 30 percent have no such staff at all.
findings.quote:
A majority of agencies (70%) reported having staff who perform internal audit 
functions, while 30% reported that they do not  have such staff.

findings.plain: Agencies split evenly on whether they have an internal audit plan, which sets out the audit work expected over a given period. DOI notes that having one is best practice.
findings.quote:
Internal audit plans enhance the ability of agencies to achieve their 
objectives, and it is best practice to have one.

findings.plain: Seventeen agencies had fewer auditors actually working than their budget allowed. Nine agencies whose budgeted audit headcount fell between January 2022 and September 2025 blamed attrition, vacancy reductions or extended vacancies and citywide budget cuts.
findings.quote:
they cited attrition, vacancy reductions or extended vacancies, and Citywide budget 
reductions, among other rea sons.

findings.plain: Sixteen of the 50 agencies reported trouble recruiting or keeping auditors, pointing to funding, salary levels and difficulty finding qualified candidates, along with hiring freezes and long hiring approvals.
findings.quote:
numerous 
agencies cited issues of funding, salary and financial compensation, and identifying 
qualified candidates.

findings.plain: Most agencies said their auditors issue written reports and make recommendations for improvement, and several described tracking corrective action through follow-up audits, management reviews and tools for open action plans.
findings.quote:
the majority of agencies also reported that their auditors 
make recommendations for improvement.

findings.plain: Seven agencies said their auditing staff reported findings from completed audits to DOI during the year.
findings.quote:
Seven agencies also reported that in the last year, the ir respective  auditing 
staff/departments had made a report to DOI regarding findings from performed or 
completed audits.

findings.plain: Twenty-one of the 50 agencies had hired outside auditors in the past five years. Agencies without internal auditors were not more likely to buy external audits: of the 15 agencies with no internal audit staff, only one had procured an external audit in that period.
findings.quote:
agencies without inte rnal auditors were not more likely to hire external 
auditors.

audits.title: Twenty-First Report for the Monitoring Period July 1, 2025 to December 31, 2025
audits.plain_title: New leaders at Rikers, but no material change in risk of harm
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The court-appointed independent monitor's 21st compliance assessment of the Department of Correction under the Nunez court orders, covering July through December 2025, with narrative updates on leadership, use of force, security practices, staff misconduct and deaths in custody plus compliance ratings for 45 court order provisions.
audits.background: Since the monitor's previous report, a new commissioner took office on February 16, 2026 and the court-appointed remediation manager began work on February 23, 2026. Much of the report covers a period under the prior city administration and before the remediation manager's appointment.

findings.plain: Despite the new leadership structure, the monitor found no material change in reducing the risk of harm in the jails as of the report's filing, with the reform effort still moving at a glacial pace.
findings.quote: no material change in ameliorating the risk of harm in the jails

findings.plain: The monitor's long list of problem centers, including normalized violence and poor security practices, no coherent operational plan, a revolving door of leadership and a perpetual state of crisis, remains essentially unchanged.
findings.quote: ...remain present with little to no change observed as of the filing of this Report.

findings.plain: The small group of persistently violent individuals responsible for most jail violence is dispersed across the jails with no dedicated management structure, and the monitor strongly urged the commissioner and remediation manager to take immediate action on classification and security deficits.
findings.quote: ...throughout the jails with no dedicated management structure in place to abate their patterns

findings.plain: Basic security failures persist, including failures to secure doors, remain on post, conduct meaningful tours, control housing areas, search and escort safely, de-escalate and activate body-worn cameras, all of which raise the risk of violence and preventable harm.
findings.quote: These deficiencies include failures to secure doors, remain on post, conduct meaningful

findings.plain: The department's Safety Plan contained some reasonable recommendations but did not provide a concrete strategy to change actual staff security practice and in several respects appeared to minimize the current state of affairs.
findings.quote: Plan did not provide a concrete strategy to change actual staff security practice,

findings.plain: A revised organizational chart took effect June 1, 2026, incorporating the remediation manager, consolidating investigations and discipline into a new division reporting to him and elevating classification, which the monitor calls a stronger foundation while cautioning that the uniformed reporting structure has reverted to its pre-2022 form.
findings.quote: The new organizational chart provides an important foundation for the reform effort.

numbers.label: Court order provisions assessed for compliance in the report
Date the court-appointed remediation manager began work

recommendations: Take immediate, specific and concrete action to mitigate the current risk of harm, focusing on the small group of individuals engaged in the largest number of violent incidents.

Provide the department with additional and new resources to support the reform effort, including administrative and project management support, policy development help and legal, compliance and operational expertise, without which reform cannot be catalyzed or sustained.

The department and the remediation manager's team must develop an overarching plan that clearly defines reform priorities and how leadership, staffing and resources will be allocated to address them in a deliberate, concrete and systematic way.
audits.agency_response: The department's new leadership worked with the remediation manager and monitoring team to revise the organizational chart, appointed the remediation manager's choice to lead the new investigations division and is considering the monitor's recommendation to reinstitute a deputy commissioner of classification.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor reports the risk of harm in the jails remains unreasonably high for incarcerated people and staff, with the department's entrenched problem centers showing little to no change despite years of work and multiple court orders.

audits.title: 2026 Healthcare & Life Sciences Report
audits.plain_title: Loosening zoning rules so hospitals can modernize
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the New York Building Congress, a membership association for the city's building and construction industry, arguing that New York City's zoning and land use rules make it hard to rebuild aging hospitals to modern clinical standards. It is subtitled "Building a Healthier Five Boroughs" and closes with eight proposals for changing city rules.
audits.background: The report says health care and social assistance accounted for 1,016,400 jobs in New York City as of January 2026 and more than 7 percent of the city's gross domestic product, with life sciences adding 18,800 jobs. It says the 1961 Zoning Resolution gave hospitals and other community facilities special bulk treatment in residential districts, a framework the group argues has not kept pace with modern medicine.

findings.plain: Health care is one of the city's largest employers, and an analysis the report cites puts the yearly economic activity of city hospitals and health systems above $123 billion, with more than $21 billion in tax revenue.
findings.quote: accounted for 1,016,400 jobs in New York City as of January 2026

findings.plain: Many hospitals are putting off capital work. A 2022 hospital association survey found that more than three quarters were delaying or cancelling capital improvement projects because of finances.
findings.quote: A 2022 joint hospital association survey reported that 77% of hospitals are delaying or cancelling capital...

findings.plain: The city's public hospital buildings are old. A 2014 Center for an Urban Future count found their average construction year was 1957.
findings.quote: New York City’s public hospital buildings were, on average, built in 1957.

findings.plain: State and federal design standards now require more floor area per patient and per procedure. Single-bed rooms must be at least 120 square feet, and a standard operating room approved since 2010 must be at least 400 square feet, against 270 square feet under the older state hospital code.
findings.quote: that a standard operating room must be at least 400 square feet, with more complex specialty operating rooms at

findings.plain: Because a hospital cannot shut down while it is rebuilt, modernization is staged around live clinical operations, which the report says makes the work slower and costlier per square foot than comparable construction.
findings.quote: These projects are complex and expensive for a simple reason: A hospital cannot close to renovate.

findings.plain: Case studies inside and outside New York show hospital floor area growing much faster than bed counts, and in some cases with no added beds at all.
findings.quote: require considerable bulk growth even without programmatic expansion.

findings.plain: Discretionary land use review takes years. The report cites a Citizens Budget Commission finding on the median timeline, and says Board of Standards and Appeals cases can add up to two more years.
findings.quote: the median discretionary land use application took two and a half years from formal filing with City Planning

recommendations: Create an as-of-right pathway for healthcare modernization projects that need added bulk to meet modern standards, where net bed growth is 20 percent or less.
Raise the allowable floor area ratio broadly for healthcare community facility uses to match the space modern hospitals need.
Create targeted bulk and floor area allowances for safety-net, public and community hospitals, paired with faster approvals and more capital support for institutions serving high-need communities.
Streamline the Uniform Land Use Review Procedure and related reviews for healthcare modernization projects, including through City Charter revision where appropriate.
Create a healthcare-specific allowance for mechanical space so modern hospital equipment fits inside zoning envelopes, even where mechanical space is already excluded from floor area ratio.

Streamline environmental review for hospital modernization projects.
Encourage healthcare growth in all five boroughs by giving hospitals, outpatient centers and other care facilities more flexibility to expand where New Yorkers live and work.

audits.title: How Did He Do It?
audits.plain_title: What the fiscal 2027 executive budget does and does not fix
audits.what_they_audited: A Citizens Budget Commission report analyzing Mayor Zohran Mamdani's fiscal year 2027 executive budget for New York City.
audits.background: The budget is balanced, as the law requires, and it corrects years of underbudgeting to give a fuller picture of the city's spending obligations.

findings.plain: Most of the actions used to balance the fiscal 2026 and 2027 budgets do not stabilize the budget over the long run, including one-shot resources and delayed payments.
findings.quote: Sixty-one percent of the budget balancing actions over fiscal years 2026 and 2027 do nothing to stabilize the budget long term

findings.plain: Projected gaps in later years grow, before accounting for employee raises or new programs.
findings.quote: Projected budget gaps grow from $7.1 billion in fiscal year 2028 to $9.8 billion in fiscal year 2030

findings.plain: Stretching out pension contributions lowers payments in the near term but raises them substantially in the 2030s.

findings.plain: The savings program under Executive Order 12 produces savings over two years, but only about a quarter of the initiatives increase efficiency.
findings.quote: Executive Order 12 initiatives save $1.8 billion over two years, but only 26 percent increase efficiency.

findings.plain: Delaying the state class size reduction mandate saves money now but leaves an annual cost later.
findings.quote: Delaying the Class Size Reduction mandate saves money for now, but leaves the City to ultimately spend $1.4 billion annually

findings.quote: The budget increases headcount by 869 full-time positions, with the elimination of 2,268 vacancies offset by 3,137 new positions

findings.plain: The budget adds new spending, part of it for administration priorities such as housing production and childcare and the rest to support existing programs.

audits.auditor: Center for New York City Affairs
audits.title: City FY2027 Budget Estimate: City Must Address Child Care Budget Gap for Low-Income Families and Low-Wage Workers
audits.plain_title: What it would cost the city to cut the childcare waitlist
audits.what_they_audited: A budget memo from the Center for New York City Affairs at The New School estimating what it would cost the city, in city fiscal year 2027, to cut the waitlist for the Child Care Assistance Program and to set up a stabilization grant fund for family child care providers.
audits.background: The memo says the state fiscal year 2027 budget included a $4.5 billion statewide investment in child care but did not include a workforce fund, and that more than 25,000 children from low-income families are on a city waitlist for the Child Care Assistance Program, which subsidizes child care for low-income families.

findings.plain: More than 25,000 children are on the waitlist for the Child Care Assistance Program, and the center's earlier modeling found the waitlist growing by about 1,500 children a month between June 2025 and March 2026.
findings.quote: trends from June 2025 to March 2026 demonstrate a monthly growth of 1,500 children on the CCAP waitlist

findings.plain: Families on the waitlist generally cannot use the city's public school early education programs, because their children fall outside the age ranges, they work outside a 9-to-5 schedule or there are no seats nearby.
findings.quote: because their children do not fit into those age ranges, they work hours outside of the 9-to-5 schedule, or there are no available seats near them

findings.plain: The memo says the state budget's $3 billion for the city's Child Care Assistance Program in federal fiscal year 2027 is not enough to run the program at full capacity.
findings.quote: this is insufficient for a fully operational CCAP program

findings.plain: Family child care providers are the lowest paid part of the sector. The center estimates the median provider earned $6.01 per hour in 2023, rising to $11.20 for a provider with good enrollment.
findings.quote: CNYCA estimates the median FCC providers earned $6.01 per hour in 2023

findings.plain: Only about 20 percent of family child care providers take part in public school programs such as 3-K and 2-K, while about 70 percent serve families who use Child Care Assistance Program vouchers.

audits.title: Review of the City’s Animal Population Control Efforts
audits.plain_title: City spay and neuter program is underfunded and little known
audits.agency: Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: This was a review rather than a standard audit. The team evaluated how effectively the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene runs the city's Animal Population Control Program, which subsidizes free or low-cost spay and neuter surgeries for eligible pet owners, and looked at approaches other cities use.
audits.background: City law requires the health department to run a program that reduces the stray dog and cat population by offering no- or low-cost sterilization, funded by a surcharge on licenses for unsterilized dogs. To deliver the services the department contracted with the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) for up to $3 million, covering as many as 24,000 surgeries at $125 each through 2028.

findings.plain: The health department set up the required low-cost spay and neuter program but has not been proactive about animal population control overall, relying on a single funding source and not seeking other public or private money it is allowed to pursue.
findings.quote: DOHMH has not been proactive in pursuing animal population control overall

findings.plain: The program's sole funding source, a surcharge on licenses for unsterilized dogs, brought in $950,819 over fiscal years 2022 to 2024, well short of the $1.5 million anticipated. As a result the ASPCA performed 6,733 sterilization surgeries, 37% fewer than its 10,660-surgery target.
findings.quote: The ASPCA performed a total of 6,733 sterilizations during FYs 2023 to 2025, 3,927 (37%) less than the 10,660 sterilizations anticipated under the contract.

findings.plain: Dog licensing outreach was heavily concentrated: five zip codes, about 3% of the city's more than 170, hosted 73% of the 192 licensing events held. Only about 70,000 dogs are licensed out of an estimated 500,000 pet dogs.
findings.quote: DOHMH concentrated its outreach and education efforts in only five (3%) of the City’s more than 170 zip codes

findings.plain: Oversight of the ASPCA contract is thin. The department reviews invoices but has no performance metrics, no way to verify the ASPCA's reported outreach and no record that required reports explaining the surgery shortfall were ever filed.
findings.quote: DOHMH provided no mechanism for verifying the reported outreach figures, stating instead that they rely on trust.

findings.plain: The department does not publicly report any data on the program's activities or outcomes, such as how many surgeries were performed or where the recipients live.
findings.quote: DOHMH does not publicly report any data regarding the activities and outcomes relating to the Program

findings.plain: In a survey conducted by the review team, 70% of respondents did not know the free or low-cost spay and neuter program exists and 61% did not know dog licenses are mandatory.
findings.quote: 74 (70%) stated that they were not aware that qualifying residents of the City could have their pet cats or dogs spayed or neutered free of charge or at low-cost through the Program

findings.plain: The city spends almost $54 million a year sheltering animals while the program meant to address a root cause of shelter crowding received an average of about $316,000 a year. Other cities use multiple funding streams and city-backed trap-neuter-return programs, which New York City does not support.
findings.quote: received an average of only $316,000 in each of the last three fiscal years reviewed

audits.background: Fair Fares NYC uses city money to give a half-fare discount on buses and subways to people living at or below 150 percent of the federal poverty level (FPL).

findings.plain: Eliminating bus fares would cost the city more than $900 million in the first year, with costs rising after that.
findings.quote: Eliminating bus fares would cost more than $900 million in the first year, with costs rising thereafter

audits.title: Access Denied: Challenges to DOI's Oversight of the City's Child Welfare System
audits.plain_title: State law blocks watchdog scrutiny of child welfare cases
audits.agency: New York City Administration for Children's Services
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined how New York State Social Services Law and the state Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS) restrict DOI's access to Administration for Children's Services (ACS) records, hindering its City Charter-mandated oversight of the child welfare system.
audits.background: ACS investigates reports of child abuse and maltreatment, while OCFS, a state agency, regulates many of ACS's policies and maintains the statewide child abuse hotline register. DOI is the city's inspector general and investigates systemic failures, criminality, corruption and inefficiencies at city agencies.

findings.plain: Five provisions of the state Social Services Law significantly restrict DOI's access to ACS records essential for rigorous oversight, including investigations of systemic failures, criminality and corruption.
findings.quote:
five provisions in the law  significantly restrict DOI’s access to records of the City Administration for Children’s 
Services (ACS) that are essential for rigorous oversight

findings.plain: Three provisions require OCFS authorization before DOI can access almost any records about children who had contact with ACS, and OCFS often exercises that discretion in ways DOI found more restrictive than the law requires, delaying investigations for months.
findings.quote:
OCFS’s responses 
to DOI record requests are often more restrictive than what the applicable laws intend or require

findings.plain: Two other provisions bar DOI entirely from records of abuse reports ACS deemed unfounded and reports diverted to the CARES alternative-to-investigation program, so DOI cannot investigate, for example, whether an employee failed to investigate abuse because of a bribe.
findings.quote:
Two other provisions of State law prohibit DOI from accessing certain categories of ACS records 
altogether

findings.plain: In 2025 DOI was notified of 18 child fatalities where ACS had prior involvement with the family in the past decade, but state law barred access to the full ACS history in 17 of them. The numbers were 13 of 16 in 2024 and 19 of 25 in 2023.
findings.quote: current state law bars DOI from accessing the full ACS history in 17 of those matters

findings.plain: Unfounded and diverted reports are precisely where lapses in ACS supervision or decision-making would likely appear, and the restrictions also prevent DOI from reviewing alleged systemic unfairness such as racial disparities.
findings.quote:
unfounded reports , and reports diverted to 
CARES, are exactly where one c ould expect to find lapses in ACS supervision or decision- making.

findings.plain: Years of negotiations with OCFS have produced no tangible improvements; the authorization process has grown more burdensome over time, even when ACS itself referred the allegations to DOI and is cooperating.
findings.quote:
the authorization process has become more burdensome over time, even in cases 
where ACS itself referred the initial allegations to DOI and is cooperating with the investigation.

audits.auditor: New York City Board of Correction
audits.title: Third Report and Recommendations on 2025 Deaths in New York City Department of Correction Custody
audits.plain_title: Missed tours and abandoned posts before three jail deaths
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The New York City Board of Correction (BOC), the city's jail oversight board, investigated the deaths of Edwin Ramos, Aramis Furse and Kyron Randall, three people who died in November and December 2025 in the custody of the New York City Department of Correction (DOC). Board staff reviewed DOC, medical, medical examiner, emergency medical and hospital records, surveillance and body-worn camera video, and interviewed staff and people in custody.
audits.background: The New York City Charter and city rules require the Board to investigate deaths in DOC custody and to recommend measures to DOC and NYC Health + Hospitals/Correctional Health Services (CHS) that could prevent the circumstances that contributed to a death. The Board says these investigations look for systemic flaws and policy failures rather than criminality, and this is its third report on the 15 people who died in custody in 2025.

findings.plain: Officers left their assigned housing area posts repeatedly during the tours in which Mr. Furse and Mr. Randall died, without logging that they had told a supervisor. In one case the officer was away from the post for nearly three hours.
findings.quote: the oﬃcer was oﬀ post for two hours and 44 minutes

findings.plain: The officer assigned to Mr. Randall's housing area did not tour as DOC policy requires, which calls for a visual check for signs of life in every person in a cell area twice an hour.
findings.quote: conduct visual observations at 30-minute intervals

findings.plain: Logbook entries in Mr. Randall's unit recorded 30-minute tours that video shows did not happen, because the officer was not on the post at the times logged.
findings.quote: logbook entry, the “B” oﬃcer was oﬀ post

findings.plain: When Mr. Randall was found in medical distress, the housing officer left him alone in his cell for 24 minutes, contrary to DOC rules requiring staff to stay close to a person needing medical attention.
findings.quote: unsupervised, for 24 minutes while he experienced a medical emergency

findings.plain: CHS emergency responders also stepped away from Mr. Randall twice while he was in distress, which CHS policy on emergency response does not allow.
findings.quote: CHS emergency response staﬀ left Mr. Randall unattended while in distress

findings.plain: Supervision lapses let people in Mr. Furse's unit stay out of their cells after the 9:00 pm mandatory lock-in, gather in single cells assigned to someone else, cover fixed cameras with tissues and pass items that looked like rolled cigarettes. Video in Mr. Ramos' unit also showed apparent drug paraphernalia in use.

findings.plain: Cell windows in Mr. Furse's housing area were blocked, obstructing officers' view into the cells, which DOC's own rule book prohibits.

recommendations: To CHS 1: CHS should reinforce and retrain staff on the requirement to continuously monitor people in custody who are in medical distress, as set out in CHS Medical Policies Section 10 on emergency response.
To DOC 1: Reinforce and retrain staff on basic supervision, touring and logbook practices, including staying on post, staying alert and accurately documenting breaks, meals, tours and incidents.

To DOC 2: Facility leadership must assign supervisors to periodically review surveillance video to spot officers who tour and document poorly, require those officers to meet with leadership before returning to post and schedule refresher training when needed.

To DOC 3: Housing area staff must immediately notify a supervisor when they see contraband and step in to confiscate it, and DOC must then arrange an unscheduled search of the unit and drug test the people housed there.

To DOC 4: DOC must address the findings of the 2023 cell door audit cited by the Nunez federal monitor, conduct an updated audit if needed and develop an action plan for securing cell doors and promptly reporting broken ones, to be shared with the Board at least 30 days before it is put in place.

To DOC 5: Staff must tell people in custody to remove cell window coverings, notify a supervisor and log the encounter if that does not work, have a supervisor physically remove the coverings, and have supervisors regularly monitor housing areas and audit logbooks.
To DOC 6: Post and distribute notices telling people in custody to comply with the security bulletin on cell window obstruction or risk losing the items used to block the view.
To DOC 7: Use the Video Monitoring Unit as intended to help facilities spot security problems including drug and tobacco use, and improve records tracking people found with prohibited items.
To DOC 8: Enforce the Board's Minimum Standard barring more than one person from occupying a single cell.

To DOC 9: Report refusals to lock in at 9:00 pm to the Central Operations Desk and respond as the lock-in and lockout directive requires, which may include calling in other DOC units, and improve reporting to track housing areas where people refuse to lock in.
To DOC 10: Send out teletypes restating that officers may not leave their assignment without a supervisor's approval or being relieved.
To DOC 11: Retrain staff who do not follow the rule requiring them to stay close to a person needing medical attention so the person stays under close observation until medical responders arrive.
To DOC 12: Stay alert on post as the rules require and report anyone seen tampering with DOC equipment.
audits.agency_response: In a letter appended to the report, CHS accepted the single recommendation directed to it and said it will continue to reinforce with clinical staff the need to continuously monitor patients in medical distress. The report does not include a DOC response.

To DOC 8: Enforce the Board's Minimum Standard barring more than one person from occupying a single cell.

To DOC 12: Stay alert on post as the rules require and report anyone seen tampering with DOC equipment.

audits.title: Privacy and Security of Student Data
audits.plain_title: How well the school system protects student data
audits.what_they_audited: Whether New York City Public Schools consistently followed all laws and regulations on the privacy and security of student data. The audit covered March 2020 through September 2025.
audits.background: New York City Public Schools, the largest school district in the country with about 1,600 schools and over 900,000 students, holds students' personally identifiable information and must follow federal and state privacy rules, including a state requirement to adopt a data security policy aligned with the National Institute of Standards and Technology Cybersecurity Framework.

findings.plain: The school system's data security and privacy policy does not fully align with the national cybersecurity framework, and it lacks written policies in some fundamental areas.
findings.quote: NYCPS does not have written policies covering the areas of data classification, risk assessment, and backup and recovery

findings.plain: The school system did not always report data breaches or notify affected people on time. Of 141 breaches reviewed from January 2023 through February 2025, reporting to the State Education Department was late for 48% and notification to affected individuals and families was late for 11%.
findings.quote: NYCPS delayed reporting 48% (67 of 141) of breaches to SED and delayed notifying affected individuals and families about 11% (16 of 141) of breaches

findings.plain: There is no documented data classification policy, only an informal practice, which could slow the school system's ability to figure out what sensitive data was involved in a security incident.
findings.quote: NYCPS does not have a documented data classification policy.

findings.plain: The school system does not keep a comprehensive list of the applications each school uses. Of 524 schools that answered a survey, 42% said they used at least 70 different student information system applications beyond the central systems.
findings.quote: Of the 524 responding schools, 218 (42%) stated they used at least 70 different SIS applications

findings.plain: Only 73% of employees completed required annual data privacy and security training in 2024, and the school system does not check that everyone with access to personally identifiable information has completed it.
findings.quote: in 2024, only 73% (117,763 of 161,337) of employees completed the training

findings.plain: Auditors identified weaknesses in technical controls over selected information systems, detailed in a confidential draft report.
findings.quote: We identified weaknesses in technical controls that need to be corrected

findings.plain: The audit team had trouble getting information and meetings from the school system, with some document requests taking over five months and meeting requests taking two months.
findings.quote: some documentation requests taking over 5 months to fulfill, and meeting requests taking 2 months to be scheduled

numbers.label: Students in New York City Public Schools, over
Breaches or unauthorized data releases reviewed

Employees who completed required privacy training in 2024

recommendations: Use the applicable national cybersecurity framework to identify gaps and improvements to the overall security posture.
Build a mechanism to ensure notifications of breaches or unauthorized releases of personal information always go out within required time frames.
Complete a written data and asset classification policy covering all systems and data, and classify all of the school system's data.
Develop a way to account for every student information system used at schools.
Put in place monitoring to ensure all employees with access to personally identifiable information complete privacy and security training every year.
Implement the technical control fixes detailed in the confidential draft report.
Cooperate more promptly with authorized state oversight inquiries.

audits.title: Status Report on Local Law 42
audits.plain_title: New jail leaders and pilot projects reshape the solitary law fight
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: A status report from the court-appointed independent monitor in Nunez v. City of New York updating the court on the evaluation of Local Law 42, a city law changing jail practices on restraints, escorts, de-escalation, lock-ins, out of cell time and restricted housing, and on new pilot projects meant to advance the law's goals.
audits.background: Local Law 42's requirements overlap with the Nunez court orders on security and operations, and several policy areas require the monitor's consultation or approval. Since the monitor's January 14, 2026 report, the mayor appointed a new correction commissioner who took office February 16, 2026 and a new corporation counsel, and the court-appointed remediation manager began work on February 23, 2026.

findings.plain: After evaluating the law, the monitoring team raised concerns that some of Local Law 42's requirements may not be safe to put into practice and could make conditions in the jails worse.
findings.quote: some of the requirements of LL42 may not be safe to implement and could

findings.plain: The monitor is encouraged by the city's newly installed jail leadership but remains gravely concerned about dangerous conditions that continue to put people in custody and staff at risk of harm.
findings.quote: remains gravely concerned about the dangerous conditions in the jails

findings.plain: The monitoring team provided confidential draft findings to the parties identifying where Local Law 42 conflicts with the Nunez court orders and explaining its safety concerns, but says more work is needed before it can make final decisions on what it will approve.
findings.quote:
Additional work remains before the Monitor can 
render final determinations on what may be approved

findings.plain: Two pilot projects are being developed to test whether parts of the law can work safely: one to improve the department's restricted housing program and one to add due process protections, including legal representation, for people referred to restricted housing.
findings.quote:
one focused 
on an improved restricted housing model and the other focused on enhancing due process 
protections for people in custody who are referred to restricted housing

findings.plain: The monitor cautioned that the department's history is full of pilot projects that failed, citing a recent door security pilot that collapsed despite strong leadership attention, and said the new pilots must be designed differently to be scalable and sustainable.
findings.quote:
The record in this case is rife with examples of 
pilot projects that were ineffective, not scalable, not sustainable or were simply abandoned

findings.plain: The department is closing the North Infirmary Command jail, which the monitor says resolves long-running concerns about its cell-within-a-cell housing layout that was not conducive to programming and contributed to prolonged isolation.
findings.quote:
The closure of NIC resolves the 
concerns about the physical plant

Meet and confer sessions convened with the Local Law 42 parties

The monitoring team and remediation manager team should determine when a detailed joint position on the stayed Local Law 42 provisions can be completed and provided to the parties and the court.

The department, remediation manager team and monitoring team should continue engaging the Local Law 42 parties, including at least one meet and confer session and a confidential written submission to the City Council intervenors.
The city should deploy additional resources and staff, including skilled project management support, to advance both the Nunez court orders and Local Law 42 obligations.

audits.title: Implementation of Selected Aspects of the Climate Mobilization Act
audits.plain_title: Enforcing the city's building emissions law
audits.agency: New York City Department of Buildings
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Buildings has taken steps to ensure private building owners comply with selected parts of the Climate Mobilization Act by the mandated deadlines. The audit covered November 2019 to June 2025.
audits.background: The Climate Mobilization Act, enacted in 2019, aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions from the city's largest buildings 40% by 2030 and reach net zero by 2050. Its centerpiece, Local Law 97, sets emissions limits for large private buildings starting in 2024, and the Department of Buildings oversees implementation and enforcement.

findings.plain: While the department has made outreach efforts, including hiring third parties, it has not closely monitored either that outreach or building owners' compliance, so there is no assurance owners will meet the law's deadlines.
findings.quote: it has taken a hands-off approach to monitoring its outreach efforts and the building owners’ compliance with the requirements

findings.plain: The department could not substantiate its own outreach letters until after the audit's closing conference, and only a quarter of the addresses it supplied were on the list of buildings actually required to comply.
findings.quote: only 150 of the 602 addresses (25%) were on the CBL

findings.plain: A 2024 phone initiative to advise owners ahead of the first reporting deadline reached only 8% of the buildings required to comply.
findings.quote: DOB contacted only 1,118 of 13,269 (8%) of those required to comply.

findings.plain: In a survey auditors sent to 151 building owners, several respondents said they were unaware of the law or had never been contacted, and 20 of the letters came back undeliverable.
findings.quote: five respondents stated they were unaware of the CMA, seven said they were never contacted by DOB

findings.plain: The department refers owners to a service provider for help but does not follow up on referrals and has no documentation of what assistance the provider gave.
findings.quote: they do not follow up on the referrals

findings.plain: Auditors visited 55 buildings and found 24% had not posted the required energy efficiency label, while 31% of those that did post labels put them where the public could not see them, including one label inside a desk drawer. The department does not inspect for the labels.
findings.quote: found 13 (24%) did not have their energy efficiency labels posted as required

Reassess the resources assigned to contacting building owners about compliance.
Create a system to track referrals to the service provider, record what assistance was given and follow up on buildings at risk of missing emissions requirements.
Educate building owners on where energy efficiency labels must be posted.
Inspect buildings to verify a label is posted near each public entrance where the public can see it.

audits.title: Review of Schools’ Food Donation and Composting Efforts
audits.plain_title: How schools handle donating leftover food and composting waste
audits.agency: New York City Public Schools (Department of Education)
audits.what_they_audited: This was a review, not a full audit. The comptroller's office examined whether New York City Public Schools tracks data on its food donation and composting programs, how it promotes those programs and what school administrators say about participating in them.
audits.background: New York City Public Schools, the nation's largest school system, serves about 940,000 free meals a day and spent $600 million on food in fiscal year 2025, 12% of its operations budget. Two units, the Office of Food and Nutrition Services and the Office of Energy and Sustainability, are responsible for preventing food waste.

findings.plain: The school system does not centrally track how many meals are prepared and discarded, so it cannot measure whether its food waste prevention efforts are working.
findings.quote: NYCPS has no idea how successful its overall efforts to prevent food waste are

findings.plain: Only 67 of 1,319 school buildings, or 4%, donated food to outside organizations in fiscal year 2025, and central management does not compile records of which organizations receive donations.
findings.quote: in FY2025 only 67 (4%) of NYCPS’ 1,319 school buildings donated food to outside organizations

findings.plain: Composting has grown dramatically. Participating schools went from 725 in fiscal year 2017 to all 1,715 in fiscal year 2024, and compostable material collected nearly quadrupled over that period.
findings.quote: from 6,278 tons collected in FY2017 to 24,477 tons in FY2024

findings.plain: Most school food waste still is not composted. A Department of Sanitation study found only about 37% of food waste generated at schools was captured for composting, and 28% of what was collected was contaminated, versus a 4% contamination rate citywide.
findings.quote: The study found that 28% of the organics collected from schools were contaminated, well above the citywide organics contamination rate of 4%.

findings.plain: The school system's own sustainability survey showed low engagement. Of 1,182 schools surveyed, 15% engaged in none of six food waste prevention activities and 87% engaged in no more than three.
findings.quote: 15% of all schools engaged in none of the six activities, and most schools—87% in total—engaged in no more than three of the six activities

findings.plain: In the review team's own survey of school administrators, only 33% said their schools donate uneaten leftovers and 59% said they have a food sharing table. Schools cited lack of funding and staffing as the main barriers.
findings.quote: Only 33% of respondents who answered the question stated that their schools donated unused food to school families, staff, or outside organizations.

recommendations: Set system-wide targets for participation in composting, food donation and other food waste reduction programs.
Compile system-wide data to measure progress against those targets.
Conduct and publish a centralized assessment of progress by school and by program, identify barriers and develop strategies for improvement.
Develop system-wide training and outreach to increase participation, encourage idea sharing among sustainability coordinators, capture more food waste as compost and reduce contamination.
Visit schools to verify that recycling and composting bins are properly placed in cafeterias and classrooms.
Identify schools without appointed sustainability coordinators, fill those positions and support the new coordinators.

audits.title: OIG-NYPD Twelfth Annual Report
audits.plain_title: Police watchdog tallies 275 recommendations, most adopted
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation's (DOI) Office of the Inspector General for the New York City Police Department (OIG-NYPD) issued its annual report, required by Local Law 70, discussing the 25 public reports and one statement of findings it issued between 2015 and December 31, 2025 and the status of 275 recommendations to the New York City Police Department (NYPD).
audits.background: Local Law 70 established OIG-NYPD within DOI to oversee the NYPD. The annual report catalogues the office's investigations and tracks how NYPD and the Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) have responded to its recommendations; some recommendations made in late 2025 are not assessed.

findings.plain: NYPD has fully implemented 159 of the 275 recommendations, about 57.82 percent, partially implemented or accepted in principle 53, rejected 47 and is still considering seven. Nine are no longer applicable because of technology or procedure changes, and two CCRB recommendations were implemented.
findings.quote:
NYPD has  fully implemented 159 recommendations, or approximately 57.82 
percent; partially implemented or accepted in principle 53 recommendations, or approximately 19.27 percent

findings.plain: More than 75 percent of OIG-NYPD's recommendations have been implemented, partially implemented or accepted in principle, which the acting commissioner attributed to the office's consistent follow-up.
findings.quote: more than 75 percent of the recommendations being implemented, partially implemented, or accepted in principle

findings.plain: On the January 2025 social media report, NYPD accepted all six recommendations on April 28, 2025 and has implemented five; the staff training recommendation remains partially implemented until OIG-NYPD confirms all staff with account access are trained.
findings.quote:
NYPD accepted the six recommendations on April 28, 2025, and OIG-NYPD 
determined that NYPD has implemented five of them.

audits.title: Facilitated Programs to Assist Small Businesses
audits.plain_title: Helping small businesses get financing
audits.agency: New York City Department of Small Business Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Small Business Services provided the services available under its programs to help small businesses obtain funding to open, operate and expand. The audit covered July 2019 to November 2023.
audits.background: The department contracts with Industrial Business Service Providers and Business Solutions Centers to help businesses analyze finances, package loan applications and get training. During the four fiscal years from 2019 to 2022, the department reported the programs facilitated about $220 million in financing.

findings.plain: The department monitors its contractors' expenses and outputs but does not develop or review operational data that would show how the programs are helping small businesses reach their goals.
findings.quote: it does not include the development and review of operational data that would enable the agency to determine how its programs are helping small businesses reach their goals

findings.plain: The 76 businesses auditors reviewed obtained facilitated loans of $97,363,816, but the department collected no data on what the financing accomplished, such as new jobs or stronger operations.
findings.quote: SBS did not collect data on the beneficial effects of this financing, such as the creation of new jobs or strengthening of the businesses’ operations

findings.plain: Program results such as the number and amount of facilitated loans are self-reported by vendors and the department does not verify them.
findings.quote: the program results are self-reported by the vendors

findings.plain: Contractor files were incomplete. Fifteen sampled businesses received 24 loans worth $23,113,349 with no lender proof letter on file, and three others had loan amounts that did not match their proof letters.
findings.quote: did not have a proof letter from the lender in Dynamics

findings.plain: Some loans went to businesses that may not have qualified. Auditors found 158 facilitated loans worth $10,242,747 went to businesses outside New York City or lacking documentation of a city presence.
findings.quote: 158 of the 2,129 facilitated loans, valued at $10,242,747, were made to businesses located outside of New York City or there was no documentation to support a presence in New York City

findings.plain: Controls over training enrollment and attendance need improvement. Attendance records were missing for 13% of counted participants, 18% of attendees with records did not stay for at least half the session and before 2023 the department did not run post-course surveys.
findings.quote: we found that 173 attendees (18%) did not stay for at least half of the course/session
