audits.auditor: CUNY Institute for State and Local Governance
audits.title: The Criminal Justice Investment Initiative: Synthesizing a Decade of Innovation
audits.plain_title: What a decade of Manhattan DA grants taught about services
audits.what_they_audited: A series of six briefs from the CUNY Institute for State and Local Governance, the research center that manages the Criminal Justice Investment Initiative, drawing lessons from a decade of grants the Manhattan District Attorney's Office made to New York City community organizations. Each brief ends with its own set of recommendations addressed to funders, policymakers and service providers, and they are listed here brief by brief.
audits.background: The Criminal Justice Investment Initiative was created by the Manhattan District Attorney's Office to spend $250 million seized in international financial crime prosecutions on community projects in three areas: crime prevention, diversion and reentry and support for crime survivors. Since 2015 it has backed more than 50 programs serving more than 34,000 people, and CUNY ISLG manages the grants and measures performance.

findings.plain: The initiative put forfeiture money from financial crime prosecutions into community programs, funding, expanding or evaluating more than 50 of them and reaching more than 34,000 people across the city since 2015.
findings.quote: evaluate over 50 innovative community programs serving more than 34,000 people across New York City

findings.plain: Even in a city with many community organizations, service silos kept people from getting the full range of help available, and coordination between organizations did not happen unless it was paid for.
findings.quote: Yet, organizational siloes mean people may nonetheless struggle to fully benefit from all that’s available.

findings.plain: Trust between staff and participants, and between partner organizations, was what made referrals across organizations work.
findings.quote: Trust is the lubricant for transcending service siloes.

findings.plain: Contact with the criminal legal system is itself a source of trauma, and standard intake and assessment procedures can compound it.
findings.quote: Involvement in the criminal legal system is inherently traumatic .

findings.plain: Groups that are shut out of services face different barriers from one another, so programs designed around a single model reach fewer of them.
findings.quote: Barriers and needs vary across specific populations .

findings.plain: Many community-based organizations lack the infrastructure to collect and analyze their own data, and the briefs trace that gap back to funding requests that do not pay for data capacity or technical assistance.
findings.quote: This gap begins at the funding level, with many requests-for-proposals (RFPs)

findings.plain: Linking data across agencies for evaluation was possible but heavy going even inside a well-funded initiative, and 33 of the 52 funded programs got an outside evaluation.
findings.quote: labor-intensive within the well-resourced CJII, but

People served by funded programs since 2015
Funded programs that got an outside evaluation
Interviews used to design the initiative

recommendations: Invest in coordination: pay providers specifically for the time and staffing it takes to collaborate, and build planning time into grants so partnerships are a good fit before work starts.
Reassess partnerships on a regular schedule, with routine check-ins and periodic reviews from all sides, so collaborations can change as needs and funding shift.
Support the development of data management systems that cross organizational lines, ideally a shared system, so partners can coordinate services and track their impact.
Have partners and funders build learning communities that spread best practices and help programs survive past one grant.
Tailor trauma-responsive programs to the specific populations being served rather than applying one treatment model to everyone.
Combine clinical and non-clinical interventions, including art groups, family events and recreation, to provide more holistic care.
Create employment pathways into the helping professions for people from groups now underrepresented in them, including survivors of trauma.
Build flexible program policies, including a mix of remote and in-person options and formal and drop-in services, to meet participants where they are.
Dedicate funding to longer-term care so treatment is not cut off before people have worked through their trauma.
Hire and onboard people with lived experience as staff, and create paths for participants to become staff themselves.
Make programming flexible and individualized so each participant's plan matches their own needs and can change as they progress.
Facilitate communication and networking across service providers and other city agencies so referrals out of a program actually land.
Foster continuous and comprehensive care, with coordinators or case managers who stay with a person through the transition back to the community.
Provide comprehensive staff training and hire staff with experience, including lived experience, working with people involved in the criminal legal system.
Address material needs such as food and housing as part of programming, alongside longer-term work on employment, education and health.
Allow flexibility, multiple points of entry and re-engagement, so people can come back to a program after a lapse without being penalized.
Increase community awareness of these programs, invest in provider responsiveness and highlight the benefits, to improve recruitment and attendance.
Monitor and address inequities in who engages with and completes programs, since uneven participation can widen existing disparities.
Deploy data-driven approaches to assess impact on recidivism and other measures, and adjust programs accordingly.
Have requests for proposals prompt applicants to describe their data capacity and their data and research staffing.
State clearly in requests for proposals whether evaluation is a condition of funding.
Involve data, research and program staff from applicant organizations in contract negotiations, not just development and legal teams.
Assess an organization's actual data capacity at the time of funding, including through site visits and video calls.
Assess whether a program and its evaluator are a good fit before the contract is executed.
Dedicate money and hands-on data support as part of the funding package rather than leaving data work unfunded.
Offer ongoing assistance, support and training on data to grantees throughout the grant.
Make performance measurement participatory, with grantee staff reviewing and shaping reporting templates.
Support a data-driven culture inside grantee organizations rather than treating data as a reporting chore.
Address the historical injustices that shape how communities view research, rather than assuming trust.
Develop realistic evaluation timelines that match how programs actually start up and run.
Plan evaluations around what data will actually be available.
Emphasize participatory evaluation approaches that treat programs as active stakeholders in the research design.
Be flexible about research design, considering regression discontinuity, longitudinal and propensity score matching approaches where a randomized trial does not fit.
Address research ethics directly and openly, including disagreements over consent, random assignment, data ownership and what gets published.
Connect stakeholders' data across programs and agencies so evaluations can show a fuller picture of impact.
Standardize data-sharing agreements within a jurisdiction, including a common template and shared data definitions across city agencies.
Center participant stories in reporting, using mixed methods and first-person accounts alongside administrative data.
Reach people where they are by moving technical detail into appendices, requiring mid-evaluation reports and producing short practitioner briefs and presentations.
Adopt flexible, low-barrier, hybrid service delivery models, both virtual and in person, as a standard feature of program design.
Allocate unrestricted, flexible funding streams that pay for physical spaces and adaptive programming rather than narrow outputs.
Build system literacy and self-advocacy by having participants co-create their own service plans and exercise real choice in how they engage.
Establish formal systems for bringing staff with direct lived experience into service delivery and leadership at all levels, and invest in professional pathways for those roles.
Invest in the workforce through fair pay, staff wellness, reasonable caseload limits and comprehensive training.
Minimize the burden research places on participants by replacing traditional high-demand data collection with co-designed, low-barrier and incentive-based alternatives.
Employ reflexive knowledge-sharing throughout the research cycle, with continuous feedback loops involving staff and participants.

Provide comprehensive staff training and hire staff with experience, including lived experience, working with people involved in the criminal legal system.
Address material needs such as food and housing as part of programming, alongside longer-term work on employment, education and health.
Allow flexibility, multiple points of entry and re-engagement, so people can come back to a program after a lapse without being penalized.
Increase community awareness of these programs, invest in provider responsiveness and highlight the benefits, to improve recruitment and attendance.
Monitor and address inequities in who engages with and completes programs, since uneven participation can widen existing disparities.
Deploy data-driven approaches to assess impact on recidivism and other measures, and adjust programs accordingly.
Have requests for proposals prompt applicants to describe their data capacity and their data and research staffing.
State clearly in requests for proposals whether evaluation is a condition of funding.
Involve data, research and program staff from applicant organizations in contract negotiations, not just development and legal teams.

Assess whether a program and its evaluator are a good fit before the contract is executed.
Dedicate money and hands-on data support as part of the funding package rather than leaving data work unfunded.
Offer ongoing assistance, support and training on data to grantees throughout the grant.
Make performance measurement participatory, with grantee staff reviewing and shaping reporting templates.
Support a data-driven culture inside grantee organizations rather than treating data as a reporting chore.
Address the historical injustices that shape how communities view research, rather than assuming trust.
Develop realistic evaluation timelines that match how programs actually start up and run.
Plan evaluations around what data will actually be available.
Emphasize participatory evaluation approaches that treat programs as active stakeholders in the research design.

Center participant stories in reporting, using mixed methods and first-person accounts alongside administrative data.

Allocate unrestricted, flexible funding streams that pay for physical spaces and adaptive programming rather than narrow outputs.
Build system literacy and self-advocacy by having participants co-create their own service plans and exercise real choice in how they engage.
Establish formal systems for bringing staff with direct lived experience into service delivery and leadership at all levels, and invest in professional pathways for those roles.
Invest in the workforce through fair pay, staff wellness, reasonable caseload limits and comprehensive training.
Minimize the burden research places on participants by replacing traditional high-demand data collection with co-designed, low-barrier and incentive-based alternatives.
Employ reflexive knowledge-sharing throughout the research cycle, with continuous feedback loops involving staff and participants.

audits.title: New York City Housing Authority Monitorship: Monitors' Report (Second Annual Report, Seventh Overall)
audits.plain_title: Year seven: pests and mold improve, elevators and IT go backward
audits.what_they_audited: The federal monitors' annual review of the New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) for the seventh year of the monitorship, January 31, 2025 to January 31, 2026. It covers the six property areas of the 2019 agreement with the federal government, heat, elevators, pests and waste, mold and leaks, lead paint and inspections, plus the 47 initiatives in NYCHA's Transformation Plan, capital spending and the monitors' own budget.
audits.background: On January 31, 2019 NYCHA agreed with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the City of New York to fix housing conditions, and a monitor was appointed. About two-thirds of NYCHA's funding comes from federal grants, and the monitors write that contemplated federal budget cuts could cost NYCHA as much as $100 million starting next year.

findings.plain: Pest response times improved sharply while pest populations went the other way. NYCHA answered 87% of mouse, cockroach and bed bug complaints within seven calendar days, a 22 percentage point jump, and kept meeting its rat targets at 98% within two business days. But its estimated populations rose 19% for rats, 39% for mice, 21% for bed bugs and 4% for cockroaches compared with Year 6, though all four remain far below where they stood at the start of the monitorship.
findings.quote: increased from Year 6, with a 19% increase for rats, 39% for

findings.plain: Mold work improved but stayed far short of the standard. NYCHA met the agreement's mold timeframes 29% of the time, up from 9% in Year 6 and well below the 95% requirement, and average remediation time fell from 120 days in Year 4 to 12 days. Severity remains a problem, with 85% of complaints involving mold covering ten square feet or more, and the combined mold and leak backlog is over 65,000 open work orders.
findings.quote: mold and leak backlog—over 65,000 open work orders—

findings.plain: NYCHA finished its boiler obligation a year early, replacing 198 boilers itself and transferring 698 to private partners who replaced 462, but heating outages rose. There were 307 unplanned central heating outages in the first half of the 2025-2026 season against 206 a year earlier, affecting 61% of occupied apartments compared with 54%.
findings.quote: there have been 307 unplanned central heating outages,

findings.plain: Elevator performance stalled or declined after three years of gains. NYCHA finally completed its obligation to replace or modernize 275 elevators, a year late, and restored service within ten hours for 89% of unplanned outages, but the average outage lasted 6.5 hours, 16% worse than the 5.6 hours of the prior year.
findings.quote: elevator outages in an average of 6.5 hours per outage,

findings.plain: HUD inspection results improved markedly. NYCHA passed 64 of 89 inspections in 2025, or 72%, compared with 46% of 138 inspections in 2024, and completed annual self-inspections in 95% of occupied apartments, up from 91%. The monitors found HUD had flagged problems NYCHA's own inspectors could have caught, such as missing smoke detectors and kitchen and bathroom outlets without ground-fault protection.
findings.quote: passed 64 of 89 inspections (72%), a signiﬁcant

findings.plain: A large lead paint remediation backlog remains open. Of 19,835 remediation work orders identified in December 2024, NYCHA completed 9,412 and cancelled 610, leaving 9,813 open, many unresolved because NYCHA cannot get into the apartment or more work is needed. Separately, NYCHA has completed X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) testing in about 97% of units known or presumed to have lead paint.
findings.quote: remediation work orders. Of 19,835 remediation work

findings.plain: NYCHA's biggest technology project collapsed. The replacement of its Resident Case Management System, first due to go live in April 2025, has no launch date after NYCHA terminated the vendor's contract in 2025, and two other major systems also slipped. The monitors traced the failure to vendor selection, heavy customization and weak vendor management, and NYCHA paid $350,000 for a second outside technical assessment.
findings.quote: either select vendors with more public housing experience or take

recommendations: Keep replacing boilers and invest in the heating distribution system, which NYCHA estimates would take $4 billion in additional funding to fully repair or replace.
Improve the quality of pest control treatments, not just their timeliness, so pest populations actually fall.
Strengthen annual self-inspections so health and safety problems are caught and fixed before HUD inspectors arrive.

audits.agency_response: NYCHA agreed to adopt several of the monitors' performance evaluation recommendations in the cycle that began in January 2026, including a four-point rating scale and review by next-level supervisors, and plans to use key performance indicators in evaluations in 2027. It declined to add training for low-rated employees, saying that kind of follow-up is already part of its traditional progressive management of staff. NYCHA also agreed to share the monitors' technology findings with candidates for new information technology leadership.
audits.compliance_note: The monitors found NYCHA built on earlier progress and should be commended, but that performance regressed in several areas and full compliance will require both continued cultural and organizational reform and enough money for operations and capital work. audits.title: Review of the Small Business Forward Initiative and Its Impact on Violations Enforcement
audits.plain_title: Did small business fine reforms actually reach small businesses?
audits.agency: Mayor's Office, Department of Small Business Services and six enforcement agencies
audits.what_they_audited: This was a review, not a full audit. The comptroller's office checked the status of the 116 regulatory reforms recommended under the Small Business Forward initiative and, where possible, whether the projected savings for small businesses were actually realized.
audits.background: In January 2022 Mayor Eric Adams signed Executive Order 2, directing six city agencies to reform business regulations to reduce fines for small businesses; the agencies recommended changes to 116 of 232 regulations reviewed, with estimated savings of about $8.9 million a year. Many reforms were codified in Local Law 151 of 2023, and Mayor Mamdani extended the initiative in January 2026 with Executive Order 11.

findings.plain: The city never defined "small business" for the initiative, and the agencies carrying it out generally did not consider the impact on small businesses when choosing regulations to reform. No agency tracks violations by business size.
findings.quote: the agencies charged with implementing Small Business Forward generally did not consider the potential impact on small businesses when identifying regulations for potential reform

findings.plain: The claimed outreach behind the reforms, including a survey of nearly 1,000 small business owners, could not be verified. No agency produced the survey or any documentation of consultation.
findings.quote: none of the entities contacted during this review could substantiate that the survey or consultation with small businesses occurred

findings.plain: Most of the regulations picked for reform were rarely or never enforced. Only 36 of the 116 were regularly used as the basis for violations in calendar year 2021, and 59 produced no violations at all that year.
findings.quote: only 36 (31%) had related violations that were issued frequently during CY 2021

findings.plain: No one has measured the initiative's full financial impact because agencies did not collect the needed data. Using the data available, auditors estimated the reforms cut fines for all businesses of any size from $14.5 million to $12.1 million over 15 months, a 17% reduction.
findings.quote: went from $14.5 million (pre-adoption) to $12.1 million (post-adoption), a 17% reduction

findings.plain: Of the 30 regularly enforced regulations whose changes were implemented, 14 related to health and safety, such as hazardous materials and emergency exits. Auditors could not tell whether softer penalties slowed how quickly violations were fixed.
findings.quote: Of the 30, 14 (47%) related to health and safety issues.

findings.plain: No single agency was put in charge of the initiative, no performance indicators were set and no impact assessment was ever conducted, even as the program was rebooted in 2025 and extended in 2026.
findings.quote: There appears to be no single entity responsible for overseeing the SBF initiative

findings.plain: The administration's projection of roughly $8.9 million in annual savings for small businesses had no documented methodology and could not be substantiated.
findings.quote: the SBF report’s estimated annual savings of approximately $8.9 million cannot be verified or relied upon as accurate

numbers.label: Regulations recommended for reform under the initiative
Of those 116 regularly enforced in the year before reform
Estimated fine reduction, January 2024 through March 2025

recommendations: Formally designate a lead agency to oversee and coordinate the initiative, track savings and ensure it stays effective.
Publish regular public reports on the initiative's progress, realized savings for small businesses and compliance rates, with clearly defined indicators and methods.
Adopt a uniform definition of "small business" used by all participating agencies.
Have agencies prioritize violations and reforms based on their impact on businesses that fit that definition, not on businesses generally.
Develop a framework for monitoring both financial savings and non-financial impacts such as reduced administrative burden and time savings.
Have the six regulatory agencies consider adding a small business identifier to their systems to track violations, fine reductions, waivers and cure periods for small entities.
Create a formal, documented methodology for calculating projected and realized savings from the reforms.
Implement a formal protocol to monitor whether reduced penalties or extended cure periods affect how quickly health and safety violations are fixed.
Have the lead agency review the reforms already implemented to determine whether the financial savings actually benefited small businesses.
audits.agency_response: The Mayor's Office agreed with six of the nine recommendations, agreed in principle with two and did not address one, and the Department of Small Business Services deferred to the Mayor's Office. The Fire Department disagreed with the recommendation on prioritizing reforms by small business impact.

audits.title: Oversight of Language Access Services
audits.plain_title: Interpretation and translation at the health department
audits.agency: New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene adequately serves people with limited English proficiency, complies with state regulations and local laws and provides sufficient oversight of its language access services. The audit covered January 2019 through December 2024.
audits.background: An estimated 1.7 million New York City residents have limited English proficiency, and local law requires the health department to provide free language access services, including telephone interpretation in at least 100 languages and translated key documents in the top 10 citywide languages. The department's Language Services Unit creates and distributes these resources for all public-facing programs.

findings.plain: The department has no centralized system for recording and tracking the language services it provides, so requests may be underreported and the needs of clients with limited English proficiency may not be fully known.
findings.quote: DOHMH does not have a centralized system for recording and tracking LAS

findings.plain: Officials do not know how many calls are dropped or how often an interpreter cannot be found.
findings.quote: DOHMH officials are unaware of the number of dropped calls and instances where an interpreter could not be found.

findings.plain: Some bilingual staff provide clinical services in a non-English language without passing the department's required fluency assessment, and the department reports its assessment numbers inconsistently.
findings.quote: there are uncertified bilingual staff providing clinical services in a non-English language

findings.plain: In a survey of 50 restaurants and food establishments, many owners and workers did not know about available language services or the Business Owner's Bill of Rights, which covers the right to language help during inspections.
findings.quote: many owners and workers were unaware of available LAS resources or the Business Owner’s Bill of Rights

findings.plain: When multilingual state auditors called department facilities unannounced, they hit barriers including staff not trying to connect them to interpreters, hard-to-navigate automated systems, disconnected calls, long waits and missing website translations.
findings.quote: DOHMH staff not attempting to connect callers to an interpreter.

findings.plain: Visits to 10 public-facing facilities found inadequate or missing signage for giving feedback and complaints, plus delays, technical problems and apparent shortages of language access equipment at some sites.
findings.quote: Installation delays and technical issues with LAS equipment

numbers.label: Estimated city residents with limited English proficiency
Minimum languages required for telephone interpretation

recommendations: Develop a system-wide database to collect and track clients' language preferences across all facilities and work with vendors to gather data on service delivery and unfulfilled requests.

Make sure all communications aimed at people with limited English proficiency, including automated phone systems, signage, surveys and feedback boxes, are available in the appropriate languages and always accessible.
Ensure all bilingual staff who provide interpretation complete the department's fluency assessment.
Periodically assess each program and facility's language access equipment and connection needs.

audits.auditor: Center for New York City Affairs
audits.title: NYC Budget Cost Estimate for Closing The Human Services Pay Equity Gap
audits.plain_title: What pay parity for nonprofit human services workers would cost
audits.what_they_audited: A budget brief from the Center for New York City Affairs at The New School estimating what it would cost the city budget to pay nonprofit human services workers on city contracts the same as city agency employees doing comparable work.
audits.background: The brief builds on the center's January 2025 report, which found that the nonprofit human services workforce, which is predominantly women of color and highly educated, earns 25-30 percent less than similarly educated counterparts in city human services agencies.

findings.plain: The center finds pay for nonprofit human services workers on city contracts trails pay for comparable city agency employees by 25 to 30 percent.
findings.quote: the pay of nonprofit human services workers lags 25-30 percent behind that of comparable City human service agency employees

findings.plain: Closing that gap would cost an estimated $965 million to $1.35 billion, a 19 percent increase over current city-funded compensation costs at the low end and 26.7 percent at the high end.
findings.quote: The low-range estimate represents a 19 percent increase over the current City-funded compensation costs; the high-range estimate translates into a 26.7 percent increase.

findings.plain: Roughly three-quarters of the cost would go to raising pay for social workers, counselors and related direct service professionals, who make up 51 percent of the 64,500 full-time equivalent contract workforce.
findings.quote: Roughly three-quarters of the cost would go to level up the pay for nonprofit human services professionals

findings.plain: The brief says the pay gap comes from city contracting practices rather than market forces, because pay in this sector is set by city budget and procurement policy.
findings.quote: pay for nonprofit human services workers is determined entirely by City budget and procurement policies that have historically prioritized low cost over fair compensation

findings.plain: The gap is largest among workers with bachelor's or master's degrees rather than the lowest-paid staff, so the brief frames parity as mainly a question of professional pay.
findings.quote: the most profound compensation inequities are among highly professional and experienced workers, those with a bachelor’s or master’s degree

findings.plain: The brief notes City Council legislation, Introduction 452, that would require city human services contracts to include enough funding to pay workers on a par with city employees with comparable education and responsibilities.
findings.quote: Intro. No. 452 mandates that City human services contracts include sufficient funding

recommendations: Establish salary parity by aligning pay for nonprofit human services workers with city agency job titles and pay levels, so they are paid on a par with public sector employees doing comparable work.

Once parity is set on a job title basis, build automatic adjustments into city human services contracts based on citywide collective bargaining increases, and include future fringe benefit increases so total compensation reaches comparability with city employees.
Phase the estimated $965 million to $1.35 billion cost into the city budget over three years as service contracts are renewed.

audits.title: DOI's Investigation into the Reclamation of Vacant NYCHA Apartments
audits.plain_title: Vacant public housing units are a growing safety risk
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined the public safety risks posed by the growing number of vacant New York City Housing Authority (NYCHA) apartments and how well NYCHA secures those units against illegal occupancy.
audits.background: Vacant NYCHA apartments rose from about 2,840 in January 2022 to 6,740 as of May 2025, with the average vacancy lasting about a year, while 165,000 applicants sit on the public housing waitlist. Lead and asbestos abatement requirements and funding constraints drive the lengthy turnover process.

findings.plain: Vacant apartments without adequate security create opportunities for illegal occupancy, and some unauthorized occupants use the units as a base for illegal activities.
findings.quote:
vacant apartments, without adequate security measures, create opportunities for illegal occupancy by 
unauthorized individuals, some of whom use the apartments as a base for illegal activities.

findings.plain: From January 2022 to May 2025, the New York City Police Department reclaimed 548 apartments from unauthorized occupants, 60 through joint efforts with DOI, and those joint efforts produced 81 arrests on charges including trespassing, drug possession and weapon possession.
findings.quote:
the NYPD reclaimed 548 apartments  from 
unauthorized occupants, 60 of which were reclaimed through joint efforts  by the NYPD and DOI.

findings.plain: NYCHA does not proactively inspect vacant apartments throughout the turnover cycle, which lets trespassing and other illegal activity go undetected and delays the discovery of unauthorized occupants.
findings.quote:
NYCHA does not proactively inspect vacant apartments to ensure that the unit is in fact vacant 
throughout the entirety of the apartment turnover cycle.

findings.plain: NYCHA procedure requires every vacant apartment in a development to use the same lockset and key, so anyone with the key can enter any vacant unit. Some employees instead use a generic "65 key" that also opens utility rooms and management offices authority-wide, adding to the risk.
findings.quote:
presenting the risk that individuals could, upon acquiring a key, access any vacant unit in the 
development.

findings.plain: Turning over an apartment costs about $52,000 on average, including roughly $17,000 for lead abatement, $25,000 for asbestos abatement and $10,000 for general renovations, and funding constraints make it hard for NYCHA to shorten the process.
findings.quote: The average cost to complete the turnover process is approximately $52,000

numbers.label: Vacant NYCHA apartments as of May 2025
Vacant apartments in January 2022
Apartments reclaimed from unauthorized occupants
Arrests from joint NYPD-DOI reclamation efforts
Applicants on the public housing waitlist

recommendations: NYCHA should revise its apartment turnover procedure to require monthly property management inspections of vacant apartments not yet ready for rental, secure windows and door locks during those inspections and report any unauthorized occupants to NYCHA's law department within 72 hours.

NYCHA should evaluate alternative locksets or security technologies such as electronic locks, and meanwhile require each development to rotate among at least two or three versions of move-out cylinders and keys, with no two developments sharing the same keys.

NYCHA should revise its Resident Watch guidelines to require volunteers to report suspected unauthorized inhabitants or illegal activity in vacant apartments to their supervisor, who should inform property management by the end of the shift and log the reports.
When property management receives such a report from a Resident Watch supervisor, it should immediately seek to confirm it and, if verified, report to NYCHA's law department within 72 hours.
If NYCHA receives additional refurbishment funding, it should deploy the money to shorten the time needed to complete apartment turnovers.
audits.agency_response: NYCHA accepted all five recommendations, noting it will need about a year to build automated work orders for the monthly inspections, six months to a year to update the Quality of Life form and that the funding recommendation is subject to available money.

audits.title: From Degree to Career
audits.plain_title: Turning CUNY degrees into careers through employer ties
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, on why graduates of the City University of New York struggle to reach well-paying jobs, and what the city, the state and the university could do to build stronger employer partnerships. It ends with 14 proposals.
audits.background: The report draws on more than 80 interviews with CUNY leaders, faculty, career advisors, employers and nonprofit intermediaries, along with data from the CUNY Wage Dashboard, the New York State Department of Labor and the U.S. Census Bureau.

findings.plain: The entry-level job market has contracted sharply. Postings requiring little or no prior experience fell 37.4 percent between 2022 and 2024, from 72,484 to 45,354, and internship postings across the five boroughs fell 37.1 percent from 2019 to 2024.
findings.quote: entry-level job postings plummeted from 72,484 (2022) to 45,354 (2024), a 37.4 percent drop

findings.plain: Few CUNY students get the paid work experience employers look for. Just 12 percent of undergraduates do a paid internship, compared with a national average of nearly 57 percent.
findings.quote: Just 12 percent of CUNY undergraduates participate in paid internships—up from 10 percent two years ago, but still far below the national average of nearly 57 percent.

findings.plain: Outcomes after graduation are uneven. About two thirds of graduates find consistent employment within a year, and one in ten alumni are in retail or food service five years out, rising to 13 percent for community college graduates.
findings.quote: just two thirds of CUNY graduates find consistent employment within a year of finishing their degree

findings.plain: The Inclusive Economy Initiative, which embeds industry specialists and hybrid academic-career advisors in academic departments, reaches only around 40 of CUNY's 450 departments, fewer than 9 percent.
findings.quote: exist in only around 40 of 450 departments across CUNY, or fewer than 9 percent

findings.plain: Career services are stretched thin and often separated from academic departments, with ratios of 1,100 students to one staff member described as common.
findings.quote: Career services are overwhelmed—with ratios of 1,100 students to one staff member common—and frequently siloed from academics.

findings.plain: Employers describe CUNY as hard to work with, and the university lacks a systemwide customer relationship management platform to coordinate employer contacts across its 25 colleges.
findings.quote: CUNY still lacks one of the most fundamental tools for managing employer relationships

audits.title: Putting the “Rec” Back in NYC Parks & Recreation
audits.plain_title: Rebuilding public recreation across New York City
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, on the long decline of public recreation in the city and 11 ideas for rebuilding it. It draws on budget, staffing, facility and programming data provided by NYC Parks and more than 75 interviews.
audits.background: Recreation once made up close to a third of the budget of the Department of Parks and Recreation, which shortened its public-facing name to NYC Parks in 2011. In 2025 recreation accounted for 5.3 percent of the agency's budget, about $32.8 million out of roughly $618 million.

findings.plain: Recreation staffing has fallen sharply over six decades. The recreation division had 1,949 workers in 1964 and 659 in 2025, a 66 percent decline.
findings.quote: In 1964, the NYC Parks’ recreation division had 1,949 workers. In 2025, there were only 659, a 66 percent decline.

findings.plain: Attendance is well below pre-pandemic levels. Public pool attendance is down 43 percent, recreation center visits in 2024 were 38 percent below 2019 and attendance at recreation programs is down 19.6 percent since 2019.
findings.quote: the average has dropped to 929,475, or a 43 percent decrease

findings.plain: Programming has been cut roughly in half. NYC Parks offered nearly double the programming in 2019 that it offered in 2024, with declines of more than 60 percent on Staten Island and in the Bronx.
findings.quote: In 2019, NYC Parks offered nearly double the amount of programming as in 2024.

findings.plain: Facilities are aging, with more than $400 million in known capital needs for major facilities alone and, the report says, likely hundreds of millions more not yet identified.
findings.quote: more than $400 million in known capital needs for major facilities alone

findings.plain: New York has far fewer recreation centers per resident than peer cities. Most large American cities have one center for every 50,000 residents or fewer, while New York's ratio is more than 200,000 to one.
findings.quote: Practically every major city in the U.S. has one recreation center per 50,000 residents or fewer; meanwhile, the ratio in New York City is more than 200,000 to 1.

findings.plain: Access to athletic facilities is very uneven. Five community districts that together house more than 600,000 residents have only 205 athletic facilities among them, fewer than a single well-equipped district elsewhere.
findings.quote: these five districts are home to more than 600,000 New Yorkers but have just 205 athletic facilities combined

findings.plain: The variety of programming differs greatly by borough. Manhattan had 927 different kinds of classes or workshops in 2024, compared with 299 in the Bronx and 165 on Staten Island.
findings.quote: Manhattan had the greatest variety of programming in 2024, with 927 different kinds of classes or workshops to attend

recommendations: Make a long-term commitment to recreation, meeting the mayor's pledge to spend 1 percent of the city budget on parks, setting a goal of directing 20 percent of an expanded parks budget to recreation and funding a citywide recreation master plan that maps assets, identifies gaps and includes a marketing campaign.

Activate more existing public infrastructure for recreation, using the 2026 World Cup to launch a cross-agency effort that opens school gyms and fields after hours, scales open space projects on NYCHA campuses, expands waterfront access and boating, widens Summer Streets and revives Weekend Walks, explores recreation hubs at Interborough Express stations and brings programming to senior centers.

Commit to a 10-year capital campaign to modernize every major recreation facility and build new ones, paired with a citywide facilities assessment and zoning changes that make it easier to build recreation space.

Launch Rec Pass, a partnership with the public library system modeled on Culture Pass, letting library cardholders take a set number of free classes or activities each month at recreation centers, pools and partner nonprofits.
Scale up NYC Parks summer day camps to serve at least 5,000 children a year by expanding to more recreation centers and park facilities.
Create RecRx, a multi-agency effort with the health department, Health + Hospitals, NYC Parks and insurers that lets healthcare providers prescribe recreation as preventive care.

Build a Recreation Investment Fund, potentially with the New York City Economic Development Corporation, to channel private, philanthropic and corporate dollars into programming, equipment and facility upgrades in the neighborhoods that need them most.

Reverse staffing cuts by baselining funding for the 77 programming positions cut in recent budget reductions and adding 75 more staff a year for four years, so more athletic facilities can open seven days a week.

Pilot RecCorps, a workforce pipeline into recreation careers that links CUNY campuses, career and technical education high schools and the Summer Youth Employment Program, with stipends or wages for students.

Create a trusted partner program for nonprofits that provide regular recreation services, offering multi-year permits, streamlined access to space and equipment plus basic marketing and funding support.

Bring recreation equipment directly to neighborhoods through mobile and modular amenities such as vending machines stocked with handballs or jump ropes, pop-up kiosks and mobile concessions renting gear.

audits.title: Creating and Capturing Real Estate Value to Generate Dedicated Funding for NYC’s Parks
audits.plain_title: Five ways to fund parks by capturing real estate value
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, proposing five ways to raise new dedicated revenue for the city's parks by capturing a share of the real estate value that parks and public investment help create.
audits.background: The report says the city faces a $2.2 billion shortfall in the current fiscal year and a $10.4 billion gap in fiscal 2027, and that the mayor's preliminary fiscal 2027 budget reduces funding for NYC Parks by roughly $33 million compared with last year's adopted budget.

findings.plain: Parks add measurably to property values. The report cites research finding homes within 500 feet of a park carry an estimated $15.2 billion in additional property value, generating roughly $101 million a year in extra property tax revenue.
findings.quote: homes located within 500 feet of a park enjoy an estimated $15.2 billion in additional property value, generating roughly $101 million in additional annual property tax revenue

findings.plain: The city already captures real estate value for public space, but only in scattered places. Development revenues cover most of the operating budget for Brooklyn Bridge Park, and business improvement districts steward space in commercial corridors.
findings.quote: these efforts remain one-off and geographically constrained, rather than part of a coordinated, citywide strategy

findings.plain: Other American cities dedicate more real estate and development revenue to parks, including roughly $120 million a year in Seattle and more than $80 million a year in Minneapolis.
findings.quote: generating roughly $120 million annually in Seattle and more than $80 million a year for Minneapolis’s park system

findings.plain: Residents report uneven park conditions. Forty-four percent of city residents rate their local parks fair or poor, rising to 63 percent in the Bronx.
findings.quote: 44 percent rate the condition of their local parks as fair or poor, including 63 percent in the Bronx

findings.plain: The Real Property Transfer Tax brings in about $1.4 billion a year, and the report estimates an added 0.25 percentage point could produce roughly $250 million to $300 million a year for parks.
findings.quote: An additional 0.25 percentage point on property transaction values could generate roughly $250 million to $300 million each year for parks maintenance, operations, and programming.

findings.plain: New York has used value capture before. Development in the Hudson Yards financing district now generates roughly $490 million a year in dedicated value-capture revenues.
findings.quote: is now generating roughly $490 million annually in dedicated value-capture revenues

numbers.label: Added property value for homes within 500 feet of a park
Estimated added annual property tax from that value
Annual revenue from the Real Property Transfer Tax
Estimated yearly yield of a 0.25 point transfer surcharge
Residents rating their local parks fair or poor
Annual value-capture revenue in the Hudson Yards district

recommendations: Tie new development from upzoning to dedicated funding for park maintenance, operations and programming, by letting developers buy density above existing limits in exchange for contributions to a citywide parks fund and by writing similar contributions into future neighborhood rezonings.

Capture value along the Interborough Express by creating a district that dedicates part of the new property tax revenue from development near stations to sustaining nearby parks and creating new ones, with some of the money directed to parks elsewhere in Brooklyn and Queens.

Create a modest community parks surcharge on the Real Property Transfer Tax or the Mortgage Recording Tax, or dedicate a share of existing real estate revenues to parks, with a maintenance-of-effort provision so the money adds to rather than replaces city parks funding.

Make it easier to establish Parks Improvement Districts by creating a streamlined process led by NYC Parks or another public space entity, and launch a pilot that matches locally raised assessments with city dollars at a multiple based on neighborhood need.

Establish a Parks Improvement Trust to receive and allocate new park revenues under a transparent formula that balances reinvestment near the source with citywide need, overseen by a mixed public and private board with reporting requirements.

audits.title: Twenty-Ninth Report of the Independent Monitor: Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Stop and frisk compliance snapshot for spring 2025
audits.what_they_audited: A quarterly visual "compliance snapshot" updating the monitor's Twenty-Eighth Report on the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, covering the second quarter (April to June) of 2025.
audits.background: The report covers the second quarter of 2025 and in several slides compares it to the second quarter of 2024. It draws on the monitor team's audits of 100 stop reports per month and quarterly body-worn camera video audits, plus audits by the NYPD Quality Assurance Section, command self-inspections and first-line supervisor reviews.

findings.plain: In the second quarter of 2025, the monitor's audits found 91% of reported stops, 79% of frisks and 77% of searches lawful. The monitor said compliance had not changed substantially from previous quarters and that frisks and searches continued to have unacceptably low compliance rates.
findings.quote: 91% of stops, 79% of frisks, and 77% of searches were assessed as lawful

findings.plain: Self-initiated stops remained less lawful than stops from radio runs or witnesses: 85% of self-initiated stops were lawful, with frisks during them at 71% and searches at 60%.
findings.quote: Frisks during self-initiated stops were lawful 71% of the time

findings.plain: By the department's own audits, 87% of commands had stop compliance above 85%, but only 56% cleared that bar for frisks and 44% for searches. The monitor noted that 100% compliance is the goal and each command should achieve at least 85% as a minimum.
findings.quote: 87% of commands had a compliance rate for stops greater than 85%

findings.plain: Supervision remained poor. The monitor found 9% of stops, 21% of frisks and 23% of searches unlawful, while reviewing supervisors flagged only 2% of stops, 4% of frisks and 4% of searches.
findings.quote: the reviewing supervisors found that only 2% of stops, 4% of...

findings.plain: Officers failed to complete stop reports for 27% of stops identified in the monitor's audit (11 of 40), down from 37% in the second quarter of 2024, suggesting stop reporting may be improving.

findings.plain: Body-worn camera compliance kept improving: officers recorded 96% of stops in their entirety, up from 92% a year earlier.
findings.quote: the NYPD properly recorded the stop in its entirety

findings.plain: Housing Bureau officers' compliance was 82% for stops, 84% for frisks and 80% for searches, with trespass arrests at 98% compliance on the reason to approach and 100% on probable cause.

audits.title: Explainer: Charter Revision Commissions Appointed by Prior Mayors
audits.plain_title: What a mayor can do about a prior mayor's charter commission
audits.what_they_audited: A question-and-answer explainer by Citizens Union and Reinvent Albany, two good-government groups, on charter revision commissions appointed by a mayor on the way out of office. It was prompted by the commission former Mayor Adams established on December 31, 2025.
audits.background: Section 36 of the New York Municipal Home Rule Law gives mayors, city councils and voters the power to create a charter commission and sets how commissions place questions on the ballot. A charter commission can block, or bump, ballot questions submitted by the City Council or by voter initiative.

findings.plain: State law, not the New York City Charter, governs how charter revision commissions are created and how they put questions before voters.
findings.quote: commissions are governed by state

findings.plain: The groups write that the State Legislature and the governor could amend the Municipal Home Rule Law to deal with commissions appointed by a departing mayor, including commissions that already exist.
findings.quote: we believe that the Legislature and Governor can amend the Municipal Home Rule

findings.plain: On whether a sitting mayor can remove commissioners appointed by a predecessor, the Q&A concludes it might be possible in some cases but would likely be settled in court.
findings.quote: POTENTIALLY IN SOME CASES, BUT IT WOULD BE INADVISABLE

findings.plain: State law does let a sitting mayor fill any vacancy on a commission that a previous mayor appointed.
findings.quote: shall be filled by the mayor

findings.plain: Nothing in the law requires a mayor to fund or support a commission created by a predecessor, so a commission can be left without money, space, legal advice or data.
findings.quote: The law allows a mayor to “starve” a mayoral charter commission of government resources,

findings.plain: A commission is not required to propose any ballot questions, yet its existence alone can block questions put forward by the City Council or by voters.
findings.quote: The mere existence of a mayoral charter revision commission introduces the threat that it

findings.plain: Whether a charter commission may accept private donations is unsettled, and the Office of Management and Budget has discretion over city agency bank accounts.
findings.quote: It is unclear how this section applies in the context of private contributions.

numbers.label: Window a proposed state amendment would give a new mayor
Donations to agencies reported yearly to the ethics board

recommendations: Amend the state Municipal Home Rule Law so that a charter revision commission appointed in the last six months of a mayor's term must be affirmed by the incoming mayor within 90 days or dissolve.

Do not attempt to remove charter commissioners appointed by a previous mayor without cause, which the groups say would open the door to routine political purges of bodies that have operated independently.
Consider using an executive order to bar direct donations to mayoral charter revision commissions and the creation of affiliated nonprofits to raise money for them.

audits.title: 2025 End of Year Monitor Update
audits.plain_title: After twelve years, NYPD still not in compliance on stop and frisk
audits.what_they_audited: The monitor's year-end summary of the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) 2025 efforts to comply with the federal court's 2013 order requiring constitutional policing in the Floyd, Ligon and Davis stop and frisk cases, covering accountability, self-initiated stops, underreporting, discipline, Fourteenth Amendment compliance and community engagement.
audits.background: A federal court ordered the NYPD in 2013 to bring its stop, question and frisk practices in line with the Constitution and appointed an independent monitor. The monitor writes that ongoing compliance problems fall into three main categories: lack of meaningful accountability, unlawfulness of self-initiated stops and persistent underreporting of Terry stops.

findings.plain: After twelve years of oversight, the department has yet to reach substantial compliance with the court's 2013 order. The monitor called the report a wake-up call and said there should not be a permanent monitor.
findings.quote: the NYPD has yet to reach substantial compliance

findings.plain: Supervisors still approved nearly everything. In the first half of 2025, reviewing supervisors found 99% of stops, 95% of frisks and 94% of searches compliant, while the monitor's audits found only 89% of stops, 73% of frisks and 73% of searches lawful.
findings.quote: 99% of all stops, 95% of frisks, and 94% of searches compliant

findings.plain: Discipline remained rare. In the first half of 2025, commands took no action in 97 of 305 cases where the Quality Assurance Section found a stop unlawful, issued command discipline in only 8 cases and in 29 cases rejected the audit finding outright, a practice the monitor said undermines compliance efforts.
findings.quote: command discipline (“CD”) issued in only 8 cases

findings.plain: Self-initiated stops, nearly half of all reported stops, were far less lawful (79.4% for stops, 64.0% for frisks and 53.3% for searches in the first half of 2025) than stops from radio runs or witnesses. Specialized units performed worst, with only 75% of Neighborhood Safety Team stops and 64% of Public Safety Team stops lawful, and the monitor's preliminary audits show the department is unlikely to meet the compliance targets of 85% by the third quarter of 2025 and 90% by year end. The department eliminated its Public Safety Teams on November 7, 2025.
findings.quote: self -initiated stops ( 79.4% stops, 64.0% frisks, 53.3% searches)

findings.plain: Underreporting improved but nearly one-third of stops still went undocumented: the monitor's 2025 audits found 71% of stops reviewed were properly documented, up from 61% in 2024.
findings.quote: The Monitor’s 2025 audits showed  that 71% of the...

findings.plain: Work on police discipline reform stalled. The Discipline Working Group of plaintiffs, the City and the monitor had to be paused after the City sought to revamp the process at the end of 2025 and said it could agree to only a few of the recommendations in Judge James Yates' September 2024 discipline report.
findings.quote: the DWG had to be paused because at the end of 2025, the City sent a letter

findings.plain: The department advanced a Fourteenth Amendment compliance plan, delivering a revised plan on December 31, 2025 that includes a Racial Disparities Review Committee, and hired academic advisors to analyze racial disparities in stops. Separately, in five bias cases where the Civilian Complaint Review Board sought charges, the police commissioner found the conduct improper but not racially motivated and declined to bring charges.
findings.quote: This plan includes a Racial Disparities Review...

audits.auditor: New York City Board of Correction
audits.title: Injury Response in NYC Jails: Board of Correction Analysis of 2024 Data
audits.plain_title: Jail injury counts still do not match and reports run months late
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The New York City Board of Correction (BOC) checked whether the New York City Department of Correction (DOC) and New York City Health + Hospitals/Correctional Health Services (CHS) followed the Board's minimum standard on injury response during calendar year 2024. The review combined analysis of administrative data, the agencies' monthly and annual reports and a random sample of 99 Injury-to-Inmate forms.
audits.background: The Board published a report on serious injuries in 2019 that found DOC underreported serious injuries and had no single reliable count, and it then adopted rules requiring the two agencies to build a shared electronic injury tracking system and file joint monthly injury reports. Those requirements were phased in through August 2022, making 2023 the first full year of data collection after implementation.

findings.plain: Both agencies have written injury policies, which technically satisfies the standard, but the Board found the policies do not set deadlines for closing investigations or explain how investigative findings feed into preventing future injuries.
findings.quote: The lack of a formal definition for “prompt” and “expeditious” in

findings.plain: Injury investigations closed in nine days on average, but the spread ran from same day to about three months, and one in ten sampled forms carried date problems: missing dates, a closure date before the injury date or dates from before 2000. The Board says bad dates undercut its ability to sequence events and follow up.
findings.quote: a mean closure time of nine days

findings.plain: Most narratives read as neutral, with 86 of 99 rated fully objective, but people in custody declined to take part in the investigation in 97 of the 99 sampled cases.
findings.quote: people in custody refused to participate in the investigation process

findings.plain: The shared electronic injury tracking system the rules require still does not exist. DOC and CHS keep separate systems, and for 2024 CHS counted 29,405 injuries against DOC's 28,273, a gap the agencies say cannot be reconciled month to month because each counts a different set of cases.
findings.quote: The agencies continue to maintain separate systems

findings.plain: Self-harm reporting runs through three separate unreconciled figures in the same joint monthly report, two from CHS and one from DOC, with no explanation of the differences. CHS shares self-injury data with DOC but not its mental health self-harm data, so some self-harm incidents are never investigated by DOC.
findings.quote: these numbers match, and the report does not include an explanation or footnote

findings.plain: Reporting to the Board was late and incomplete. DOC first supplied 23,664 of the 28,273 injury forms for 2024, or 84 percent, rising to 94 percent after it uploaded missing May 2024 forms in November 2025, and the joint monthly reports slipped from an average 17 days late in 2023 to 72 days late in 2024.
findings.quote: In 2023, the average delay was 17 days, increasing substantially to 72 days in 2024.

findings.plain: DOC's 2024 annual injury review attributed a 4 percent rise in injuries to a growing jail population, but the Board's own rate calculation shows injuries per 1,000 people in custody fell from 372 in 2023 to 365 in 2024. recommendations: DOC and CHS should update their policies on addressing and preventing injuries so they line up with the investigation, coordination and reporting requirements of Minimum Standard 3-16.
DOC policies should spell out how investigative findings are used to inform injury prevention, tying investigation results to corrective action.

CHS policies should spell out expected timelines for injury response, documentation such as Injury-to-Inmate forms and reporting such as the joint monthly injury report and the monthly public self-harm report.
DOC should digitize the Injury-to-Inmate form with required fields, room for supporting evidence such as video and electronic signatures, to cut down on missing data and handwritten sign-offs.
DOC should set up internal monitoring of investigation timeliness, including clear deadlines for closing an investigation, to address the cases that run long.
Given how often people in custody decline to take part, DOC should look for ways to engage them during investigations while respecting their rights and the standards.
DOC and CHS should voluntarily give the Board detailed minutes or summaries of the quarterly meetings the rules require, showing the data review, trends identified and quality assurance work.
DOC and CHS must build and maintain the coordinated electronic injury tracking system the rules require, covering serious and non-serious injuries in one reconciled platform.
DOC and CHS should put internal controls in place to submit Injury-to-Inmate forms and joint monthly injury reports on time.
DOC and CHS should reconcile their differing injury and self-injurious behavior counts into a single joint monthly injury report with all required breakdowns.

DOC should make its required annual review of the joint monthly reports document compliance findings, systemic issues and corrective action plans with steps and timelines, and should publish the annual reports as well as send them to the Board.
CHS should make its monthly public self-harm reports consistently break the data out by seriousness, separating serious from non-serious injuries as the minimum standards require.

audits.title: 2026 Policy Agenda
audits.plain_title: The building industry's 2026 policy priorities for New York
audits.what_they_audited: An annual policy agenda from the New York Building Congress, a construction industry membership association, setting out the proposals it will push for in 2026. Items are labeled as federal, state or city, and cover infrastructure funding, housing, transportation, energy, resilience, procurement, workforce and technology.
audits.background: The group describes itself as a membership association that brings together architects, engineers, contractors, subcontractors, labor, owners and consultants, and it says the federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Law expires in 2026.

findings.plain: The group names three top priorities for the year: a new federal surface transportation funding bill, changes to the 485-x housing tax break, and sustained capital budgets for state and city agencies including the Metropolitan Transportation Authority and the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey.
findings.quote: Securing a strong federal infrastructure bill and long-term infrastructure investments, namely

findings.plain: The group says New York City is on track to add far fewer homes than it believes are needed, and that closing the gap statewide would take a much larger number by 2030.
findings.quote: may only see about 21,000 new units in 2026,

findings.plain: The group says the 485-x tax incentive, created after the 421-a program expired, is not producing homebuilding at the level it thinks New York needs, and that developers are responding by building projects of exactly 99 units to stay under regulatory thresholds.
findings.quote: expected to have a surge in — developments of

findings.quote: up to 90% of that electricity is generated

recommendations: Release federal infrastructure money faster and give New York a share reflecting its population, transit systems and contribution to federal taxes and gross domestic product.
Add worker training provisions to the next federal infrastructure bill, including new grants for industry partnerships and H-1B visa cap exemptions for government-funded infrastructure work.
Track and disclose federal infrastructure spending more fully.
Streamline and speed up environmental reviews and permitting for infrastructure projects at every level of government, and adopt changes that reduce construction costs.
Stabilize the federal Highway Trust Fund with predictable revenue so states can plan multi-year projects.
Write lasting changes to the National Environmental Policy Act into law and widen the set of projects that qualify for categorical exclusions, supporting the SPEED Act and the RESTART Act.
Expand the categories of actions exempt from review under the State Environmental Quality Review Act and adopt the state bill creating exemptions for qualifying infill and transit-oriented housing.

Create a National Infrastructure Reserve Board, an independent body modeled on the Federal Reserve with a standing appropriation, to fund state-of-good-repair and replacement needs outside the annual budget cycle.
Reevaluate, expand and fine-tune the 485-x zones for projects of 150 units or more, vary the income and wage requirements by neighborhood, and add a new bracket for the largest projects.
Treat projects using 485-x as Type 2 actions under the State Environmental Quality Review Act.
Fast-track environmental assessments for new housing and housing-related infrastructure.
Allow affordable housing to be built as of right in districts where less than 10 percent of housing rents below market.
Extend zoning exemptions in Special Transit Land Use Districts to a full half mile around each transit zone, as in the original City of Yes proposal.
Have state lawmakers prioritize senior housing in the suburbs.
Create the NYC Affordability Fund proposed by the city comptroller, deploying about $2.5 billion in pension capital toward up to 75,000 affordable homes.
Keep and expand the incentives behind office-to-residential conversions, including the City of Yes changes and the 467-m program.

Create an Interborough Express transit-oriented development special district covering land within a half mile of each planned station, and set up a Rail-to-Roof air rights market that lets nearby owners sell unused floor area into that district.
Adopt a statewide transit-oriented development framework modeled on the Massachusetts MBTA Communities law, with base densities above 15 units per acre.

For the Manhattan plan, raise residential floor area in the Special Hudson Yards District from 4 to at least 18, raise floor area around 125th Street ahead of Second Avenue Subway phase 2, reexamine historic districts for where more housing could go, sharply raise residential floor area caps to enable office conversions in districts such as the Financial District and Midtown, and deck over roadways such as the FDR Drive and tunnel approaches for housing.

Expand the budget of the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, specifically Community Development Block Grants, the HOME Investment Partnerships Program and the Public Housing Capital Fund, and support the Pro-Housing Act, the INCREASE Housing Affordability Act and the Build More Housing Near Transit Act.

Accelerate the Brooklyn Marine Terminal project, including swift state approval of the General Project Plan and a federal decision to review it through an environmental assessment rather than a full environmental impact statement.
Speed up MTA change orders and invoice payments and create a formal feedback loop with the building industry to identify bottlenecks.
Rebalance risk in MTA contracts, including insurance, indemnification and bonding terms, so more qualified firms bid.
Use qualifications-based selection for MTA procurements, giving technical merit more weight with transparent scoring.
Commit to full Americans with Disabilities Act compliance across the MTA network, prioritizing high-ridership and transfer stations and publishing timelines and progress.
Expand transit-oriented development tools such as Zoning for Accessibility so private development helps pay for station accessibility while adding housing.

Fund the Gateway Program, advance the Penn Station overhaul, start Second Avenue Subway phase 2 and plan phase 3 and a 125th Street crosstown extension, advance Interborough Express design and environmental work, and pursue a full redesign of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway with federal funding commitments.
Reuse the abandoned LIRR Rockaway Beach Branch between Rego Park and Ozone Park for both a new subway connection and a park.
Increase state funding for renewable energy projects, including onshore and offshore wind and a renewable energy hub on Rikers Island after the jails close.

Create a state-financed renewable energy fund in the budget rather than funding upgrades through utility ratepayers, pointing to bills that would tax large crypto miners and create a separate utility class for large data centers.

Shorten permitting and grid interconnection timelines at NYISO and the Office of Renewable Energy Siting and Electric Transmission, add staff, and treat clean energy projects as Type 2 actions under the State Environmental Quality Review Act.
Prioritize transmission upgrades, including directing the New York Power Authority to invest in them.
Increase funding and incentives for battery storage.
Encourage renewable natural gas where electrification is difficult and allow blending.
Run streamlined NYSERDA procurements with quarterly solicitations for large-scale renewables.
Expand large-scale geothermal in New York City through more funding, technical support and inclusion in long-term capital and energy planning.

Fully implement the streamlined federal licensing created by the ADVANCE Act to deploy advanced nuclear facilities such as small modular reactors, and support the state's 5 gigawatt nuclear goal and its advanced nuclear master plan.
Advance planning and design for the Army Corps of Engineers' New York and New Jersey Harbor and Tributaries study of storm surge barriers.
Increase the Clean Water State Revolving Fund to finance water infrastructure upgrades.
Continue the Lower Manhattan Coastal Resiliency project.
Strengthen sewage and drainage systems, targeting neighborhood-scale green infrastructure and Bluebelt-style drainage upgrades in areas that flood repeatedly.

Keep practical exemptions, flexibility and clearer good-faith guidance in Local Law 97, particularly for public health and safety facilities and nonprofits, and earmark noncompliance penalties for grid improvements or energy-efficiency retrofits.
Streamline land use reviews for hospitals and related health care facilities, along the lines of the City of Yes zoning changes.
Give health care facilities flexible Local Law 97 compliance schedules.
Create a protocol that automatically adjusts emissions calculations for health care facilities when utilities require or recommend changes in energy use during grid instability.
Improve hiring at New York City agencies by speeding up Office of Management and Budget review and approval of positions and making salaries more competitive with the private sector.
Add engineering and technical staff at the New York City comptroller's office to speed dispute determinations and improve communication about claim status.
Streamline payment requisitions and change order processing across all procurement agencies.

Create a set of pre-approved best practices for contract processes that any procurement department can adopt, with the Office of Management and Budget giving agencies flexibility to choose the approach that fits a project.
Add requisition numbers to city payments on Checkbook NYC.
Shorten bid cycles and clarify procurement so firms can recruit and retain staff.
Set more project funding as multi-year commitments with clear capital plans.
Reduce insurance and indemnification requirements so pricing reflects actual project risk.
Change the Dormitory Authority of the State of New York's procurement and risk requirements and allow public-private partnership models for university facilities.

Have government agencies buy and store critical materials up front for large projects, include larger contingency line items for material price escalation, and offer tax credits when material costs rise enough to stall a project.

Convert the New York City Department of Design and Construction into a public authority, modeled on the School Construction Authority, with multi-year bonding capacity and flexibility in project delivery methods.
Have the state authorize one-step progressive design-build for all project types and city agencies, and remove cost from the evaluation criteria for those procurements.
Expand CM-Build beyond the project types the Department of Design and Construction may now use it for, and make it available to all city agencies.
Continue the New York City Capital Process Reform Task Force under the new administration.
Have the state legislature extend authorization for joint bidding in city procurements.
Guarantee timely contract payments, especially to minority and women-owned business enterprises.
Make minority and women-owned business enterprise certification reciprocal between the state and New York City.
Create a single centralized procurement portal for minority and women-owned business enterprises across government entities.

Create a federal H-1B visa cap exemption and fast-track approval program for government-funded infrastructure, targeted at United States-educated workers in fields such as engineering, architecture, construction management and planning.
Fund childcare centers that open at 6 a.m. so early work hours do not keep people out of the workforce.
Lower fees for federal certification and required training courses, particularly those from the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
Expand Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act programs for youth, adults and dislocated workers.
Increase funding for public and nonprofit apprenticeship, STEAM education and job training programs in all five boroughs, and increase support for statewide training programs.
Have state lawmakers create an artificial intelligence in construction and engineering task force, with the group's innovation council represented.
Require a standard 'Human Reviewed' certification on drawings, blueprints and project plans, and set industry-wide best practices for human oversight.

Fully build out the city's 3D underground mapping initiative as a central, city-run repository of subsurface data in BIM-compatible formats, generally meeting or exceeding Quality Level B under the ASCE 38-22 standard.

audits.title: 5 Revenue-Raising Ideas for NYC
audits.plain_title: Five ways the city could raise money on its own
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, proposing five ways the city could generate new recurring revenue using tools it says are largely within the city's own control rather than Albany's.
audits.background: The report says the city faces widening budget gaps and federal funding cuts while most spending is already locked into fixed costs such as employee pay, education, healthcare and social services.

findings.plain: The report says the five ideas together would raise more than $1.4 billion a year, or about $5.6 billion over four years.
findings.quote: $1.4 billion in new revenue

findings.plain: The City University of New York (CUNY) controls large amounts of surface parking that the report says could be ground-leased for infill housing while the land stays publicly owned.
findings.quote: CUNY controls more than 80 acres of surface parking.

findings.plain: Driverless ride-hailing is being tested in the city under temporary permits, and the report says New York captured little revenue when app-based ride-hailing scaled up in the 2010s.
findings.quote: benefit of hindsight and the chance to act earlier.

findings.plain: The Mayor's Office of Climate and Environmental Justice identified 47 city-owned sites suitable for battery storage in 2023, but the report says no solicitation has followed.
findings.quote: has not put out a single RFP soliciting bids for energy

findings.plain: Fewer than 2.5 percent of the city's street parking spaces are metered, which the report calls the largest untapped revenue option that needs no state approval.
findings.quote: just 80,000 of these are metered, or fewer than 2.5

findings.plain: Across more than 30,000 acres of parkland the city licenses only a handful of restaurant concessions and cafes, and more than half of all park concessions are carts or trucks.
findings.quote: city licenses just 15 restaurant concessions

numbers.label: New annual revenue the five ideas together would raise
CUNY surface parking that could be partly redeveloped
City sites identified in 2023 for battery storage
Metered street parking spaces in the city today
Restaurant concessions licensed across city parkland

recommendations: Develop infill housing on underused portions of City University of New York (CUNY) campuses through long-term ground leases, and steer the lease revenue to campus infrastructure and economic mobility programs.

Set an autonomous vehicle impact fee, combining a per-trip surcharge with annual permit fees, before driverless services scale up, and dedicate part of the money to charging infrastructure, street safety and support for current for-hire drivers.

Site battery storage on city-owned property, including by directing the Department of Citywide Administrative Services to issue requests for proposals for at least 40 of the 47 sites identified by the Mayor's Office of Climate and Environmental Justice.
Expand paid street parking by metering more commercial corridors, launching dynamic pricing in central business districts and piloting residential parking permits.
Expand park concessions and sponsorships, including at least 20 new destination concessions, share the revenue through designated partners and standardize the rules across agencies.
