audits.title: Audit Report on the NYC Department of Veterans’ Services’ Coordination of Housing Assistance
audits.plain_title: Veterans agency housed 153 people but tracked its work poorly
audits.agency: New York City Department of Veterans' Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Veterans' Services (DVS) is efficiently and effectively helping veterans find housing and avoid homelessness, focusing on its housing assistance services in fiscal year 2025.
audits.background: New York City is home to more than 129,000 veterans. DVS was created in 2016 to connect veterans with city services including housing, and the city has cut its homeless veteran population by nearly 90%, from 4,677 in 2011 to 624 in 2024.

findings.plain: DVS effectively helped 153 veterans secure permanent housing in fiscal year 2025, a 21% increase over the prior year, and provided required aftercare services to veterans housed through Collaborative Case Management vouchers.
findings.quote: the agency effectively helped 153 veterans secure housing in FY2025.

findings.plain: More than a quarter (27%) of veterans' housing assistance requests were not answered within the agency's five-business-day target, and 52 requests took at least 21 business days to get a first contact attempt.
findings.quote: DVS failed to respond to more than a quarter (27%) of veterans’ housing assistance requests within its five-business-day target.

findings.plain: DVS lacked written standard operating procedures and formal training for its housing work, and its housing guide was outdated, referring to subsidies that have not existed since 2019. It provided a new policy manual only after the exit conference.
findings.quote: DVS has not developed written standard operating procedures governing its operations, including the Veteran Peer Coordinator Program and Aftercare Assistance

findings.plain: Tracking errors meant DVS overstated its work. Its tracker listed 1,582 housing assistance requests but 41 were duplicates, so it actually received 1,541. In a sample of 60 clients, 25 were recorded as still housed but case notes supported only 11.
findings.quote: although 1,582 housing assistance requests were listed in the tracker, DVS in fact received only 1,541 requests in FY2025.

findings.plain: DVS reported in the Mayor's Management Report that it provided 509 veterans with homelessness prevention and aftercare assistance, but after removing duplicates the real number was 447. The agency acknowledged the error and asked City Hall to correct it.
findings.quote: After subtracting these 62 discrepancies, the actual number of veterans assisted appears to be 447.

findings.plain: DVS gave auditors four different answers over four months about how often staff were supposed to make aftercare check-in calls, showing its internal guidance was unclear.
findings.quote: DVS also offered inconsistent information regarding the frequency with which staff were to make aftercare service calls.

findings.plain: As of December 1, 2025, DVS had not filed its legally mandated annual report to the City Council since 2023 or its three most recent semiannual reports on veteran resource centers. It submitted all outstanding reports on December 15, 2025 after receiving the draft audit.
findings.quote: On December 15, 2025, following the issuance of the Draft Report to the agency, DVS submitted all outstanding required reports and published them on its website.

Submit the annual services report and biannual veteran resource center reports on time as required by Local Laws 44 of 2019 and 215 of 2018.

audits.title: New York City Bike Share Program – Oversight of Revenue Collection and Monitoring
audits.plain_title: Whether the city collects and checks its Citi Bike money
audits.agency: New York City Department of Transportation
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department of Transportation collects the revenues it is owed from the Citi Bike bike share program under its agreement with the vendor and whether it monitors the vendor's compliance with the contract. The audit covered July 2019 to October 2024.
audits.background: The city launched the bike share program in 2013 as a public-private partnership: a vendor operates the system while the department handles planning, outreach and oversight. The program generates revenue from rides, sponsorship and advertising, liquidated damages and a fixed $1 million a year to replace lost parking meter revenue.

findings.plain: The department monitors Citi Bike passively. It does not run scheduled monitoring of its own, conduct program reviews or audits, or do its own calculations to check the accuracy of what the vendor reports.
findings.quote: DOT takes a passive approach to monitoring the Citi Bike program.

findings.plain: Department officials responsible for monitoring were not familiar with the vendor's reports and, despite real-time access to program information, could not explain key elements of them.
findings.quote: Despite having real-time access to program information, DOT officials were not able to explain key elements of the reports.

findings.plain: Errors went unnoticed until the audit. Faulty database queries wrongly excluded 900,829 trips from the ridership count used to figure the department's share of revenue, and on all 203 days of data reviewed the daily data feed did not match the vendor's reported figures.
findings.quote: Errors in the queries (questions used to retrieve and analyze data from databases or information systems) resulted in the erroneous exclusion of 900,829 trips from the ridership count

findings.plain: The contract called for the main sponsor to pay $54.9 million in sponsorship revenue, but auditors found evidence that only $33.6 million was received, a $21.3 million gap.
findings.quote: we only found evidence that $33.6 million in sponsorship revenue was received—a difference of $21.3 million.

findings.plain: The department could not show it counted $26.7 million in accelerated fees the vendor paid to extend the contract, and it had no evidence that the $1 million annual deposit of lost parking meter revenue was made for 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2024, a total of $4 million.
findings.quote: DOT did not provide evidence that the annual deposit of $1 million in lost parking meter revenue was deposited into the City’s bank account for 2019, 2020, 2021, and 2024—totaling $4 million.

findings.plain: For the one year with records, the department treated the $1 million parking meter payment as a bookkeeping credit rather than a bank deposit, which could leave funds unavailable for program improvements and operating costs.
findings.quote: believes that creating a liability in its general ledger satisfies the requirement for the annual deposit

Gap between sponsorship revenue owed and evidence of receipt
Accelerated fees with no proof they were counted
Lost parking meter deposits with no evidence for four years

Make sure payments are received according to the terms of the agreement.
Set up a process to track revenues from each source and ensure all money due to the city is deposited into the right accounts and transferred to the city's general fund as the agreement requires.

audits.title: New York City Housing Authority Monitorship: Monitors' Report (Sixth Report)
audits.plain_title: Heating outages spike and a chimney falls as mold work improves
audits.what_they_audited: The federal monitors' sixth quarterly report on the New York City Housing Authority's (NYCHA) compliance with its 2019 agreement with the federal government, covering heat, elevators, pests and waste, mold and leaks, lead paint and inspections, plus organizational change and capital spending. It reports data for August 1, 2025 to October 31, 2025.
audits.background: On January 31, 2019 NYCHA agreed with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the City of New York to improve housing conditions, and a monitor was appointed to evaluate compliance. Neil Barofsky and Matthew Cipolla of Jenner & Block LLP began a five-year term as co-monitors on February 28, 2024.

findings.plain: The heating season opened badly. There were 30 unplanned central heating outages in October 2025 compared with four in October 2024, affecting 13% of occupied apartments rather than 2%, though NYCHA still resolved them in an average of 7.3 hours. findings.plain: A 20-story exterior chimney serving the boiler room at Mitchel Houses in the Bronx collapsed on October 1, 2025. No one was hurt, but 38 apartments were evacuated, about 88 residents went to hotels and gas service to the whole development was shut off. The Fire Department, the Department of Buildings and the Department of Investigation are all investigating.
findings.quote: approximately 88 residents were temporarily relocated to hotels

findings.plain: Mold response kept improving from a very low base. NYCHA removed mold within five business days 24% of the time in the third quarter of Year 7, up from 7% a year earlier, and met the agreement's combined mold timeframes 28% of the time across three quarters versus 8%. The requirement is 95%.

NYCHA answered 86% of mouse, cockroach and bed bug complaints within seven calendar days, 27 percentage points better than a year earlier, yet its estimated rat population rose about 33% and the cumulative rat reduction stood at 48%, short of the 75% target.

audits.title: Report on the New York City Conflicts of Interest Board's Advisory Opinion and Moonlighting Waiver Practices
audits.plain_title: Ethics board quietly cleared a top official's second job
audits.agency: New York City Conflicts of Interest Board
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined how the New York City Conflicts of Interest Board (COIB) interprets the city Conflicts of Interest Law's "moonlighting restrictions" and whether COIB makes its advisory opinions public as the law requires.
audits.background: The city's Conflicts of Interest Law, known as Chapter 68, generally prohibits full-time city employees from holding second jobs with firms that do business with the city. DOI looked into the issue after learning COIB issued an advisory opinion letting First Deputy Mayor Randy Mastro continue serving as an outside attorney for the Madison Square Garden Group (MSG) in a lawsuit against a former New York Knicks player.

findings.plain: DOI found no legal authority supporting COIB's apparent position that the moonlighting restrictions do not apply to city-employed attorneys acting as outside counsel to entities with city business, and concluded COIB overlooked those restrictions in the Mastro opinion.
findings.quote:
DOI is unaware of any legal authority supporting COIB’s view and found that COIB overlooked the 
law’s “moonlighting restrictions” in its advisory opinion issued to First Deputy Mayor Mastro.

findings.plain: DOI's position, based on the plain language of Chapter 68, is that COIB could only have permitted the arrangement through a public waiver, which would have disclosed both the attorney-client relationship and COIB's permission. Instead COIB issued what it considered a confidential advice letter.
findings.quote:
it is DOI’s position, supported by the plain language of Chapter 68,  that the law requires 
COIB to do so via public waiver.

findings.plain: COIB does not comply with Chapter 68's requirement to publish advisory opinions in redacted form and has not published one since 2018 despite issuing hundreds of written opinions since then.
findings.quote: has not done so since 2018 despite having issued hundreds of written advisory opinions since then.

findings.plain: The fact that COIB cleared the first deputy mayor to represent a powerful local business became public only through the press and litigation, which DOI said points to COIB operating less transparently than the law envisions.
findings.quote:
COIB is operating in a less transparent manner 
than Chapter 68 envisions.

findings.plain: DOI did not investigate Mastro himself, noting he continued the representation only after obtaining COIB's permission and was entitled to rely on the board's advice even though DOI believes that advice was legally flawed.
findings.quote:
Mastro was entitled to rely on the advice he received from COIB, even though 
DOI believes that the advice was legally flawed.

numbers.label: Last year COIB published a redacted advisory opinion
Recommendations DOI issued to COIB

recommendations: COIB should review the advice it gave First Deputy Mayor Mastro on his MSG representation to ensure it is consistent with the moonlighting restrictions, and amend the advice and issue a waiver if appropriate.

COIB should review its previously issued advisory opinions to determine whether it has permitted other city-employed attorneys to represent private firms with city business, and where that conduct is ongoing, reconsider and amend the advice and issue waivers if appropriate.
Alternatively, if COIB maintains that the moonlighting restrictions apply only to in-house attorneys of firms with city business, it should issue a formal rule saying so.
COIB should publish waivers on its website in a searchable format so the public does not need to file Freedom of Information Law requests to see them.

COIB should comply with the City Charter's requirement to publish its advisory opinions, including the March 2025 Mastro opinion, either with redactions or as summaries omitting the parties' identities.
audits.agency_response: DOI noted that the board has already implemented some changes in response to its review, particularly changes to COIB's website concerning its advice practices. COIB takes the position that its advisory opinions are confidential and would not produce them to DOI.

rec_display.text: COIB should review the advice it gave First Deputy Mayor Mastro on his MSG representation to ensure it is consistent with the moonlighting restrictions, and amend the advice and issue a waiver if appropriate.

COIB should review its previously issued advisory opinions to determine whether it has permitted other city-employed attorneys to represent private firms with city business, and where that conduct is ongoing, reconsider and amend the advice and issue waivers if appropriate.
Alternatively, if COIB maintains that the moonlighting restrictions apply only to in-house attorneys of firms with city business, it should issue a formal rule saying so.
COIB should publish waivers on its website in a searchable format so the public does not need to file Freedom of Information Law requests to see them.

COIB should comply with the City Charter's requirement to publish its advisory opinions, including the March 2025 Mastro opinion, either with redactions or as summaries omitting the parties' identities.

audits.title: Audit Report of the New York City Department of Education’s Oversight of Its Contracted Bus Services
audits.plain_title: Schools barely police the companies running their buses
audits.agency: New York City Department of Education
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Education (DOE) has proper operational controls over its contracted school bus vendors to ensure that bus service is adequately provided to New York City schoolchildren and complies with laws, regulations and contract requirements.
audits.background: DOE's Office of Pupil Transportation coordinates busing for public, charter and nonpublic schools. In school year 2023-24 it bused about 68,742 students on stop-to-school routes and about 56,446 students on curb-to-school routes for students with disabilities, with $1.7 billion of DOE's budget dedicated to transportation.

findings.plain: DOE does not adequately oversee its school bus vendors or hold them accountable for poor performance. Despite having global positioning system (GPS) and complaint data, it does not proactively use it to enforce contract terms, spot problem vendors or routes or improve service.
findings.quote: DOE does not proactively or systematically use readily available global positioning system (GPS) or complaint data to oversee school bus vendors, enforce contract terms, identify trends and problematic vendors or routes, or improve performance.

findings.plain: Complaints to the Office of Pupil Transportation rose nearly 82% in three years, from 84,849 in school year 2021-22 to 154,376 in 2023-24, yet DOE did not analyze the data or require any vendor to adopt a corrective action plan.
findings.quote: The number of complaints reported to OPT increased by nearly 82% over the three-year period between 2021 and 2024.

findings.plain: Special education students were disproportionately hurt. Curb-to-school routes serving students with individualized education programs averaged 11.5 delays per route versus 5.6 for general education routes, accounted for 99% of "problem run" delays and had far more delays over an hour.
findings.quote: students with IEPs were disproportionately impacted by unreliable bus service.

findings.plain: On the 10 routes with the most no-show and late-service complaints, all serving students with disabilities, DOE staff generally closed complaints after talking to vendors instead of checking GPS data, and route changes did not fix the problems. After modifications, buses still ran four minutes to 2 hours and 20 minutes late.
findings.quote: After modifications, delays ranged from four minutes to 2 hours and 20 minutes.

findings.plain: DOE did not ensure practice "dry runs" happened before the first day of school. Nineteen vendors failed to comply, one skipped dry runs on all 24 of its routes, and DOE waived at least an estimated $268,691 in liquidated damages it could have assessed.
findings.quote: For SY2023–24, the audit team estimated that, at minimum, DOE failed to assess liquidated damages of $268,691.

findings.plain: Drivers often failed to log in so parents could track buses, and DOE collected penalties in only 5.5% of 200,556 violations, leaving almost $42.6 million in damages unassessed. Roughly 11,209 pre-K students rode buses without real-time tracking devices.
findings.quote: This means that DOE was entitled to assess almost $42.6 million in damages but failed to do so.

findings.plain: DOE did not hold Via Transportation, whose contracts total $51.7 million, accountable for delivering route optimization and student boarding-tracking technology that was due in December 2021 and still has not been implemented. DOE meanwhile creates special education routes with an unsupported legacy system built in 1994.
findings.quote: This technology was expected to be implemented in December 2021 but to date, this has not happened.

Review and use prior complaints as part of investigations to identify trends in vendors' poor performance.
Consistently maintain the vehicle numbers serving each route and use them to run a GPS review for every no-show or late-service complaint.
Routinely compare planned route start and end times to actual times to check compliance with contracts and individualized education programs, issuing violations and penalties as appropriate.

Consider enhanced minimum performance standards in new bus contracts, including monthly metrics for on-time performance and ride times, a tiered penalty scale, GPS-based liquidated damages and taking routes away from the poorest performers.

Ensure DOE recovers any money paid to Via Transportation for required work that was not performed.

Provide vendors with reports comparing planned and actual route times, discuss them and document the discussions.
Formally document and keep records of all performance discussions with vendors.

audits.title: Audit on the Department of Investigation’s Background Investigations for City Employees
audits.plain_title: City background checks lagged years behind hiring
audits.agency: New York City Department of Investigation
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Department of Investigation, the city's watchdog agency, conducts background investigations of high-level and sensitive city hires well enough to identify adverse information in a timely way. The audit covered July 1, 2022 through December 31, 2024.
audits.background: Mayoral executive orders require the Department of Investigation to run background checks on city employees appointed to positions of responsibility, such as those earning more than $125,000 or with authority over contracts, but agencies generally hire candidates before the check is finished. By July 1, 2019 the department had accumulated a backlog of 6,479 pending investigations.

findings.plain: Backlogged cases took years to resolve. Backlogged investigations closed during the audit period had been pending an average of 5.7 years, with delays ranging from three to eight years.
findings.quote: backlogged investigations closed during the audit scope period were pending for an average of 5.7 years, with delays ranging from three to eight years

findings.plain: Two in five backlogged cases were closed without a completed investigation because the person had already retired or otherwise left city government.
findings.quote: 40% of all cases closed during this period were administratively closed because the subject of the investigation had already left City service or retired

findings.plain: People with criminal histories or other red flags served in positions of trust while their checks sat pending. Auditors found evidence of criminal history in 27 of 30 sampled backlogged files, and those cases were pending almost six years on average.
findings.quote: auditors found evidence of criminal history in 27 of 30 sampled files, including petty larceny, driving while intoxicated, attempted criminal possession of a controlled substance, and aggravated unlicensed operation of a motor vehicle

findings.plain: The department does not advise agencies on whether a candidate is suitable and does not track what agencies do when a check turns up adverse information, which the audit calls a gap in oversight.
findings.quote: DOI does not track whether candidates with adverse information are retained by agencies.

findings.plain: Case files were incomplete. Of 50 sampled files with completed investigations, 30 were missing required documents or evidence that steps such as tax checks or education verification were taken.
findings.quote: Of the remaining 50 sampled files, 30 (60%) were missing required documents or evidence that certain investigation steps were performed.

findings.plain: Fingerprint records that must be destroyed within three months of closing a case were still in 31 of 75 sampled files, an issue a state review also flagged in 2021.
findings.quote: Fingerprint results were found in 31 (41%) of 75 sampled files.

findings.plain: New investigations are on track. The department has prevented a new backlog from forming since July 1, 2019 and completed 99% of routine checks in under 180 days.
findings.quote: DOI completed 99% of the routine background investigations it received in under 180 days.

Consider tracking appointment dates to determine whether agencies submit applications within required timeframes.

Ensure Kaseware, the department's new case system, has adequate documentation, including a data dictionary.

audits.agency: New York City Campaign Finance Board
audits.what_they_audited: A report from Citizens Union, a good-government group, analyzing independent expenditure spending in the 2025 New York City general election, drawn from disclosures to the New York City Campaign Finance Board and the New York State Board of Elections.
audits.background: Independent spending groups, called Independent Expenditure Entities in New York, may not coordinate with candidate campaigns. The report covers June 25, 2025, the day after the primary, through December 1, 2025, and follows a companion report on the primary.

findings.plain: Outside spending across the 2025 cycle set a record for New York City, roughly double the 2021 total.
findings.quote: These groups spent a total of $82.95 million to influence races up and down the ballot

findings.plain: Nearly all general election outside spending went to the mayor's race, and the number of active groups doubled compared with the primary.
findings.quote: general election, 98% of it on the mayoral race.

findings.plain: Most of the outside money in the mayoral race supported one candidate, which the report calls the largest sum ever spent by such groups to support a single candidate in the city.
findings.quote: $28.4 million, or 83% of all outside spending in the race.

findings.plain: The winning candidate had by far the most individual contributors and the smallest average donation, and reached the matching funds program's private fundraising cap two months before Election Day.
findings.quote: Zohran Mamdani had more contributors than any other candidate

findings.plain: A large share of outside spending went to negative advertising, nearly all of it from groups aligned with one candidate.
findings.quote: Super PACs spent at least $17.1 million on

findings.plain: Outside spending in City Council races dropped sharply from the primary, and no negative ads were run by these groups in Council contests.
findings.quote: In total, Super PACs spent $863,000 on Council races in the 2025 general election.

findings.plain: Donors routed money through intermediary committees so that the required top-three-donor disclaimers on ads did not identify the original funders.

audits.title: Explainer: How to Increase Elected Officials’ Salaries in New York City
audits.plain_title: How the city sets pay for its elected officials
audits.what_they_audited: An explainer from Citizens Union, a good-government group, on how salaries for New York City elected officials are normally set, written as the City Council moved a bill to raise those salaries by 16 percent.
audits.background: Under a 1986 law, the mayor must create a Quadrennial Advisory Commission for the Review of Compensation Levels of Elected Officials every four years. The commission holds public hearings, consults experts and recommends salary levels, and the Council then sets pay by local law.

findings.plain: The Council is moving a bill that would raise elected officials' salaries by 16 percent, retroactive to January 1, 2026.
findings.quote: The New York City Council is advancing legislation to increase the salaries of elected officials by 16% in the final weeks of the Council term.

findings.plain: Every raise in the past half century followed a review by an independent compensation commission.
findings.quote: Every increase in elected officials salaries over the past fifty years has been enacted after an independent commission of experts reviewed compensation levels and offered recommendations.

findings.plain: Several mayors have skipped the required commission, and no commission has met since 2015.
findings.quote: Since no commission has been convened since 2015, salaries have remained unchanged for nearly a decade.

findings.plain: There is no penalty when a mayor does not appoint the commission, short of a lawsuit.
findings.quote: There is no enforcement mechanism if the mayor refuses to implement this law, except for legal action through the courts.

findings.plain: Citizens Union writes that the Council's bill comes with no published analysis behind the 16 percent figure.
findings.quote: It offers no supporting analysis for the proposed 16% pay increase.

findings.plain: The Council may set its own pay except between general election day and December 31 in an election year, and the group says the current schedule of a December hearing and a January vote raises questions about that restriction.
findings.quote: The City Council has full discretion over setting salaries for elected officials, including for themselves,

audits.agency: New York City Landmarks Preservation Commission
audits.what_they_audited: A letter report assessing how the Landmarks Preservation Commission processes applications for permits to do work on landmarked properties, covering July 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025.
audits.background: The commission regulates changes to more than 38,000 landmarked properties and reported receiving 12,211 permit applications in fiscal year 2023 alone. In March 2024 it launched Portico, a web portal that lets owners of landmarked buildings apply for permits and track their applications electronically.

findings.plain: The commission generally followed its own procedures. Of 50 sampled applications, 47 resulted in permits, and the three that did not had open violations, were withdrawn or lacked required documents.
findings.quote: auditors concluded that LPC satisfactorily complied with its protocols when processing permit applications and issuing permits

findings.plain: Processing got faster after the Portico portal launched. Average processing time for certificates of no effect dropped 33% and the share of permits issued on time rose for all four permit types reviewed.

findings.plain: Two of the 47 sampled applications that received permits were missing the commission's required approval stamp.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Office of City Clerk’s Enforcement of the Lobbying Law
audits.plain_title: Weak spots in how the city polices lobbying
audits.agency: New York City Office of the City Clerk
audits.what_they_audited: How the Office of the City Clerk administers and enforces the city's Lobbying Law, including lobbyist registration, audits of filings and investigations of unregistered lobbying. The audit covered January 1, 2022 through June 30, 2025.
audits.background: The office's Lobbying Bureau registers lobbyists, audits their filings and investigates unreported lobbying activity. According to the office's annual report, entities spent $138.4 million on outside lobbying in New York City in 2024, an all-time high.

findings.plain: The office generally meets the law's core requirements, auditing registered lobbyists each year and publishing the required annual report.
findings.quote: the Office of the City Clerk (OCC) generally complies with the requirements of the Lobbying Law by conducting audits of registered lobbyists and by publishing the required annual report

findings.plain: The burden of catching unregistered lobbying falls on the office because the law does not require city officials or employees to report contacts that may be lobbying. The office has discussed amendments with the City Council.
findings.quote: Instead, the burden to detect unregistered lobbying falls on OCC.

findings.plain: Searches for unregistered lobbyists skip high-risk areas such as land use applications and non-competitive contracts. Auditors found 11 of 45 private land use applicants in 2024 were not registered, and the office's follow-up has already produced $120,480 in accumulated late filing penalties for two entities.
findings.quote: The audit team found that 11 (24%) of the 45 ULURP applicants during CY2024 had not registered with the Lobbying Bureau

findings.plain: Outreach emails to 1,863 recipients of City Council discretionary funds drew only 58 responses and produced no new registrations, and the office does not ask recipients to state whether they lobby.
findings.quote: OCC sent emails to 1,863 such recipients and received only 58 (3%) responses. These efforts did not result in the registration of any new lobbyists.

findings.plain: Investigations of unreported lobbying are limited in scope. All nine closed cases auditors reviewed ended with findings of no probable cause, and files showed no evidence that staff contacted the officials who were allegedly lobbied.
findings.quote: the files contained no evidence that staff attempted to reach out to the City agencies or officials that were allegedly the subject of lobbying

findings.plain: The Lobbying Bureau lacks detailed written policies for staff and is short-staffed, with five people, three vacancies and a budget the office says does not allow new hires.
findings.quote: OCC has not developed written policies and procedures outlining OCC’s key requirements and responsibilities as they pertain to the Lobbying Law.

Regularly review land use applicants and vendors awarded non-competitive contracts to determine whether they lobbied, registered as lobbyists and accurately recorded their lobbying activity.

audits.title: DOI Investigation into the NYPD's Compliance with Local Laws Restricting City Assistance with Immigration Enforcement
audits.plain_title: One of five incidents broke immigration cooperation limits
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with local laws and executive orders restricting assistance with federal civil immigration enforcement, investigating five specific incidents and the department's related policies.
audits.background: The investigation was prompted by a June 2025 referral from City Council Speaker Adrienne Adams and Oversight and Investigations Committee Chair Gale Brewer after media reports raised questions about NYPD involvement in civil immigration enforcement. City laws limit such assistance while permitting cooperation with federal criminal investigations.

findings.plain: DOI concluded that NYPD's current policies, particularly as strengthened by reforms in 2025, comply with city law, but identified one incident of five in which an officer violated local law by assisting federal civil immigration enforcement.
findings.quote:
DOI identified one incident in which an officer violated local law  by providing assistance to federal 
authorities in connection with enforcement of the federal civil immigration law

findings.plain: In November 2024, an NYPD officer on a Homeland Security Investigations task force placed alerts on a list of people subject to potential civil immigration enforcement so he would be emailed if they interacted with the NYPD, violating policy and local law. The officer was removed from the task force and discipline is ongoing.
findings.quote:
The officer honored that request in 
violation of NYPD policy and local law.

findings.plain: In three other incidents, including the transfer of Merwil Gutiérrez Flores to Federal Bureau of Investigation custody and the disclosure of Leqaa Kordia's sealed arrest records, DOI found no violation of the sanctuary laws, though the Kordia records should not have been shared because they were sealed.
findings.quote:
the prior arrest information should not have been disclosed to HSI because the arrest records were 
sealed.

findings.plain: NYPD does not comply with Local Law 228, which requires documenting each request for assistance with civil immigration enforcement: its documentation is underinclusive and it does not send all required information to the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs for quarterly reports.
findings.quote:
the NYPD does not comply with this law, because its documentation of requests is 
underinclusive and does not contain the level of detail required by local law and other City policies.

findings.plain: NYPD has not adopted a policy limiting non-local law enforcement agents' access to city property as Local Law 246 of 2017 requires, though it began drafting one when DOI raised the issue. It does comply with Local Law 59's annual detainer reporting requirement.
findings.quote:
DOI found that the NYPD has not 
adopted such a policy, apart from general policy statements prohibiting the use of City property to 
assist in immigration enforcement

found gaps in the NYPD’s current policies and practices that raise the risk of

audits.title: Enforcement of Local Law 144 – Automated Employment Decision Tools
audits.plain_title: How the city enforces its law on automated hiring tools
audits.agency: New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department of Consumer and Worker Protection has designed and put in place an effective system to enforce Local Law 144, the city law governing automated employment decision tools. The audit covered July 2023 through June 2025.
audits.background: Local Law 144 of 2021 requires employers and employment agencies that use automated employment decision tools to conduct a bias audit within a year before using a tool, post a summary of the results on their website and notify candidates that a tool will be used. The department enforces the law with civil penalties of $500 to $1,500 per day and has an agreement with the city Office of Technology and Innovation for technical help.

findings.plain: The department's complaint process does not ensure that complaints about violations reach it, and after its initial stakeholder education it has done no further outreach. That approach will not catch employers that simply skip the law's requirements, such as posting bias audits.
findings.quote: DCWP’s AEDT complaint process is ineffective in ensuring that all complaints related to non-compliance with LL144 are routed to DCWP.

findings.plain: The department received only two complaints about automated employment decision tools during the audit period but did not look into whether its complaint intake process was working.
findings.quote: DCWP did not investigate whether the complaint intake process worked.

findings.plain: When the department surveyed the websites and bias audits of 32 companies it found a single compliance issue. Auditors reviewed the same companies and found at least 17 instances of potential non-compliance. The department's review skipped the formal procedures its technology partner created and did not cover all of the law's requirements.
findings.quote: We reviewed the same companies and identified at least 17 instances of potential non-compliance under LL144.

findings.plain: Department officials lack the technical expertise to evaluate how these tools are used, yet they did not consult the Office of Technology and Innovation when making determinations about them.
findings.quote: DCWP officials did not consult with OTI when making determinations about AEDTs.

recommendations: Implement processes to make sure complaints about automated employment decision tools are properly handled and routed.
Implement mechanisms to make sure such complaints received by 311 are properly routed to the department.
Research and test why so few complaints about the tools come in and take steps to address those factors.
Make sure the department's bias audit reviews address all potential non-compliance, including by using existing Office of Technology and Innovation resources such as the Enforcement Workbook.
Create and implement a process to improve enforcement by identifying potential violations through research and other leads, not just complaints.
Use the Office of Technology and Innovation's expertise to evaluate the technical workings of suspected automated tools in support of enforcement.

audits.title: Oversight of Housing Discrimination Complaints
audits.plain_title: How the human rights agency handles housing bias complaints
audits.agency: New York City Commission on Human Rights
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Commission on Human Rights reviewed and addressed housing discrimination complaints on time and in line with its own policies and the law. The audit covered July 2019 through March 2025.
audits.background: The commission enforces the New York City Human Rights Law, which bans housing discrimination based on race, source of income, disability and other protected classes. From July 2019 through July 2024 it received 51,702 housing discrimination inquiries, of which 474 had been filed as formal complaints as of July 31, 2024.

findings.plain: The commission does not adequately monitor how housing discrimination inquiries and complaints are handled and has no benchmarks for timeliness. In a sample of 29 cases, determinations came more than 2 years on average after complaints were filed, and where submission dates were documented, decisions took over 3 years on average, with one case lingering more than 7 years.
findings.quote: for the 18 inquiries where the submission date was documented, decisions took over 3 years on average—including one that lingered for more than 7 years.

findings.plain: Staff often failed to respond to people alleging discrimination within the expected 14 days. In 12 of 25 sampled inquiries with dates recorded, the first contact attempt came about 39 days after the commission was contacted, and in one case not until 165 days later.
findings.quote: they did not contact the inquirer until approximately 39 days after CCHR was contacted.

findings.plain: The commission has no policy requiring timely intake appointments. Where appointment dates were documented, intake took almost 3 months on average from submission, and in one instance almost 9 months.
findings.quote: LEB staff did not conduct an intake appointment for these inquiries until, on average, almost 3 months (84 days) from the day the inquiries were submitted.

findings.plain: Guidelines say attorneys should draft a complaint within 14 days of the intake appointment, but officials did not monitor this. For the six sampled cases with dates recorded, drafts took nearly 4 months on average, and one attorney took more than 11 months.
findings.quote: on average, attorneys took nearly 4 months (115 days) to submit a draft complaint to their supervisor.

findings.plain: When an assigned attorney left or was removed from a case, the commission was slow to assign a new one, taking over 11 months on average for five of 36 sampled complaints and over 2 years in one case.
findings.quote: it took CCHR over 11 months (348 days) to reassign a new attorney to five of 36 sampled complaints.

findings.plain: The commission did not ensure staff documented and kept evidence that sampled housing discrimination cases were being supervised.
findings.quote: CCHR did not ensure its staff documented and maintained evidence of case supervision for sampled housing discrimination complaints.

numbers.label: Housing discrimination inquiries received over five years
Inquiries filed as formal complaints as of July 31, 2024
Longest wait to reassign an attorney to an open case

recommendations: Develop policies and procedures to reduce delays in processing housing discrimination complaints, including setting time frames for each step of intake, filing and investigation, monitoring dates in the case management system, analyzing its data and assessing resources to find bottlenecks, and strengthening policies and monitoring compliance.
Establish a procedure that prioritizes attorney reassignments to minimize disruption to investigations.

Make sure staff use available tools for thorough case management, including documenting evidence of case supervision and recording all intake and investigation activities and essential documents in the case management system.

audits.title: Creative New York
audits.plain_title: The state of the city's arts and creative economy
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, examining the size and health of the city's arts and creative economy and setting out ten proposals for city and state policymakers.
audits.background: The creative sector accounts for more than 7 percent of private sector employment in the five boroughs and spans ten core industries, from performing arts and film to advertising, design and architecture.

findings.plain: The creative sector remains one of the city's largest employers, with a workforce of more than 326,000 in 2024.
findings.quote: arts and creative industries employ more than 326,000 New Yorkers

findings.plain: The number of working artists has dropped since the pandemic began, with especially steep declines among dancers and actors.
findings.quote: the city has seen an 18.8 percent decline in dancers, an 8 percent

findings.plain: Film and television employment grew steeply before 2020 and has fallen since, a reversal seen in advertising, architecture and design as well.
findings.quote: film and TV jobs in New York City are down by 19.1 percent

findings.plain: The city is losing share of the national creative workforce.
findings.quote: creative economy has declined from 9.3 percent to 8.6 percent since 2019.

findings.plain: Cultural venues have closed in significant numbers since 2020, with operators citing changed audience habits and rising insurance costs.
findings.quote: Nearly 50 theaters, music clubs, museums, and galleries have shuttered since 2020

findings.plain: Creative workers earn well below the national average once the cost of living is counted, and the gap has widened over a decade.
findings.quote: about 23 percent less than the national average after adjusting for the city’s high cost of living

findings.plain: The report also documents growth, including new venues and a sharp rise in cultural nonprofits outside Manhattan.
findings.quote: nonprofits have grown 73.8 percent in Queens

Decline in creative economy employment since 2019

recommendations: Tackle the affordability crisis with a large increase in housing production, building on the City of Yes zoning reforms with more as-of-right zoning near transit, an end to remaining parking minimums, faster permitting and review, broader legalization of accessory dwellings and stronger preservation tools.

Create 5,000 artist-preference housing units by 2030, with clear guidance from the Department of Housing Preservation and Development, a biennial artist survey, a citywide artist live/work standard, artist set-asides in office-to-residential conversions and an artist housing accelerator.
Launch the city's first five-borough cultural festival, coordinated by the city and using streets, plazas, parks and city-owned properties, with streamlined permitting for outdoor programming.
Launch a portable benefits pilot for freelancers and self-employed artists, administered by a nonprofit partner and funded proportionally by employers, platforms and public dollars.
Establish a city-facilitated pooled insurance program that lets cultural organizations and small venues buy coverage together at lower rates, with subsidies for the smallest organizations.

Create a Cultural Ownership Fund to help mission-driven groups keep or acquire space, expand shared back-office services and shared spaces, and reform the Temporary Place of Assembly permitting process.

Expand the Economic Development Corporation's creative industries work into a core pillar of its strategy, dedicate at least 1 percent of capital budgets to public art or creative placemaking, and expand shared production hubs and signature industry events.
Expand the Public Artists in Residence program tenfold and create full-time civic artist positions in agencies that have never hosted one, each with its own art initiative.

Create dedicated recurring revenue for the arts, such as a voluntary hotel stay surcharge feeding a parks and culture fund and pilot cultural districts, and make Cultural Development Fund payments timelier with a new tier of grantees for midsized organizations.

Launch a Creative Pathways and Talent Pipeline Initiative spanning public schools and CUNY, including a creative economy focus in FutureReadyNYC, sequential arts learning in every grade band, and paid internships and mentorship for CUNY students.

audits.title: The High Cost of Free Job Training in NYC
audits.plain_title: Why people drop out of free job training programs
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, on the everyday costs that keep low-income New Yorkers from finishing tuition-free job training, based on interviews with 29 workforce development organizations.
audits.background: Most nonprofit career training programs in the city charge no tuition, but participants still face costs such as childcare, transit fares and lost wages while they train. The report calls these supports wraparound services.

findings.plain: Costs outside the classroom, rather than tuition, are what put training out of reach for many New Yorkers.
findings.quote: the everyday costs of childcare, subway rides, and groceries make even “free” programs out of reach

findings.plain: Few training organizations can afford to offer childcare help, stipends or transit coverage to their participants.
findings.quote: only three provide childcare support to their participants (10 percent)

findings.plain: Where programs have measured it, stipends produced sizable gains in graduation rates.
findings.quote: Per Scholas saw an 18 percent jump in graduation rates after offering a $1,000 stipend

findings.plain: One construction training program saw a large completion gap between cohorts that received stipends and those that did not.
findings.quote: 79 percent for those with stipends versus 57 percent for those without stipends

findings.plain: The city's childcare voucher process can take longer than a training program lasts, so parents often cannot use it in time.
findings.quote: can take months to access

findings.plain: The report says training will matter more as automation reshapes work.
findings.quote: AI and automation could transform or eliminate at least one-quarter of all jobs by 2030

numbers.label: Workforce organizations interviewed for the report
Rise in graduation rates after a $1,000 stipend
Rise in completions among stipend recipients at one program
Stipend size the report proposes per learner

recommendations: Create NYC Workforce Supports, a program funding free OMNY cards, childcare vouchers and other supports for training participants, paired with a pilot that rigorously tests and evaluates which supports work.
Establish an NYC Skills Grant providing stipends of up to $1,000 per learner in evidence-backed training programs to cover nontuition costs.
Create a childcare for workforce program that lets proven training providers hand city-backed childcare vouchers directly to their learners, modeled on Promise NYC.
Launch a zero-interest workforce loan program offering up to $3,000 for living costs during training, repayable only after a participant lands a stable, well-paying job.
Build a navigator staff line and a wraparound services budget line into all new city workforce development requests for proposals.
Expand the Work Progress Program to cover adults in career training so they can receive stipends while enrolled.
Expand the CUNY Community Navigator Institute to train 50 workforce navigators and place them at training organizations across the city.
Pay for these supports through expanded paid street parking and, at the state level, a 0.05 percent employer payroll surcharge modeled on a Massachusetts training fund.

audits.title: NYC’s Safety Net on the Brink
audits.plain_title: Federal cuts and the city's social service nonprofits
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City think tank, on how federal budget cuts and executive actions are hitting the city's human services nonprofits, based on interviews with leaders of more than 40 organizations.
audits.background: The report focuses on the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed in July 2025, whose largest cuts take effect in 2027, along with grant terminations and executive actions already in force.

findings.plain: Nonprofits surveyed for the report depend heavily on federal money, on average close to a third of their budgets.
findings.quote: these organizations receive, on average, 29 percent of their funding from the federal government

findings.plain: Food programs have already lost large amounts of federal food and grant money while demand at pantries keeps climbing.
findings.quote: Food Bank for New York City has received 10 million pounds fewer of food this year

findings.plain: Visits to pantries and soup kitchens have risen sharply over five years, before the effects of the federal shutdown.
findings.quote: the city’s food pantries and soup kitchens have seen a 90 percent increase in visits over the past five years

findings.plain: New Medicaid eligibility rules are expected to strip coverage from a large number of New Yorkers, which also cuts the reimbursements many nonprofits live on.
findings.quote: 1.2 million New Yorkers across the state to lose health insurance coverage

findings.plain: Supportive housing providers expect to lose federal grants as a large share of a federal homelessness program shifts to temporary housing.
findings.quote: two-thirds of the funding for this permanent housing program will end January 1

findings.plain: Immigration enforcement and related fear have cut attendance at English classes, daycare and senior centers.
findings.quote: has declined by about 40 percent since the fall of 2024

findings.plain: The city owes nonprofits a large backlog of payments for work already done, pushing organizations to take out bridge loans.
findings.quote: The city currently owes more than $1 billion in unpaid invoices

Federal food the city's food bank did not receive this year
Rise in pantry and soup kitchen visits over five years

recommendations: Establish a New York City nonprofit stabilization fund, setting money aside in the January 2026 financial plan and adding to it in the adopted budget, to cover urgent gaps in 2027 and 2028.

Reduce the administrative burden of city contracting, applications and reporting, starting by directing every contracting agency to identify three requirements it can eliminate or consolidate in 2026.
Launch a citywide Keep New Yorkers Covered initiative that uses early-warning recertification systems, outreach and technical assistance to keep eligible residents enrolled in benefits.
Convene top city leaders and human services organizations early in 2026 for contingency planning on how limited resources will be allocated as federal cuts land.
Pay nonprofits within the required contract period, clear invoices more than a year old, and publish a dashboard of contract processing times and payment delays.

Establish a federal risk and response unit within the Office of Management and Budget to track federal changes, issue rapid impact assessments and advise nonprofits.

audits.title: Oversight of the Practice of Funeral Directing
audits.plain_title: State and city oversight of funeral directors
audits.agency: New York State Department of Health and New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the state Department of Health effectively oversees the practice of funeral directing under state law and whether the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene effectively oversees selected aspects of the practice. The audit covered April 2019 through November 2023.
audits.background: Under the Public Health Law, only licensed and registered funeral directors working at registered firms may handle the care, preparation and burial or cremation of the dead. Deaths outside New York City are registered in the state's Electronic Death Registration System and deaths in the city in the city's eVital system; together the systems recorded 801,421 deaths statewide during the audit period.

findings.plain: Some funeral directors interviewed said they do not use the tests prescribed by regulation to verify that death has occurred, and some said they do not always label or otherwise identify the bodies in their care, raising the risk of misidentification.
findings.quote: some said they don’t always label or otherwise identify the bodies in their care, increasing the risk that bodies may be misidentified.

findings.plain: The state health department has reduced or no assurance that some funeral firms met, or still meet, the required standards for their preparation rooms.
findings.quote: DOH has reduced or no assurance that some firms initially met or continue to meet standards for their preparation rooms.

findings.plain: In more than 2,500 cases, deaths were registered after the bodies had already been buried or cremated, according to the two vital records systems.
findings.quote: There were more than 2,500 cases in which deaths were registered after the disposition of bodies

findings.plain: Auditors found two instances where a firm may have been practicing at an unknown or unregistered location and over 23,000 death certificates issued in the state and city systems by unregistered or unknown funeral directors or firms.
findings.quote: over 23,000 death certificates that were issued in both DOH and DOHMH’s systems by unregistered or unknown funeral directors and/or firms.

findings.plain: Auditors identified 7,484 death certificates with duplicated or missing Social Security numbers, which undermines the certificates' accuracy and their usefulness in post-death arrangements.
findings.quote: We identified 7,484 death certificates (2,785 EDRS, 4,699 eVital) with duplicated or no SSNs

findings.plain: The state's practices for learning about and following up on funeral firm closures give it little assurance that it has the information needed to investigate risks.
findings.quote: DOH’s practices for learning about and following up on firm closures provide little assurance that it has the information it needs to investigate any risks identified.

numbers.label: Deaths recorded statewide during the audit period
Death certificates issued by unregistered or unknown directors or firms
Death certificates with duplicated or missing Social Security numbers

recommendations: To the state Department of Health: take steps to better ensure funeral directors and firms know about and comply with required death tests and minimize the risk of misidentifying human remains.
To the state Department of Health: take action to gain greater assurance that firms meet requirements for their preparation rooms.
To the state Department of Health: work with the city health department on an approach to identify and follow up on the risk that bodies are buried or cremated before the death is registered.

To the state Department of Health: strengthen methods to identify and address unauthorized funeral directing by unregistered directors or firms or at unregistered locations, which might include better internal communication between its funeral directing and vital records bureaus.
To the state Department of Health: evaluate the benefit of inspecting funeral firms based on identified risks and document the results.
To the state Department of Health: take steps to improve assurance that closing or closed firms have actually stopped operating.
To both departments: improve interagency communication, which could include analyzing registration data and sharing results, to better identify and address unauthorized funeral directing activity.
To both departments: improve the completeness and accuracy of Social Security number information on death certificates in their respective systems.

audits.title: Oversight of Language Access Services
audits.plain_title: How well city hospitals serve patients with limited English
audits.agency: New York City Health and Hospitals Corporation
audits.what_they_audited: Whether New York City Health + Hospitals, the city's public hospital system, adequately serves patients with limited English proficiency, complies with state regulations and local laws and provides enough oversight of its language access services. The audit covered January 2019 through December 2024.
audits.background: Health + Hospitals, the nation's largest municipal public health care system, serves about 1 million New Yorkers a year, and the Census Bureau estimates over 1.7 million city residents have limited English proficiency. In fiscal year 2024 the system answered 2.6 million requests for language services with 35.6 million minutes of interpretation in 255 languages and dialects at a cost of $24.1 million.

findings.plain: The system did not adequately oversee its language services data. Records had missing or mislabeled information, the system could not confirm that interpretation in rarer languages was actually provided and it did not reconcile the data against vendor invoices.
findings.quote: H+H did not reconcile LAS data with billed invoices, and there are no standard review procedures for invoices.

findings.plain: The system has not fully met state regulatory requirements. It failed to perform required annual assessments of limited English proficiency needs for 2019 through 2023, workers at Bellevue Hospital missed 4,061 required annual training sessions and no training records were provided for Woodhull and Harlem hospitals.
findings.quote: H+H failed to perform required annual LEP needs assessments for years 2019–2023

findings.plain: There is no centralized list of qualified in-house interpreters and bilingual staff, and lists at individual facilities were missing or outdated. Some bilingual staff interpretation was never reported in the data.
findings.quote: H+H lacks a centralized list of qualified in-house interpreters and bilingual staff.

findings.plain: Twenty-nine facilities or programs had no language access policies at all, and at the 21 that did, policies did not always match systemwide guidelines or actual practice.
findings.quote: We found 29 facilities/programs had no LAS policies.

findings.plain: Auditors found no assurance that translations of medical records, after-visit summaries and discharge papers are managed and tracked for accuracy, and the system could not confirm that patient calls lasting 2 hours were reviewed.
findings.quote: We have no assurance that H+H manages and tracks translations of patient medical records, after-visit summaries, and discharge papers into different languages

findings.plain: Bilingual state auditors made anonymous, unannounced calls and visits and hit barriers: staff who did not try to connect them to an interpreter, hard-to-navigate automated phone systems and no language access through the system's street outreach mobile units.
findings.quote: Instances where H+H staff did not attempt to connect callers to an interpreter or to provide information.

findings.plain: Contract payments were poorly managed. The system overpaid language vendors $215,879 between January 2022 and June 2024, including phone interpretation billed at higher video rates, and would have saved $8,247,840 over two fiscal years by negotiating or using vendors with lower per-minute rates.
findings.quote: H+H made $215,879 in overpayments to vendors for LAS.

Comply with the state hospital regulation, including conducting annual assessments of limited English proficiency needs and ensuring staff complete all annual trainings.
Prepare and maintain centralized and facility-level lists of in-house interpreters and bilingual staff.
Make sure every facility and program develops language access policies or updates existing ones to match systemwide guidelines.
Ensure information in patient records is accurately translated into various languages.
Review and keep documentation for patient calls lasting over 2 hours.

audits.auditor: Center for New York City Affairs
audits.title: Dignified Pay for Quality Care: What New York’s Family Child Care Providers Need to Thrive
audits.plain_title: What New York City's home-based child care providers earn
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for New York City Affairs at The New School on the finances and working conditions of licensed home-based child care providers in New York City. It draws on a survey of 465 family child care (FCC) and group family child care (GFCC) providers and follow-up focus groups with 59 of them.
audits.background: Family child care and group family child care providers are small business owners and independent contractors who look after children in their own homes, and they are part of the city's publicly subsidized early care and education (ECE) system. Since Pre-K launched in 2014 the city has lost 1,400 of these businesses.

findings.plain: Counting only the hours their programs are open, the median family child care provider earned $7.33 an hour in 2023 and the median group family child care provider earned $5.98. The minimum wage that year was $15.
findings.quote: provider earned $7.33 and $5.98 per hour,

audits.auditor: Advocates for Children of New York
audits.title: Reconnecting to Opportunity: Advancing Educational Equity for Court-Involved Students
audits.plain_title: Schooling for young people in and leaving city detention
audits.what_they_audited: A policy brief from Advocates for Children of New York reviewing the first two years of city data on schooling for young people held in juvenile detention or placement. It covers who attends Passages Academy, the school that serves them, what instruction they receive and what happens when they return to a community school.
audits.background: A December 2023 City Council law requires New York City Public Schools and the city Administration for Children's Services to report each year on educational programming for young people in juvenile detention or placement. All students in those settings are taught through Passages Academy, a public school run by District 79, the citywide district for alternative schools and programs.

findings.plain: Students held in detention or placement are far more likely than other city secondary students to be classified as having a disability, especially an emotional disability.
findings.quote: Compared to all New York City students in grades 7–12, youth in juvenile detention or placement in 2023–24 and 2024–25 were almost twice as likely to have learning disabilities and more than 17 times as likely to be labeled as students with emotional disabilities.

findings.plain: Black students, boys, students with individualized education programs and students in foster care make up much larger shares of the Passages population than of the school system overall.
findings.quote: 61.6% were Black, though Black students comprised only a quarter of overall enrollment.

findings.plain: Reading and math screening scores on entry to Passages were far below grade level for at least half of the students tested.
findings.quote: At least half of students scored at the fifth percentile or below in reading upon entering Passages in 2023–24, meaning they performed worse than 95% of their grade-level peers; in 2024–25, at least half of students were reading at the twelfth percentile or below upon enrollment.

findings.plain: Many students with disabilities waited longer than the law allows for the plan that sets out the special education services they are to receive.
findings.quote: a total 16.5% of students with IEPs did not receive a SEP within a month of enrolling at Passages Academy

findings.plain: Nearly a quarter of students learning English received no English as a new language instruction while in city custody.
findings.quote: of the 216 ELLs who were enrolled during the 2023–24 and 2024–25 school years, nearly a quarter (23.6%) received no English as a New Language (ENL)

findings.plain: Students who returned to a community school after release attended less than half the time, with rates lowest for the oldest students.
findings.quote: In 2023–24, the median attendance rate for the 227 students for whom data are available was just 49%, meaning that at least half of these young people missed more days of school than they attended

findings.plain: The city left several data points required by the reporting law out of its published reports, without explaining the omissions.
findings.quote: The published report provides no explanation for why any such data were omitted.

audits.agency: New York City Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings
audits.what_they_audited: A letter report on whether the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings, the city's central administrative law court, provides the interpretation and translation services required by city and state language access laws. The scope ran from January 1, 2018 through October 30, 2025.
audits.background: Nearly one-half of all New Yorkers speak a language other than English at home and almost 25% are not proficient in English. Local Law 30 of 2017 requires city agencies that serve the public to provide language services in 10 designated citywide languages and to adopt a language access implementation plan.

findings.plain: The agency complies with the website translation, document translation and interpretation standards set by the relevant laws and guidelines.
findings.quote: OATH complies with the website translation, document translation, and in-person and telephonic interpretation standards prescribed by relevant laws, standards, and guidelines

findings.plain: Services generally meet the needs of residents who prefer languages other than English, who have the same access to the agency's services as English speakers.
findings.quote: the NELP population has the same access to government services as the English-speaking population

findings.plain: Its language access plan contains every key element required by Local Law 30, including a designated coordinator, telephone interpretation in over 100 languages, translated documents, staff training and complaint monitoring.
findings.quote: The LAIP contained all key aspects required by Local Law 30

findings.plain: Contracted vendors cover the required languages. The interpretation vendor offers over 250 languages and the translation vendors over 160, including the designated citywide and temporary languages.
findings.quote: Language Line can provide interpretation in over 250 languages including the designated citywide languages

findings.plain: The agency tells the public that free language services are available through signs in its offices, notices on its website and messages on its help line, and its website translates into the required languages.
findings.quote: OATH informs the public of the availability of free language access services by posting signs in conspicuous locations

audits.auditor: Data Collaborative for Justice at John Jay College
audits.title: Rikers Island and Mental Health: Pathways Toward Community-Based Diversion and Jail Population Reduction
audits.plain_title: Mental health needs at Rikers and ways to divert people
audits.what_they_audited: A research and policy brief from the Data Collaborative for Justice at John Jay College and the Katal Center for Equity, Health, and Justice presenting current data on mental health needs in the New York City jails, four case studies and 15 policy proposals for diverting people into community-based treatment.
audits.background: The City Council voted in 2019 to close the jails on Rikers Island and build smaller jails in four boroughs, and later set a legal deadline of August 31, 2027. The replacement jails plus more than 300 secure hospital beds are planned to hold about 4,200 people a day, while the current jail population is close to 7,000.

findings.plain: The share of people in the city jails receiving mental health services and the share with a serious mental illness both rose between 2020 and 2025.
findings.quote: the fraction of the jail population receiving mental health services climbed from 44% to 60%,6 and the fraction diagnosed with a serious mental illness rose from 17% to 22%

findings.plain: The authors describe Rikers as the city's largest mental health facility.
findings.quote: Today, Rikers is the largest mental health facility in New York City and among the largest in the country.

findings.plain: Most people in the jails are held before trial, and Black New Yorkers make up a much larger share of the jail population than of the city's population.
findings.quote: Currently, close to 7,000 people are held in the City’s jails, of whom 85% have been detained before trial. Black people make up 58% of the jail population, compared to 23% of the City’s general population.

findings.plain: Missed medical appointments in the jails have risen sharply since 2020.
findings.quote: In September 2025, there were 15,823 missed medical appointments compared to 3,626 in September 2020.

findings.plain: People flagged for mental health needs are held longer than other people in the jails.
findings.quote: people in the latest jail population needing mental health services had been held for 281 days, compared to 212 days for people not needing such services

findings.plain: Women in the jails need mental health services at a higher rate than men.
findings.quote: Of close to 500 women jailed at Rikers as of October 2025, 87% have needed mental health services, compared to 58% of men.

findings.plain: The city's mental health courts serve a small fraction of arraigned cases.
findings.quote: New York City’s mental health courts, which enrolled less than 360 participants (representing 0.2% of arraigned cases) in 2023

audits.title: Review of the New York City Police Department’s Body-Worn Camera Program
audits.plain_title: Police body camera footage is slow to reach the public
audits.what_they_audited: A review, rather than a full audit, of the police department's body-worn camera program: how the department handles public records requests for footage, whether officers activate cameras as required and how the program is overseen. The scope ran from January 1, 2020 through May 21, 2025.
audits.background: The 2013 federal court settlement in Floyd v. City of New York required the police department to adopt body-worn cameras to record stops and other encounters, with a federal monitor overseeing the reforms. The camera program began in April 2017 and most officers had cameras by August 2019.

findings.plain: Footage requests moved slowly. The department took an average of 133 business days to grant or deny Freedom of Information Law requests for camera footage, missed its own 95-day goal more than half the time and took as long as four years in one case.
findings.quote: On average, NYPD took 133 business days to grant or deny FOIL requests during the review period.

findings.plain: Denials rarely held up. 97% of appeals of denied footage requests were granted, and 12 of 13 decided court challenges ended with the department providing footage or being ordered to provide it.
findings.quote: NYPD’s FOIL appeal process resulted in production of BWC footage 97% of the time, and footage was provided after being challenged in court 92% of the time.

findings.plain: Footage was often missing or incomplete. In the department's own reviews of dispatched 911 calls, 36% of review determinations had no video on file, and where video existed, cameras were activated late or shut off early 18% of the time.
findings.quote: 4,319 (36%) of 12,116 review determinations had no corresponding video on file

findings.plain: Required internal checks were skipped. Precincts could not produce monthly self-inspections of camera activation for more than half of the months sampled, and nobody independently reviews the inspections that are done.
findings.quote: NYPD was unable to provide Self-Inspections for 87—more than half—of the requested months.

findings.plain: Department supervisors and the federal monitor reach very different conclusions about stops. Internal reviews found officers applied the law appropriately over 98% of the time, while the monitor found 11% to 14% of reviewed stops unconstitutional in 2020 through 2023.
findings.quote: NYPD supervisors do not assess stops correctly

findings.plain: Use-of-force paperwork is not ensured. In a sample of 25 substantiated excessive force complaints, the department acknowledged a Threat, Resistance, or Injury Report was required in 17 cases, but four of those had none.
findings.quote: for four (24%) of the 17 incidents, a TRI Report was not prepared

findings.plain: The department does not aggregate camera data or analyze trends, even though precincts with poor camera compliance overlapped with precincts with above-average substantiated excessive force allegations.
findings.quote: NYPD does not aggregate data or perform trend analyses of its Self-Inspections and ICAD reviews

audits.title: Dollars, Sense, and the 2025 Mayoral Election: Affordability, Tax Policy, and the Future of New York
audits.plain_title: A brief on city incomes, poverty and tax policy
audits.what_they_audited: A policy brief by James A. Parrott of the Center for New York City Affairs at The New School examining New York City economic trends since 2019 and two policies raised in the 2025 mayoral race: raising the minimum wage and raising city income taxes on millionaires.
audits.background: The brief was written during the 2025 mayoral campaign, in which affordability was a central issue. Part of it responds to an August 2025 Citizens Budget Commission report on New York's shrinking share of the nation's millionaires.

findings.plain: Inflation-adjusted median household income in New York City fell 4.9 percent between 2019 and 2024, the steepest drop among the nation's 10 largest cities, while nationally median household income rose slightly.
findings.quote: a sharp 4.9 percent falloff in real median household income

findings.plain: Poverty rose in New York City from 16 to 18 percent between 2019 and 2024 and child poverty rose from 22.2 percent to 24.2 percent, while poverty fell nationally over the same period.
findings.quote: it rose from 16 to 18 percent in New York City

findings.plain: The number of New York City residents receiving cash public assistance rose 85 percent between July 2019 and July 2025, the highest level this century.
findings.quote: rocketed upward by 85 percent, reaching

findings.plain: Income is heavily concentrated at the top. In 2022 city millionaires were 0.88 percent of all tax filers, held 35.3 percent of adjusted gross income and paid 40 percent of city income taxes.
findings.quote: paid 40 percent of city income taxes.

findings.plain: The city's personal income tax supplies only 19 percent of total city taxes, while property and sales taxes supply nearly three times that share. In fiscal 2022 the average marginal city income tax rate for a $60,000 household was close to the rate for a millionaire household.
findings.quote: the New York City PIT contributes only 19 percent of total city taxes.

findings.plain: Census data put New York City's Gini coefficient, a measure of income inequality, at 0.5563 in 2024, the highest among the 10 largest cities and above the national figure of 0.4809.
findings.quote: 0.5563, considerably higher than the 0.4809 Gini for the U.S. overall.

findings.plain: The average cost of child care for infants and toddlers in city family-based settings rose 79 percent between 2019 and 2024, about four times the metro area inflation rate.
findings.quote: jumped by 79 percent

findings.plain: The brief argues that New York's falling share of national millionaires tracks its slower population, labor force and economic growth, and that counting nonresident millionaire taxpayers who work in New York would put the state's share above California's.
findings.quote: a level that would boost New York’s share of the national total to 18.7 percent
