audits.title: How to Restore Public Trust and Clean City Hall: Proposals for the Next Administration
audits.plain_title: Ethics and transparency proposals for the next mayor
audits.what_they_audited: A report from Citizens Union setting out 17 proposals for the incoming mayoral administration on appointments, lobbying, oversight agencies, transparency and relations with the City Council.
audits.background: Citizens Union is a good government group that has worked on ethics, campaign finance and transparency in New York City for more than a century. The report was published ahead of the next mayor taking office on January 1, 2026.

findings.plain: The report says senior appointments under the outgoing administration reflected favoritism rather than merit, pointing to the attempted appointment of the mayor's brother as deputy police commissioner and to top officials caught up in corruption investigations.
findings.quote: appointment of the mayor’s brother as Deputy Police Commissioner

findings.plain: Incoming public servants must sever ties and divest from companies doing business with the city, but are not required to recuse themselves from matters involving former business partners, clients or employers.
findings.quote: clients, or employers

findings.plain: Lobbying oversight sits in the City Clerk's Lobbying Bureau, a small unit that reports to the City Council, the body being lobbied. The report says the Conflicts of Interest Board is a better fit.
findings.quote: reports to the City Council—the very body being lobbied

findings.plain: Oversight agencies have lost capacity. Since 2019 the Department of Investigation has lost more than a quarter of its employees and Conflicts of Interest Board staffing is down 16 percent, and the Civilian Complaint Review Board closed 1,440 complaints without full review.
findings.quote: closed 1,440 complaints without full review.

findings.plain: Records requests are slow, with some agencies averaging more than 400 days to respond to a Freedom of Information Law request.
findings.quote: with some agencies taking over 400 days on average to respond.

findings.plain: The report says press access has narrowed, citing fewer briefings, encrypted police radio channels, reporters barred from press conferences and attempts to move reporters out of City Hall and 1 Police Plaza.
findings.quote: briefings, encrypting police radio channels, barring reporters from press conferences

findings.plain: The report says recent mayors have used their control of the Charter Revision Commission to remove ballot questions proposed by the City Council or by citizens, and that the city has no clear mechanism to remove a mayor for serious misconduct.
findings.quote: Commission to remove ballot questions proposed by the City Council or citizens

audits.title: Why Am I Getting Electioneering Mailers from the City Council? An Explainer
audits.plain_title: Explainer on Council mailers about the 2025 ballot questions
audits.what_they_audited: An explainer from Citizens Union setting out what New York City law says about using public money to campaign on ballot questions, written in the context of the City Council's campaign against three housing-related proposals on the November 2025 ballot.
audits.background: The 2025 Charter Revision Commission put four housing and land use proposals on the November 2025 ballot. The Council campaigned against three of them with mailers, a website, digital ads, community board presentations, rallies and press conferences.

findings.plain: The Council's campaign against ballot questions 2, 3 and 4 included mailers to thousands of households, a website and social media toolkit, digital ads, community board presentations and public rallies. Media reports put the mailer spending at up to $2 million.
findings.quote: Media reports suggest the Council paid up to $2 million to send out those mailers.

findings.plain: Section 1136.1 of the City Charter bars public servants from using government funds or resources for a public communication containing an electioneering message, defined as a statement designed to urge the public to support or oppose a referendum question. The ban covers all elected officials, officers and city employees.
findings.quote: governmental funds or resources for a public communication that contains an electioneering message

findings.plain: The Council says its materials are meant to educate the public rather than advocate a result, and the mailers avoid phrases such as vote against, defeat or reject. Citizens Union writes that taken at face value the materials are intended to urge opposition.
findings.quote: Taken at face-value these materials are clearly intended to urge the public to oppose the ballot questions.

findings.plain: Three city bodies could in principle regulate this activity but none has stepped in. The Campaign Finance Board regulates candidate campaigns and independent expenditures rather than government communications, and Department of Investigation inquiries are confidential.
findings.quote: There are a few, but none have stepped in to regulate this activity:

findings.plain: The Conflicts of Interest Board can interpret and enforce only Chapter 68 of the City Charter, while the ballot question electioneering ban sits in Chapter 49. Press reports say the board advised the Council that the Chapter 68 rule applies only to campaigns involving candidates or parties.
findings.quote: while the explicit ban on ballot question electioneering appears in Chapter 49 of the City Charter.

findings.plain: The Council ran a similar campaign against ballot questions from a prior Charter Revision Commission in 2024, and a Council member filed a complaint with the Department of Investigation alleging a violation of the electioneering law.
findings.quote: In 2024, the City Council ran a similar campaign against ballot questions proposed by a prior Charter Revision Commission.

findings.plain: Intentional or knowing violations of the electioneering ban are punishable as misdemeanors under the Charter.
findings.quote: intentional or knowing violations of the electioneering ban are punishable as misdemeanors

numbers.label: Reported Council spending on the mailers
City Charter section banning electioneering messages

recommendations: Amend the City Charter either to let the Conflicts of Interest Board enforce ethics provisions outside Chapter 68 or to move the electioneering ban into Chapter 68 so the board can enforce it directly.

rec_display.text: Amend the City Charter either to let the Conflicts of Interest Board enforce ethics provisions outside Chapter 68 or to move the electioneering ban into Chapter 68 so the board can enforce it directly.

audits.title: Twenty-Seventh Report of the Independent Monitor (Corrected): Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Stop and frisk compliance snapshot for late 2024
audits.what_they_audited: A visual "compliance snapshot" updating the monitor's Twenty-Fourth Report on the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) compliance with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, covering the fourth quarter of 2024. This summary uses the corrected version of the report, filed November 19, 2025.
audits.background: The report covers the fourth quarter of 2024 and in several places compares that quarter to the fourth quarter of 2023. It draws on the monitor team's audits of 100 stop reports per month and 225 body-worn camera videos per quarter, plus the NYPD Quality Assurance Section's own audits.

findings.plain: In the fourth quarter of 2024, the monitor's audits found 89% of reported stops, 71% of frisks and 73% of searches lawful, with little if any improvement compared to a year earlier.
findings.quote: In the fourth quarter of 2024, 89% of stops, 71% of frisks, and 73% of searches were assessed as lawful.

findings.plain: Self-initiated activity remained the weak spot. While 96% of radio run stops and 100% of stops based on complainant information were lawful, only 81% of self-initiated stops were, along with just 58% of frisks and 60% of searches during self-initiated stops.
findings.quote: 81% of self-initiated stops were lawful, showing no change from the fourth quarter of 2023.

findings.plain: Most commands fell short of an 85% compliance rate: the department's own audits found 61% of the NYPD's 98 commands below that bar for frisks and 69% below it for searches.
findings.quote: 61% of NYPD’s 98 commands

findings.plain: Supervisors still approved nearly everything. The monitor found 11% of stops, 29% of frisks and 27% of searches unlawful in the quarter, while reviewing supervisors flagged only 1% of stops, 1% of frisks and 3% of searches.
findings.quote: approved close to 100% of all stops, frisks, and searches and barely identified any as unlawful.

findings.plain: Underreporting improved slightly but persisted: officers failed to complete stop reports for 28% of stops identified in the monitor's audit, down from 37% in the fourth quarter of 2023.
findings.quote: 28% of stops identified in the audit.

findings.plain: Housing Bureau officers improved markedly: 90% of their stops, 81% of frisks and 79% of searches were lawful in the quarter, and trespass arrests showed 96% compliance on the reason to approach and 100% on probable cause.
findings.quote: 90% of stops, 81% of frisks, and 79% of searches were assessed as lawful

recommendations: The report makes no new formal recommendations.

audits.title: Audit on the Effectiveness of the Mayor’s Office of Housing Recovery Operations’ Build It Back Program
audits.plain_title: How well Build It Back rebuilt homes after Hurricane Sandy
audits.agency: Mayor's Office of Housing Recovery Operations
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Build It Back program run by the Mayor's Office of Housing Recovery Operations (HRO) achieved its goal of helping property owners affected by Hurricane Sandy repair, rebuild or relocate, and whether it made Sandy-affected New Yorkers and communities safer and more resilient.
audits.background: Hurricane Sandy damaged or destroyed over 17,000 homes in New York City in October 2012, and the city created HRO to coordinate recovery. HRO launched Build It Back in June 2013, with $2.3 billion in federal Community Development Block Grant Disaster Recovery funding allocated for the single-family program and a stated goal of finishing construction by the end of 2016.

findings.plain: The program ultimately served only about a third of the people who applied. Of 22,436 homeowners who applied, 8,131 were served, even though only a small share were found ineligible.
findings.quote: HRO served 36% of those applicants who initially applied to participate in the program, despite excluding only a small percentage based on eligibility.

findings.plain: Processing was slow. It took HRO about two years on average to process a single application and roughly six more months to start construction.
findings.quote: HRO took two years on average to process a single application and six more months to initiate construction.

findings.plain: The program missed its own deadline. Nearly 1,600 homes, about 40 percent, were not finished by the end-of-2016 target, and 565 homes had not even begun construction by then. The last home was finished in February 2023, more than a decade after the storm.
findings.quote: HRO established a construction completion deadline of 2016, but nearly 1,600 (40.1%) homes were not completed by this time.

findings.plain: Start to finish, projects took about three years on average from the day a homeowner applied to the day construction was done, with the longest taking almost a decade.
findings.quote: On average, construction projects took three years to complete from the date an application was submitted to the date construction finished.

findings.plain: Deadline policies and an acceleration initiative introduced in 2016 cut the time to start construction from 217 days to 104 days on average, but the time to complete construction rose from 164 days to 283 days, so overall completion times did not improve.
findings.quote: the introduction of new policies and initiatives also failed to reduce overall completion times.

findings.plain: Slow timelines drove people away and kept others out of their homes. 11,140 applicants withdrew or were withdrawn, and of the 860 applicants who were temporarily relocated during construction, 627 were displaced longer than the program's 14-month limit, for 24 months on average, with 15 homeowners displaced for over four years.
findings.quote: Of the 860 applicants who were temporarily relocated, 627 were displaced from their homes for longer than 14 months.

findings.plain: HRO's controls were weak. It did not consistently track contract completion terms in its case management system, and it had no timeframe or deadline policies in place when the program started, which likely contributed to delays.
findings.quote: HRO did not ensure that TPA and Home Improvement Contract terms were consistently and accurately tracked in CMS.

recommendations: For future disaster recovery programs, document timeframes and deadlines in policies and procedures at the start so staff and contractors can monitor application processing and construction and keep them on schedule.
Establish and track performance indicators in the recordkeeping system, including timeliness measures for the contractors handling application processing and construction management.
audits.agency_response: HRO acknowledged that Build It Back encountered significant implementation challenges and agreed with both recommendations, saying it was establishing a new standard for compliance and audit readiness for future disaster recovery programs.

audits.title: Update on NYPD's Implementation of DOI's 2023 Criminal Group Database Recommendations
audits.plain_title: Gang database reforms are half done, so watchdog adds 13 more
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation's (DOI) Office of the Inspector General for the New York City Police Department (OIG-NYPD) assessed how the NYPD has implemented recommendations from OIG-NYPD's 2023 report on the Criminal Group Database (CGD), reviewing database entries and paperwork for a sample of 531 individuals.
audits.background: OIG-NYPD's 2023 report on the gang database made 17 recommendations, of which NYPD accepted 11, rejected five and placed one under consideration. As of December 2022 the database held 16,141 people, 98% of them male, identified as Black or Hispanic and under 42.

findings.plain: The database shrank 39% between December 2022 and October 2025, from 16,141 people to 8,563, while its demographics stayed largely the same: predominantly Black and Hispanic men aged 18 to 34.
findings.quote:
as of October 2025, the numbers had 
declined by 39%, to 8,563.

findings.plain: Of the eight accepted recommendations reviewed in depth, four were fully implemented and four partially implemented. NYPD updated its policies in October 2023 consistent with the accepted recommendations, though gaps remain.
findings.quote: finding four have been fully implemented and four partially implemented.

findings.plain: Renewals and deactivations still are not reviewed by a supervisor or subject to a multilevel review process, contrary to a recommendation NYPD accepted in 2023.
findings.quote:
the renewal and deactivations are not 
reviewed by a supervisor or otherwise subject to a multilevel review process

findings.plain: Despite a new parental notification process for minors added to the database, the department failed to complete any notifications; NYPD says a new procedure putting the duty on the nominating detective is still pending.
findings.quote:
Despite the updated IUP and the Chief of Detectives Memorandum, the Department failed to 
complete any notifications.

findings.plain: Review delays got worse: at least 151 entries, including 48 minors, were between six and more than 60 months past due for renewal or deactivation review. After OIG-NYPD flagged the delays, NYPD says the maximum is now eight days.
findings.quote:
delays were even 
longer with at least 151 entries (48 minors and 103 adults) between 6 and 60+ months past due

findings.plain: A vendor coding error wrongly stretched the review period from two years to three for people added at 16 or 17 who turned 18 before their review; 48 of 59 minors reviewed were delayed six to 60 months. NYPD says the error is corrected.
findings.quote:
the automated review system incorrectly extended the review time from two years to three years if a 
person was activated at 16 or 17

findings.plain: Activation paperwork improved but some officers filled forms out incorrectly, including listing themselves as one of the two required independent sources, and source justifications were often boilerplate with no specific supporting information.
findings.quote:
there wer e reporting 
officers who listed themselves as one of the two sources.

recommendations: Ensure all uniformed personnel authorized to nominate people into the database are trained on the Impact and Use Policy and the Chief of Detectives Memorandum.
Require the two independent reliable sources to give substantive explanations for their belief in an individual's criminal group membership and document those explanations on activation forms.
Clarify that the two independent sources must be different from the reporting officer.
Update the Impact and Use Policy to mirror the detailed guidelines in the Chief of Detectives Memorandum.
Establish a multilevel review process for renewals with supervisor sign-off on all renewal forms, as previously recommended and accepted, and list the required supporting documentation.
Require the nominating detective to notify a juvenile's parent or guardian within 60 days of activation into the database.
Ensure renewal and activation forms include a required field with the individual's next review date.
Create a written internal audit requirement to verify that parental notifications for minors are made, documented and recorded in a new database column.
Confirm whether anyone activated at 16 or 17 went more than two years without review because of the coding error, and review whether they should be renewed or deactivated.
Ensure supporting documentation is included for all renewals.

Review individuals renewed based on an arrest every six months to make sure renewals do not rest on arrests that were later sealed, at minimum exploring whether such an audit is feasible.
Collect, analyze and publish data annually on the number of entries added, renewed and deactivated.
audits.agency_response: NYPD promptly moved to reduce review backlogs when OIG-NYPD flagged them, saying the maximum delay is now eight days, corrected the vendor coding error and plans to shift parental notification duties to nominating detectives and strip sealed-arrest details from database forms.

Review individuals renewed based on an arrest every six months to make sure renewals do not rest on arrests that were later sealed, at minimum exploring whether such an audit is feasible.
Collect, analyze and publish data annually on the number of entries added, renewed and deactivated.

audits.title: Twenty-Sixth Report of the Independent Monitor: The NYPD's Accountability Efforts
audits.plain_title: Few consequences for officers who made unlawful stops
audits.what_they_audited: The effectiveness of the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) internal accountability systems for unconstitutional stops, frisks and searches: how commands responded to audits by the department's Quality Assurance Section (QAS), whether the court-ordered Early Intervention Program (EIP) changed officer behavior and how the department's ComplianceStat meetings held commanders accountable.
audits.background: Accountability for unconstitutional stops is key to compliance with the federal court's orders in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York. Each quarter QAS audits a sample of stop reports from every command, the court ordered an early warning system in 2020 to flag at-risk officers and the department launched ComplianceStat meetings in January 2024 to question borough and command staff on compliance.

findings.plain: There was little accountability for unconstitutional policing in 2024. Over the four quarters reviewed, QAS identified 4,458 improper stops, frisks or searches, but only eight officers received a Command Discipline and 110 got a negative entry through the Cop's Rapid Assessment Feedback Tool (CRAFT), the lowest sanction. In the other 97.5% of incidents the officer was instructed, trained or nothing was done.
findings.quote: Out of these 4,458 incidents, eight officers were given CDs and 110 officers were issued a

findings.plain: Commands responded to audit findings with training and instruction even for repeat offenders. In the 46 Precinct, where only 78% of audited stops, 57% of frisks and 60% of searches were lawful, one officer was instructed or referred for training 14 times in 12 months with no improvement, and nothing more severe was ever reported.
findings.quote: ...was instructed or referred for training 14 times...

findings.plain: The Early Intervention Program has not worked. Interventions directed by the Early Intervention Committee were minimal, follow-up was rare and officer behavior did not change.
findings.quote: EIP interventions did not impact officer behavior...

findings.plain: Officers flagged by the intervention program kept failing to document stops. For ten officers reviewed from the first quarter of 2024, the monitor found that of 43 encounters that should have had stop reports, only 17 did, leaving 60.5% of stops without reports.
findings.quote: leaving a staggering 60.5% of stops missing reports.

findings.plain: ComplianceStat pressure worked when sustained. Patrol Borough Brooklyn South was called in three times in four months for poor performance; by the third meeting an intensive borough effort had cut potentially undocumented encounters to 1% of audited videos, a precinct commander and two other supervisors were removed and one command's Neighborhood Safety Team was disbanded.
findings.quote: ...in another command, the NST team was disbanded.

findings.plain: At later ComplianceStat meetings covering Manhattan and Brooklyn North patrol boroughs, several borough and command executives were unprepared and could not answer basic questions about their specialized teams. Department leadership responded by disbanding the Brooklyn North Public Safety Team, relieving the executive responsible for compliance oversight and reassigning personnel.
findings.quote: ...command executives were unprepared for the meetings and unable to answer questions

Command Disciplines issued for those incidents

recommendations: Recognize that discipline and/or reassignment, for both officers and supervisors, may be necessary to address poor performance.
Hold supervisors accountable for identifying the unlawful actions of officers under their command.

Give the Early Intervention Program a strategic approach at the command level: commanders presenting to the committee should address not just the individual officer but what is being done to prevent other officers from engaging in triggering events.
Track the results of Early Intervention Program interventions and conduct an evaluation of the program.
audits.agency_response: The NYPD told the monitor it will begin examining how commands respond to Quality Assurance Section audits so officers with repeat deficiencies are not simply given the same training, and it acknowledged the monitor's concerns about the Early Intervention Program and is implementing new procedures. The police commissioner also issued a February 5, 2025 memorandum on discipline for repeated or intentional violations in connection with Level 3 stops.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor found meaningful accountability for unconstitutional stops, frisks and searches largely absent in 2024, with training substituted for discipline, but called the department's newer systems such as ComplianceStat and a revamped Early Intervention Program hopeful signs while saying it is too early to tell whether they will produce measurable improvement.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Office of the New York City Public Advocate’s Provision of Language Access Services
audits.plain_title: Does the public advocate serve New Yorkers in their languages?
audits.agency: Office of the New York City Public Advocate
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Office of the Public Advocate (PAO) provides services to people with a Non-English Language Preference (NELP) in the languages required by law, whether those services meet the NELP population's needs and whether NELP residents get the same access to government services as English speakers.
audits.background: Nearly half of all New Yorkers speak a language other than English at home and almost 25% of city residents aged five and over are not proficient in English. Local Law 30 of 2017 requires city agencies that provide direct public services to designate a Language Access Coordinator and develop a Language Access Implementation Plan.

findings.plain: The office generally provides the required language services, contracting with vendors for telephonic interpretation in over 240 languages and document translation in over 100 languages, and NELP residents generally get the same access as English speakers.
findings.quote: The language access services provided by PAO generally meet the needs of the Non-English Language Preference (NELP) population as intended, and the NELP population generally has the same access to government services as the English-speaking population.

findings.plain: The office was not fully compliant with Local Law 30. Its website did not say free language services were available and did not list the name and title of its Language Access Coordinator.
findings.quote: PAO’s website did not indicate whether the agency provides free language access services...

findings.plain: The reports the office publishes on its website, its most commonly distributed documents, could not be translated into the city's top 10 non-English languages. Only the report summaries could be translated, and the site did not tell visitors that translations were available on request.
findings.quote: they are not translatable documents—only the report summaries can be translated

findings.plain: The office had no Language Access Implementation Plan as the law requires. Its existing procedures left out most key elements, including annual staff training, emergency preparedness and a process for handling language access complaints.
findings.quote: PAO had not created or implemented an LAIP in compliance with LL30 prior to this audit.

findings.plain: When auditors first tested the website's translation feature in March 2025, the language dropdown menu showed blank options. The office fixed the bug promptly after being told, and a retest in April 2025 found it working.
findings.quote: the dropdown menu was not functioning properly, with language options appearing blank

findings.plain: By the August 2025 exit conference the office had made fixes, including creating a Language Access Implementation Plan, updating its website and documenting training for 12 staff members, and auditors assessed that it is now in compliance with Local Law 30.
findings.quote: Auditors confirmed that the implementations had been made and assessed that PAO is now in compliance with Local Law 30.

numbers.label: City residents aged five and over not proficient in English
Languages covered by the office's interpretation vendor
Languages the website translation feature can handle
Staff with documented language training by August 2025

recommendations: Periodically test website features to make sure they work as intended.
Going forward, make sure all frontline and managerial staff get annual language access training as Local Law 30 requires, and keep documentation such as attendance sheets and training materials.

Continue publishing reports directly on the website so the translation feature can translate them in full, or if that is not feasible, post a notice that published reports can be translated on request.
Post the newly created Language Access Implementation Plan in a conspicuous spot on the website.
Continue to keep the Language Access Coordinator's name and title posted on the website as required.

audits.title: College Readiness (Follow-Up)
audits.plain_title: Checkup on how city schools prepare students for college
audits.what_they_audited: How far New York City Public Schools has gone in carrying out the four recommendations from a 2022 state audit of how well the school system prepares students for college.
audits.background: New York City Public Schools, the nation's largest school system, served about 900,000 students in the 2023-24 school year. The initial audit found that in a cohort of 71,210 students expected to graduate by August 2019, as many as 23% did not graduate on time, 38% did not persist in college for 6 months after enrolling and 45% of a 291-student sample were not college ready.

findings.plain: The school system has made significant progress since the initial audit. All four of the original recommendations have been implemented.
findings.quote: Of the initial report’s four audit recommendations, all four have been implemented.

findings.plain: Graduation rates still outpace college readiness. In 2024, 83% of high school students citywide graduated while only 52% were considered college ready, and the system has since added a grade point average component and a career component to its readiness metric.
findings.quote: In 2024, 83% of high school students citywide graduated, while only 52% were considered college ready.

numbers.label: High school students citywide who graduated in 2024
Students considered college ready in 2024

recommendations: The report makes no formal recommendations.
audits.implementation_note: Of the four recommendations in the 2022 audit, the follow-up found all four implemented.

audits.title: Follow-Up Audit on the Equal Employment Practices Commission’s Compliance with Its Charter Mandate to Audit City Agencies
audits.plain_title: Did the equal employment watchdog fix its audit lapses?
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Equal Employment Practices Commission (EEPC) implemented the three recommendations from a 2020 audit and whether it is now meeting its City Charter mandate to audit every city agency's equal employment practices at least once every four years.
audits.background: EEPC is an independent oversight body that audits, reviews and monitors the equal employment practices of New York City government. The 2020 audit found EEPC had failed to audit 27 of the 141 city agencies under its jurisdiction during calendar years 2013 through 2016 and had erroneously claimed in annual reports that it met its mandate.

findings.plain: EEPC carried out all three recommendations from the 2020 audit, even though it had disagreed with two of them and never responded to the third.
findings.quote: the Equal Employment Practices Commission (EEPC) implemented all three recommendations made in the initial audit, despite its stated disagreement with two and non-response to the third

findings.plain: The commission caught up on its backlog and is meeting its mandate. It audited the 27 agencies it had skipped, completed audits of all 143 agencies under its jurisdiction for the 2018 to 2021 cycle and is on track to meet the mandate for the 2022 to 2025 cycle.
findings.quote: EEPC subsequently audited and evaluated the 27 City agencies that it had not audited during CYs 2013 through 2016; that it met its Charter mandate for the 2018–2021 cycle

findings.plain: The commission also resolved a long-running dispute over when an audit counts as done. At the auditors' urging it asked the city's Law Department, which said an audit can reasonably be considered complete when EEPC issues its final determination to an agency.
findings.quote: the Law Department stated that it was reasonable to interpret an audit as being completed upon EEPC’s issuance of an FD to an agency

findings.plain: In the current cycle EEPC issued 395 corrective actions to agencies whose equal employment programs fell short, and follow-up records showed 353 of them, or 89 percent, were satisfactorily implemented.
findings.quote: determined that 353 (89%) of the 395 CAs were satisfactorily implemented

findings.plain: A new problem: EEPC's website is badly out of date. None of the 124 final determinations auditors reviewed for the 2022 to 2025 cycle were posted online, and 10 of 40 sampled from the 2018 to 2021 cycle were also missing, undermining transparency.
findings.quote: none of the 124 FDs reviewed by the auditors for the 2022–2025 quadrennial cycle have been posted

findings.plain: Another new problem: the commission has no written policies or procedures for key audit practices, including how to create an audit plan or how to document policy changes such as its new definition of a completed audit.
findings.quote: There are no written policies or procedures that provide step-by-step instructions on how to create an audit plan

numbers.label: Previously skipped agencies that EEPC later audited
Final determinations issued in the 2018-2021 cycle
Corrective actions issued to agencies in the current cycle
Corrective actions satisfactorily implemented
Recent final determinations reviewed, none posted online

recommendations: Establish written procedures on when city agency audits open and close, in line with the Law Department's opinion.
Continue updating the website and make sure future updates happen in a timely manner.
Document all policy changes in writing and share them with the appropriate staff.
audits.agency_response: EEPC agreed with all three new recommendations and said it will implement them.
audits.implementation_note: Of the 3 recommendations in the 2020 audit, the follow-up found all 3 implemented.

audits.title: Preparing Every NYC Student for an AI-Powered Future
audits.plain_title: Training every new city teacher in computing skills
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future on computing education in New York City public schools and on Computing Integrated Teacher Education (CITE), a City University of New York (CUNY) program that trains future teachers to build computing and digital literacy into their lessons.
audits.background: New York City launched Computer Science for All (CS4All) in 2015, requiring every student to receive four units of computer science by the end of 12th grade. About one-third of the new teachers New York City Public Schools hires each year earned their degrees at CUNY.

findings.plain: Enrollment in computer science classes grew from 54,177 students, or 5.5 percent, in 2016 to 193,171 students, or 20 percent, in 2024.
findings.quote: increased from 54,177 (5.5 percent) in 2016 to 193,171 (20 percent) in 2024

findings.plain: Gaps remain by race and by borough. In 2024, 15.6 percent of Black students and 19.1 percent of Hispanic students took computer science, against 27.1 percent of Asian students and 20.4 percent of white students, and Manhattan had the lowest borough enrollment at 13.7 percent.
findings.quote: Just 15.6 percent of Black students and 19.1 percent of Hispanic students were taking computer science classes in 2024

findings.plain: Only 19 percent of schools meet the equity goal set by Computer Science for All, meaning the students enrolled in computer science reflect the school's overall population.
findings.quote: just 19 percent of schools are achieving CS4All’s equity goals

findings.plain: Training current teachers has been slow. Only 3,118 teachers had received computer science professional learning through Computer Science for All as of 2024, and 22 percent of those trained between 2016 and 2023 left the school system.
findings.quote: Only 3,118 teachers have received computer science-related professional learning sessions through CS4All as of 2024.

findings.plain: The CITE program has trained about a third of CUNY's teacher education faculty and reached more than 10,000 teacher candidates, but it is fully implemented at only one of CUNY's 16 colleges with education programs.
findings.quote: CITE has only been fully implemented in one of CUNY’s 16 colleges with education programs

findings.plain: Employment in the city's core tech sector more than doubled over 15 years, from 103,000 to more than 208,000 jobs, while Black and Latino workers hold 24.3 percent of tech jobs against 46 percent of the overall workforce.
findings.quote: from 103,000 to more than 208,000 jobs

audits.title: New York City Housing Authority Monitorship: Monitors' Report (Fifth Report)
audits.plain_title: New heat data: 84% of apartments lost heating service last winter
audits.what_they_audited: The federal monitors' fifth quarterly report on the New York City Housing Authority's (NYCHA) compliance with its 2019 agreement with the federal government, covering heat, elevators, pests and waste, mold and leaks, lead paint and inspections, plus organizational change. It reports data for May 1, 2025 to July 31, 2025 and serves as the annual heat report for the full 2024-2025 heating season.
audits.background: On January 31, 2019 NYCHA agreed with the U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the City of New York to improve housing conditions, and a monitor was appointed to evaluate compliance. This is the first report in which NYCHA and the monitors had an agreed method for measuring heating failures inside individual apartments, so it is also the first to show apartment-level heat performance.

findings.plain: Measured for the first time at the apartment level, heating failures turned out to be near universal. In the 2024-2025 season 84% of occupied apartments had at least one heating service interruption, the highest since the monitorship began. The monitors caution this does not mean those apartments fell below the legal minimum temperature. NYCHA also had 388 unplanned heating outages, 104 more than the prior season.
findings.quote: 2025 season, 84% of occupied apartments experienced at least one

findings.plain: Heat came back faster when it failed. Average restoration time for verified in-apartment heating complaints fell from 26.3 hours in the 2022-2023 season to 13.9 hours, and NYCHA resolved 94% of central heating outages within 12 hours and 100% within 24 hours, meeting those requirements in the first season they applied.
findings.quote: restoration times from 26.3 hours in 2022‒2023 to 13.9 hours in

NYCHA estimates it would need $4 billion in additional funding to repair or replace heating infrastructure at or past its useful life, and it is behind on boiler replacements, having done 146 of the required 297 as of July 31, 2025 and expecting to miss the December 31, 2026 deadline by about two months.
findings.quote: would require $4 billion in additional funding. Moreover, according

findings.plain: Mold repairs improved but remain far from compliance. Through the second quarter of Year 7, NYCHA met the agreement's mold timeframes 28% of the time, up from 8% in the same period of Year 6, against a 95% requirement. findings.plain: On pests, NYCHA hit two milestones and one setback. For the first time it met the requirement to send staff trained in integrated pest management to every pest complaint, and it began publishing estimated rat, mouse, cockroach and bed bug populations for each development on its website. But estimated populations for all four pests rose compared with the same period in Year 6, though they still met the agreement's reduction targets.
findings.quote: Year 7, NYCHA’s pest population estimates for rats,

findings.plain: NYCHA still shuts elevators down during protected hours with little warning, but a pilot showed a fix. There were 820 no-service conditions from planned outages during restricted hours this year, 383 fewer than the same period last year. At South Jamaica Houses, where NYCHA scheduled preventive maintenance and gave 24 hours' notice by robocall, no planned outages happened in restricted hours and residents told the monitors the elevators work better.

audits.title: DOI Investigation into DOC Correction Intelligence Bureau Investigator Assisting Federal Agents with Immigration Enforcement
audits.plain_title: Jail investigator broke sanctuary laws by helping ICE
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) investigated allegations that Department of Correction (DOC) officers on a joint federal task force helped Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents arrest a person in custody, and examined DOC's guidance and training on the city's sanctuary laws.
audits.background: New York City local laws and mayoral executive orders, referred to as "Sanctuary City" laws, limit when local officials can share information with immigration authorities about non-citizens for civil immigration enforcement. DOC policy likewise prohibits employees from using city resources to assist federal civil immigration enforcement.

findings.plain: A DOC Correction Intelligence Bureau investigator assigned to the Homeland Security Investigations Violent Gang Task Force assisted immigration authorities in the February 2025 apprehension of a person released from Rikers Island, in violation of the city's sanctuary laws and DOC policy.
findings.quote:
did in fact assist immigration authorities in 
the apprehension of Concepcion, as alleged by the complainant, in violation of New York City’s Sanctuary 
City l aws and DOC policy.

findings.plain: DOI uncovered a second incident in which the same investigator gave federal immigration authorities information about another person in custody, including a screenshot with his booking photo, criminal charges and next court date, also in violation of city law and DOC policy.
findings.quote:
CIB Investigator A 
provided information to federal immigration authorities about another PIC, Pedro Mujica Villa Nueva, in 
furtherance of immigration enforcement

findings.plain: In the arrest case, immigration authorities presented neither a civil immigration detainer nor a judicial warrant, and the man's conviction for third-degree assault did not meet the "violent or serious crime" definition that could have permitted assistance.
findings.quote:
Immigration authorities did not present either a civil 
immigration detainer or a judicial warrant

findings.plain: In both instances the investigator did not understand that the help he provided furthered civil immigration enforcement rather than a criminal investigation, a failure DOI traced to a lack of training and guidance by DOC.
findings.quote:
CIB Investigator A’s failure to inquire further 
with respect to the purpose of the assistance that HSI asked that he provide was the result of a lack of 
training and guidance by DOC.

findings.plain: DOC provided no training to officers or staff on the sanctuary laws or its own related policy, and had issued no other guidance on interacting with law enforcement agencies involved in immigration enforcement before DOI raised the issue.
findings.quote:
DOC does not provide any training to its officers or staff about NYC “Sanctuary City” laws or DOC’s 
policy issued pursuant to those laws.

findings.plain: The two immigration enforcement assistance requests were not reported to the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs or posted on the department's website as city law requires.
findings.quote:
not reported to the Mayor’s Office of Immigrant Affairs or posted on the Department’s website, as 
required by City Law.

Persons in custody whose information was improperly shared

recommendations: Provide updated guidance to DOC employees on the city's immigration enforcement laws and DOC policy, including in-person training and memorandums with DOC-specific scenarios.

Give staff specific guidance on responding to requests from law enforcement partners, including follow-up questions about the request's purpose and when to seek supervisory or general counsel approval.
Instruct all DOC staff to direct any immigration-related requests from other law enforcement authorities to the ICE Unit and the general counsel's office.
Amend Operations Order 9/19 to require the ICE Unit to regularly ask other DOC units whether they have received immigration enforcement-related requests and to require a written response.

Have senior DOC officials confer with senior officials at partner federal agencies to remind them that DOC staff are bound by city law and cannot assist civil immigration enforcement except in very limited circumstances.
Conduct a department-wide audit to determine whether there were other instances where the department, intentionally or not, assisted in immigration enforcement.
Report any previously unknown or unreported immigration enforcement-related requests to the Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs as the administrative code requires.

audits.title: A Compilation of Audits of Agencies’ Oversight of Prime Vendors’ Use of Subcontractors on Health and Human Services Contracts
audits.plain_title: Five agencies share the same subcontractor oversight gaps
audits.agency: New York City Administration for Children's Services, Department for the Aging, Department of Health and Mental Hygiene and Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: This is an overview report compiling a series of audits of how five health and human services agencies, the Administration for Children's Services (ACS), the Department of Homeless Services (DHS), the Human Resources Administration (HRA), the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH) and the Department for the Aging (NYC Aging), oversee the subcontractors their prime vendors hire.
audits.background: City health and human services agencies deliver services like foster care, homeless shelters and senior centers through contracts with providers called prime vendors, which sometimes hire subcontractors of their own. Because the city has no direct contract with subcontractors, oversight depends on agencies watching their prime vendors, and the comptroller's office launched this audit series in August 2023 after watchdog reports found a history of unapproved and unvetted subcontractors.

findings.plain: Four oversight deficiencies showed up at all five agencies, including failures to record subcontractors and their payments in city systems and to ensure timely payment, indicating the problems are systemic rather than unique to any one agency.
findings.quote: several deficiencies were found in multiple agencies, including four that were found at all five agencies, indicating that these issues were systemic in nature

findings.plain: At four agencies, prime vendors paid more than $8.6 million to 25 subcontractors that were never authorized to work on those contracts, including two used on contracts where the primes reported using no subcontractors at all.
findings.quote: subcontractors received more than $8.6 million in payments from prime contractors on contracts for which they did not obtain authorization to perform any work

findings.plain: Four agencies could not consistently show that subcontractors were vetted and background checked. Across the sampled contracts, 24 of 63 subcontractors, paid a combined $13.2 million, lacked evidence of vetting.
findings.quote: the auditors did not find sufficient evidence to indicate that vetting and background checks were consistently conducted on subcontractors by four of the agencies

findings.plain: Agencies did not make sure prime vendors got competitive bids. About half of the sampled subcontracts requiring written estimates lacked evidence of them, and the Human Resources Administration had no bid evidence for any of its 11 sampled subcontracts.
findings.quote: HRA had no evidence that bids were obtained for any of the 11 sampled subcontractors requiring them.

findings.plain: No agency ensured subcontractors were recorded and approved in the city's Payee Information Portal (PIP) on time. The Human Resources Administration had the worst delays, approving all of its sampled subcontractors at least 583 days after work started.
findings.quote: none of the five agencies ensured that all of the subcontractors on the sampled contracts were recorded and approved in PIP in a timely manner, if at all

findings.plain: Agencies do not monitor whether prime vendors pay subcontractors on time, and the Department for the Aging reimbursed primes $381,700 for subcontractor expenses the primes had never actually paid, surfacing only because caterers complained about nonpayment.

audits.background: NYC Aging contracts with nonprofit and for-profit providers, called prime vendors, that sometimes hire subcontractors to deliver services like meals for older adults. Because the city has no direct contract with subcontractors, it relies on agencies to make sure primes get approval before hiring them, and this audit is one of a series covering five health and human services agencies prompted by a 2021 Department of Investigation report on corruption vulnerabilities in nonprofit human services contracts.

findings.plain: Prime vendors paid $2,251,857 to six subcontractors that NYC Aging never approved during fiscal years 2022 through 2024, and the agency has no way to independently confirm which subcontractors its vendors are using.
findings.quote: unapproved subcontractors received more than $2.2 million in payments from prime contractors

findings.plain: Even for approved subcontractors, auditors found no proof the agency vetted them. findings.plain: The agency has no mechanism to make sure subcontractors get paid on time. For one sampled contract, 47 of 53 invoices from a meals subcontractor were paid more than 30 days after the invoice date, with delays running as long as 580 days past the 30-day target.

Prime vendors on these contracts sometimes hire subcontractors, and this audit is one of a series covering five health and human services agencies prompted by a 2021 Department of Investigation report on corruption vulnerabilities in nonprofit human services contracts.

findings.plain: Neither HRA nor DHS made sure prime vendors recorded their subcontractors in the Payee Information Portal (PIP) on time. Recording delays ran 67 to 471 days for HRA and 34 to 305 days for DHS, and many approvals were still pending as of August 2024, with the approvals that did happen taking as long as 583 days.

audits.title: DOI Investigation into Theft Involving Pension Funds Managed by the NYC Employees' Retirement System (NYCERS) and Related Recommendations
audits.plain_title: How a pension examiner stole $624,000 from retirees' accounts
audits.agency: New York City Employees' Retirement System
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined internal control failures at the New York City Employees' Retirement System (NYCERS) after a criminal investigation found a NYCERS benefits examiner stole about $624,000 from two pensioners' accounts.
audits.background: NYCERS, established in 1920, is the largest municipal public employee retirement system in the United States, with more than 430,000 active members and retirees. It suspends pension payments when checks are returned or a pensioner does not confirm they are still alive, then reactivates accounts and pays retroactive benefits.

findings.plain: Between February 2021 and January 2024, Gregory Mathieu, an Associate Retirement Benefits Examiner in the unit that verifies whether pensioners are alive, used forged electronic fund transfer (EFT) authorizations, manipulated member profiles and unauthorized account reactivations to divert about $624,000 from two retirees' accounts.
findings.quote:
exploited internal control 
weaknesses to fraudulently divert approximately $624,000 in pension funds from two retirees' 
accounts.

findings.plain: The case revealed critical vulnerabilities in NYCERS' internal controls, particularly in segregation of duties, system access controls and verification procedures.
findings.quote:
This case revealed critical vulnerabilities in NYCERS ’ internal controls, particularly 
regarding segregation of duties, system access controls, and verification procedures.

findings.plain: A $99,999.99 payment on one victim's account was returned several times, a potential fraud risk factor, but NYCERS did not flag the account or give it extra scrutiny.
findings.quote: NYCERS did not flag the account or otherwise subject it to additional scrutiny.

findings.plain: NYCERS protocols did not require bank account verification for EFT forms received by mail, and the payroll unit processed Mathieu's fraudulent request without independent checks. The same bank account used for two unrelated pensioners should have been a warning sign.
findings.quote: NYCERS protocols also do not require account verifications for EFTs received by mai l.

findings.plain: NYCERS did not keep an audit trail of account access that would have shown when Mathieu got into pension systems, and it failed to notify DOI when one victim reported in person that he had not authorized banking changes.
findings.quote:
NYCERS did not maintain an audit 
trail of account access that would have shown when Mathieu accessed various NYCERS systems

findings.plain: In separate investigations, DOI and NYCERS found rising attempted fraud through account takeovers and fraudulent loan requests on the MyNYCERS online platform, worsened by pandemic-era disruptions; more than half of members have not re-registered on the platform.
findings.quote:
more than half of NYCERS 
members have not re-registered on the MyNYCERS platform.

numbers.label: Stolen from two pensioners' accounts
Restitution the former employee agreed to pay
Recovered by NYCERS from the defendant's account
Active NYCERS members and retirees
Recommendations DOI made to strengthen controls

recommendations: Improve internal controls with regular review of reactivated suspended accounts, especially those paying $3,000 or more a month, periodic audits of retroactive payments and returned-payment patterns and regular assessment of access controls.
Periodically review all accounts suspended for three years to determine whether members are still alive, including contacting family and checking obituaries and probate court records.
Expand bank account verification to cover electronic fund transfer requests received by mail.
Provide enhanced training for NYCERS employees, including regular ethics training stressing personal responsibility in fraud prevention.
Develop internal fraud algorithms that alert staff to duplicate bank accounts or shared contact information across profiles and to transfer requests going to high-risk banks tied to past fraud.
Maintain electronic audit logs of all account access and changes, including who made them.
Require two-factor authentication when members contact NYCERS to change account information.
Notify members by email or text immediately when someone logs into their account, with device, browser and location details.
Monitor IP addresses and review or block logins from geographic regions inconsistent with prior use.
Replace mail, email and fax submission of sensitive documents with a secure upload portal using two-factor authentication and time-locked session links.
Require identity confirmation by the relevant United States consulate plus a NYCERS video interview for reactivation requests from members living overseas.
audits.agency_response: NYCERS cooperated with the investigation and has already made reforms, including two-tier approval for account reactivations, restricted access to suspended account data and the mailroom, in-person or video confirmation for reactivations, a new anti-fraud policy and an anonymous whistleblower hotline.

audits.title: Review of the Department of Sanitation’s Commercial Waste Zone Request for Proposals and Carter Selection Process
audits.plain_title: How sanitation picked carters for commercial waste zones
audits.agency: New York City Department of Sanitation
audits.what_they_audited: This is a review rather than a full audit. It examined whether the Department of Sanitation's (DSNY) request for proposals and selection of private carting companies for the Commercial Waste Zone program complied with Local Law 199 of 2019, and looked at the safety, labor and violation histories of the carters that were chosen.
audits.background: More than 90 private carting companies collect the city's commercial waste, an industry DSNY describes as disorganized and hazardous, with private garbage trucks involved in at least 43 fatalities between January 2010 and May 2019. Local Law 199 of 2019 divided the city into 20 commercial waste zones with up to three carters each, and DSNY announced 18 winning carters in January 2024, though as of January 2025 only one zone had been implemented.

findings.plain: On the basic legal requirements, DSNY complied: its request for proposals incorporated the 13 evaluation factors in Local Law 199, no zone got more than three carters, no carter got more than 15 zones, scoring was calculated accurately and evaluators justified their scores.
findings.quote: DSNY’s RFP and carter selection processes were designed to meet the requirements of LL199

findings.plain: The carters with the worst traffic and safety records fared well in selection. Eight of the 10 carters with the most violations were chosen, selected carters averaged 241 violations each over four years versus 73 for those not selected, and auditors found no evidence violation history significantly affected suitability.
findings.quote: An analysis of the 10 carters that amassed the most violations during the period reviewed by DSNY revealed that eight of them were selected for the CWZ program.

findings.plain: DSNY awarded four zones to Cogent Waste Solutions, which holds the record for the largest payout of fines to the Business Integrity Commission, $500,000, after being charged with nearly 5,000 violation counts including overcharging customers. DSNY has since assigned an independent monitor to Cogent and a related company.
findings.quote: had the highest-ever recorded payout of $500,000 in fines for violations issued by BIC in January 2023

findings.plain: Twelve of the 15 carters proposed as subcontractors had safety violations, totaling 1,490 from February 2018 through July 2022, and three subcontractors accounted for nearly 70% of them.
findings.quote: a total of 1,490 violations were issued to the 15 subcontractors

findings.plain: Several selected carters also had labor problems and lawsuits: five awarded carters had 14 labor violations, and 12 of the 18 awarded carters faced 200 civil complaints from 2018 to 2022, mostly over vehicle accidents and injuries.
findings.quote: 12 carters faced a total of 200 civil complaints from 2018 to 2022

findings.plain: Maximum prices businesses can be charged vary widely within the same zone with no explanation in the proposals. In the Staten Island zone the highest maximum monthly rate was 145% above the lowest, which conflicts with the law's goal of fair and transparent pricing.
findings.quote: In the Staten Island zone, the maximum price listed by one carter was more than double the price listed by another carter within that zone.

findings.plain: The program's work is concentrated and rankings did not decide awards: four carters filled more than 70% of zone assignments, pricing carried the heaviest weight at 40 of 100 points, and the highest ranked carter won the zone in only three of 20 cases.
findings.quote: Of the 20 zones, the highest ranked carters were selected for only three zones.

audits.title: Status Report on Remedial Relief
audits.plain_title: Monitor's blueprint for the Rikers remediation manager's role
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The court-appointed independent monitor's second report on remedial relief for the city's contempt in Nunez v. City of New York, laying out a framework for selecting and structuring the new remediation manager position, summarizing candidate vetting and compiling the parties' objections to the court's proposed remediation manager order.
audits.background: The court held the city in contempt of 18 provisions of the Nunez court orders in November 2024 and on May 13, 2025 ordered the appointment of a remediation manager to direct a phased action plan for the contempt areas while the commissioner retains responsibility for the hundreds of other provisions. The monitoring team facilitated months of negotiations over candidates and the governing order.

findings.plain: The monitor cautioned that a receiver or remediation manager is an extreme and rarely used remedy, and that evidence on whether solutions devised by other correctional receivers work and last is mixed, largely anecdotal and context specific.
findings.quote: ...sustainability of the solutions devised by other correctional receivers is mixed, largely anecdotal

findings.plain: The remediation manager's office must build the department's own capacity to meet the 18 contempt provisions rather than becoming another entrenched layer of bureaucracy on top of the obstacles that have long blocked reform.
findings.quote: the Office of the Remediation Manager itself must not become another entrenched

findings.plain: The court identified the key blockers of compliance as insufficiently resourced leadership, lack of continuity in management, failures of supervision, lack of skill or imagination to implement transformative plans and unwillingness to cooperate with the monitor; the monitoring team adds that staff deployment and staff competency must also be essential objectives.
findings.quote: ...deployment and staff competency must also be essential objectives for the Remediation

findings.plain: The monitoring team and the parties evaluated almost 30 confidential applications for the remediation manager position, and on August 29, 2025 the monitor submitted the parties' recommended candidates to the court confidentially.
findings.quote: evaluated almost 30 confidential applications for the Remediation

findings.plain: The monitor concluded the department remains in a state of flux, with urgent safety issues persisting against a backdrop of uncertainty that includes the pending motion for reconsideration, unresolved objections to the proposed order and the November 2025 city elections.
findings.quote: The Department of Correction remains in a state of flux.

numbers.label: Nunez court order provisions covered by the contempt finding
Confidential applications for the remediation manager position

recommendations: The remediation manager's team must consist of members with bona fide credentials in sound correctional practice and in stimulating the culture change needed for the department to improve practice and sustain progress.

The court should permit the monitoring team to file a submission on September 24, 2025 with the outcome of the parties' still-pending negotiations over an information-sharing provision of the proposed order.
audits.agency_response: The city's objections and proposed revisions to the court's draft remediation manager order are attached as an appendix, and the monitor reports that all parties participated fully and made good faith efforts to find areas of agreement.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor reports that urgent, time-sensitive issues tied to the jails' elevated risk of harm remain at the forefront while the department awaits the remediation manager appointment and other court decisions.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Department of Education’s Compliance with Regulations Regarding English Language Learners Audit
audits.plain_title: Schools shortchanged English language learners on required services
audits.agency: New York City Department of Education
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Department of Education followed state regulations and its own policies for identifying English language learner students, placing them in the right programs, providing required instruction and keeping records.
audits.background: State regulations require school districts, including New York City's, to give English language learner students equal access to all school programs and services. The department reported 174,014 English language learners in the 2023-24 school year, up 16.8% from 2021-22.

findings.plain: For nearly half of sampled English language learner students, the department did not provide required courses or the minimum minutes of instruction.
findings.quote: for 145 of 301 (48.2%) sampled ELL students, DOE did not provide required courses, or the minimum number of minutes of ENL, or bilingual instruction time

findings.plain: About 40% of sampled students were served by at least one teacher who lacked the certifications required for teaching English language learners.
findings.quote: 122 (40.5%) students were served by one or more teachers who did not have the required certifications

findings.plain: The department does not track whether teachers complete the professional development hours in language acquisition that state rules require, relying instead on teachers to self-report to the state.
findings.quote: DOE does not monitor whether educators meet the required CTLE hours or the percentage of CTLE hours devoted to language acquisition

findings.plain: Schools failed to keep the forms documenting parents' program choices for nearly a third of sampled students, and 34 students were placed, or may have been placed, in the wrong program.
findings.quote: DOE did not retain ELL Parent Survey and Program Agreement Forms or Default Program Placement Letters in students’ files for 110 of 349 (31.5%) sampled ELL students

findings.plain: Instead of creating required bilingual education programs, the department improperly requested waivers. Of 150 waiver requests for the 2024-25 school year, 146 exceeded the five-year limit, affecting 9,527 students in 17 districts.
findings.quote: Of those 150 waivers, 146 exceeded the five-year exemption limit.

findings.plain: Parents of many sampled students were not given information about program options at their child's school or elsewhere in the district, and the department does not centrally record or analyze parent survey responses.
findings.quote: DOE did not inform the parents/guardians of 101 (28.9%) sampled students about ELL program options

findings.plain: The department did not consistently complete the identification process for potential English language learners on time, including the home language survey, the state identification test and a required Spanish language assessment.
findings.quote: DOE did not administer the NYSITELL to 1,447 of the 43,266 (3.3%) eligible students

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report on the New York City Office of Collective Bargaining’s Responses to Requests
audits.plain_title: How the collective bargaining office handles workers' inquiries
audits.agency: New York City Office of Collective Bargaining
audits.what_they_audited: In this final audit letter report, auditors reviewed how the Office of Collective Bargaining receives, tracks and responds to questions and complaints from city workers about union representation, checking whether responses were timely and well documented from July 2022 through December 2024.
audits.background: The Office of Collective Bargaining was created in 1967 to handle issues related to public employees' union representation. It is intended to function as a neutral agency that resolves questions about union representation and adjudicates disputes over collective bargaining, retaliation and unions' duty of fair representation.

findings.plain: Before 2024 the office's tracking of responses was inadequate. Records showed only 54% of people who contacted the office got a follow-up from an agency attorney within the informal five business day target, and 38% had no record of any contact.
findings.quote: only 54% of individuals received a follow-up contact from an OCB attorney within the agency’s informal target of five business days, and 38% of people had no record of contact at all

findings.plain: The office also did not adequately track requests for Pro Se information packets, which go to city employees pursuing claims against their union or the city without a lawyer. Of 35 people who requested one before 2024, the log shows only 11 were sent one.
findings.quote: Of the 35 individuals who requested one, OCB’s Log indicates that only 11 individuals were sent one.

findings.plain: After the office switched its tracking log from Microsoft Access to Microsoft Excel in January 2024, recordkeeping and responsiveness improved markedly. All 94 inquiries logged in calendar year 2024 got an attorney response within five business days, most within one day.
findings.quote: all 94 inquiries received a response from an OCB attorney within the five-day target, including 84 (89%) who were contacted within one business day

findings.plain: The 2024 log also shows the office became more responsive on information packets: every caller who requested a Pro Se packet that year was sent one.
findings.quote: according to the Log, all 40 callers who requested a Pro Se packet were sent one

recommendations: Document the office's procedures for responding to inquiries and complaints, including how calls and responses are recorded and a target timeframe for a response.
Continue to ensure that all inquiries and complaints get timely responses and that all relevant information is documented according to those procedures.

audits.title: DOI's Findings Regarding "Skimming" of Electronic Benefit Transfer Cards that Provide Vital Funds to Low-Income New Yorkers and Related Recommendations
audits.plain_title: Benefit card skimming cost the city $48.6 million in reimbursements
audits.agency: New York City Department of Social Services
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined the theft of Cash Assistance (CA) and Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits through "skimming" of Electronic Benefit Transfer (EBT) cards administered by the city Department of Social Services (DSS).
audits.background: About 1.8 million low-income families and individuals in New York City receive cash and food benefits through state-issued EBT cards. The cards use a magnetic stripe, which makes them vulnerable to skimming devices placed secretly on card readers, and DOI began looking into the problem in June 2022 after hundreds of client reports of drained accounts.

findings.plain: Between August 2023 and March 2025, the Department of Social Services issued $48.6 million in reimbursements for reported stolen SNAP and cash assistance benefits.
findings.quote:
Between August 2023 and March 2025, DSS issued a total of $48.6 million in 
reimbursements for reported stolen SNAP and CA benefits.

findings.plain: In that period DSS processed 142,178 SNAP reimbursement applications and approved 96,048, paying $43.7 million, plus 60,337 cash assistance applications with 27,176 approved and $4.9 million paid. The true loss is likely higher because those figures exclude unreported thefts.
findings.quote:
The actual loss to New Yorkers is likely much greater, 
because th ese figures do  not include unreported losses

findings.plain: Skimming devices capture card numbers, PINs and names and transfer the data remotely by Bluetooth, so thieves never return to the store and benefits can be drained almost immediately, making the fraud hard for law enforcement to trace.
findings.quote:
there is no need to return to the retail location to collect the skimmer, and there is little if any delay in using 
the data to steal clients’ benefits after capturing the data.

findings.plain: In a recent operation, DOI and law enforcement partners found about 55 skimming devices placed on point-of-sale terminals at local retailers.
findings.quote:
found approximately 55 skimming devices that had been 
placed on POS terminals at local retailers

findings.plain: Since December 2024, federal funding to reimburse stolen SNAP benefits is no longer available, leaving thousands of victims without a way to recover benefits stolen after that date.
findings.quote:
Since December 2024, federal funding for 
reimbursements for stolen SNAP funds is no longer available

findings.plain: DOI concluded the best prevention is replacing magnetic-stripe EBT cards with chip-enabled cards, which generate a unique encrypted code for each purchase. California began issuing chip cards in January 2025 and four New York State bills would mandate the change.
findings.quote:
the best way to prevent much of this fraud is to use chip-enabled EBT cards rather than the existing 
EBT cards with magnetic stripes.

numbers.label: Reimbursed for stolen benefits, August 2023 to March 2025
Low-income New Yorkers receiving these benefits
SNAP reimbursement applications processed
SNAP reimbursement applications approved
Skimming devices found in a recent operation

recommendations: New York should urgently install EMV chips in EBT cards to reduce skimming theft, by amending the social services law to require the state Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA) to do so or by OTDA acting without legislation.

OTDA should work with the EBT card vendor to create an alert that notifies clients when an out-of-state or suspicious transaction is pending and requires them to authenticate it through the app or an automated call.
OTDA should work with the vendor on a real-time text alert when a client's PIN is changed, on by default with the option to opt out.
OTDA should create an alert triggered by repetitive transactions at common locations between midnight and 2 a.m. and promptly report it to law enforcement.
DSS should continue working with the United States Department of Agriculture and law enforcement to promptly remove and confiscate identified or suspected skimming devices.
DSS should continue its early skimming detection and analytics work and keep informing the public of risks and precautions, including through flyers and public seminars.
audits.agency_response: DSS partnered with DOI on the investigation and has taken steps to warn clients, including a website video, multilingual fact sheets and a joint seminar with the Kings County District Attorney's Office. DSS also submitted a memorandum supporting state chip-card legislation.

rec_display.text: New York should urgently install EMV chips in EBT cards to reduce skimming theft, by amending the social services law to require the state Office of Temporary and Disability Assistance (OTDA) to do so or by OTDA acting without legislation.
