audits.title: Twenty-Fifth Report of the Independent Monitor: The NYPD's Community Response Team's Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: Quality-of-life police teams made unlawful stops at high rates
audits.what_they_audited: The stop, frisk and search practices of the New York City Police Department's (NYPD) Community Response Team (CRT) units from July to December 2024, using three methods: a review of 100 body-worn camera (BWC) videos from randomly selected CRT officers, a review of 50 videos officers had labeled as Level 2 investigative encounters and an assessment of 50 CRT stop reports.
audits.background: The NYPD established the CRT in July 2022 to focus on quality-of-life issues; its officers wear modified uniforms of khaki pants and blue shirts and drive unmarked cars. An initial monitor review in early 2024 found the teams focused on illegal motorcycles, demonstrations and unlicensed marijuana shops rather than Terry stops, but community complaints and a significant expansion of the teams prompted this second audit.

findings.plain: The teams' role has shifted: rather than addressing specific quality-of-life conditions or answering calls for service, CRTs now operate like the department's Neighborhood Safety Teams (NST) and Public Safety Teams (PST), doing proactive enforcement.
findings.quote: CRTs appear to be another version of NSTs or PSTs, engaging in proactive enforcement

findings.plain: CRT officers overwhelmingly made stops based on their own observations rather than 911 or 311 calls: 96% of the stop reports CRT officers prepared in the third quarter of 2024 were self-initiated.
findings.quote: 96% of stop reports prepared by CRT officers...

findings.plain: CRT officers stopped, frisked and searched people unlawfully at higher rates than patrol officers. In this audit 84% of CRT stops, 64% of frisks and 59% of searches were lawful, compared with 92%, 89% and 77% for patrol officers in the monitor's prior report.
findings.quote: 84% for stops, 64% for frisks, and 59% for searches

findings.plain: Supervisory review was largely absent. Reviewing supervisors found a legal basis for all but one of 50 reported CRT stops and deemed every reported frisk and search lawful, even though the monitor found unlawful stops, frisks and searches in the same sample.
findings.quote: There was a lack of meaningful NYPD supervisory review of CRT stops.

findings.plain: Officers mislabeled Terry stops as lower-level encounters and skipped required stop reports. Of 13 encounters on body-worn camera that the monitor determined were Terry stops, only four (31%) had stop reports prepared at the time.
findings.quote: only four (31%) had stop reports prepared documenting the encounters.

findings.plain: The people stopped were overwhelmingly Black and Hispanic men: 97% of the persons stopped, frisked and searched during Terry stops in this audit, and 90% of all persons CRT officers encountered across the three samples.
findings.quote: Ninety-seven percent of the persons stopped, frisked, and searched by CRT officers during...

findings.plain: CRT traffic stops frequently turned into searches that found almost nothing, and officers often sought consent to search without a lawful basis. Of 119 traffic stops in the audit, 75 (63%) involved a search, contraband was recovered in only two (2.7%) and in 38.3% of consent search requests nothing in the video supported the request.
findings.quote: In 38.3% of consent searches, there was nothing evident in the BWC footage

numbers.label: CRT stops found lawful in the audit
CRT stop reports that were self-initiated, third quarter of 2024
Persons encountered who were Black or Hispanic men
Audited traffic stops that involved a search
Traffic-stop searches that found contraband
Consent search requests with no apparent founded suspicion

recommendations: CRT officers should reach the same compliance levels the monitor set for Neighborhood Safety Team officers: at least 85% by the end of the third quarter of 2025 and at least 90% by the end of the year.

The department should tell the monitor what steps it will take to keep officers within the bounds of the Fourth Amendment during traffic stops and consent searches, including any additional training, directives or monitoring that may be required.
As the department finalizes its Fourteenth Amendment compliance plans, it should ensure an analysis of CRT operations is included in the plan's implementation.
audits.agency_response: The City argued that traffic stops and consent searches are beyond the scope of the monitorship; the monitor responded that the Fourth Amendment applies equally to vehicle stops and pedestrian stops. The department agreed with the monitor that the seven mislabeled encounters in the Level 2 sample were Terry stops.
audits.compliance_note: The monitor found CRT stops, frisks and searches lawful less often than those by patrol officers and comparable to the NST and PST specialized units, and directed the teams to reach at least 85% compliance by the end of the third quarter of 2025 and 90% by year end.

rec_display.text: CRT officers should reach the same compliance levels the monitor set for Neighborhood Safety Team officers: at least 85% by the end of the third quarter of 2025 and at least 90% by the end of the year.

The department should tell the monitor what steps it will take to keep officers within the bounds of the Fourth Amendment during traffic stops and consent searches, including any additional training, directives or monitoring that may be required.
As the department finalizes its Fourteenth Amendment compliance plans, it should ensure an analysis of CRT operations is included in the plan's implementation.

audits.title: Final Audit Letter Report on the New York City Employees’ Retirement System’s (NYCERS) Other Than Personal Services (OTPS) Expenditures
audits.plain_title: How the city employees' pension system spends its non-payroll money
audits.agency: New York City Employees' Retirement System
audits.what_they_audited: In this audit letter report, auditors checked whether the New York City Employees' Retirement System (NYCERS) spent its Other Than Personal Services (OTPS) money, meaning expenses unrelated to salaries and benefits such as supplies, travel and vendor contracts, according to its own policies and city rules, and whether the spending was necessary, reasonable and well documented. They reviewed a sample of 77 OTPS expenditures from fiscal years 2023 and 2024.
audits.background: NYCERS is one of the five New York City retirement systems and administers pension benefits for more than 350,000 active members, retirees and beneficiaries. For fiscal year 2024 it reported about $101 billion in assets and spent $130 million on administrative expenses, of which $70 million (53.8%) was OTPS spending.

findings.plain: Most spending followed the rules. The auditors found the money was generally spent in line with internal policies and other regulations and that the expenses were necessary and reasonable, but NYCERS needs better procedures for approving and documenting them.
findings.quote: NYCERS’ OTPS expenditures were, for the most part, spent in accordance with internal policies and procedures and other relevant rules and regulations

findings.plain: NYCERS could not produce purchase orders or contracts for two consultants who were paid a combined $52,250, so it could not show the purchases were approved under the city's Procurement Policy Board rules for small purchases.
findings.quote: NYCERS did not provide purchase orders or contracts for two consultants whose payments totaled $52,250.

findings.plain: Vendors were often paid late. City rules require payment within 30 days of receiving an invoice, but 33 of the 77 sampled invoices, or 43%, were paid later than that with no documented justification.
findings.quote: 33 (43%) of the 77 sampled OTPS invoices were paid more than 30 days after the invoice dates, without justification

findings.plain: NYCERS paid the same $2,000 invoice twice, first with an incorrect purchase order and account number in September 2023 and again with the correct information in January 2024.
findings.quote: NYCERS officials acknowledged that this was a duplicate payment

findings.plain: Travel spending did not consistently follow Comptroller's Directive #6. Of 30 out-of-town trips totaling $54,906 that were reviewed, four employees attended conferences without documented justification, and NYCERS paid for expenses that appeared unnecessary such as extra-legroom seats, lodging above the GSA rate and plane tickets to Washington D.C. instead of Amtrak tickets.
findings.quote: NYCERS also did not provide justification for expenses that appeared to be unnecessary, such as payments for seats with extra legroom, lodging costs that exceeded the GSA rate, and plane tickets to Washington D.C., instead of Amtrak tickets.

findings.plain: NYCERS did not appear to hold its trustees to the travel rules, saying that four trustees who attended six conferences are not required to get approval for travel or file post-conference reports.
findings.quote: In addition, NYCERS appeared not to enforce Directive #6 requirements for trustees who attended conferences.

numbers.label: OTPS spending in fiscal year 2024

Sampled invoices paid more than 30 days late

Cost of the 30 out-of-town trips reviewed

recommendations: Make sure a purchase order or contract is created for every small or micro purchase.
Pay vendors within 30 days of receiving their invoices.
Recoup the $2,000 overpayment from the vendor or have it credited to NYCERS' account.
Make sure all out-of-town travel costs are approved, including lodging that exceeds GSA rates and extra-legroom charges.
Get all necessary documents before processing payments and reimbursements to avoid paying unnecessary expenses.
Get post-travel attendance reports from everyone who attends out-of-town conferences to show how what they learned benefits NYCERS.
audits.agency_response: NYCERS agreed with five of the six findings and recommendations and disagreed with one, saying its trustees are not employees and do not need formal travel approval or post-travel reports. The auditors maintained that NYCERS should still collect post-travel reports from everyone who attends conferences.

audits.title: Audit of the Behavioral Health Emergency Assistance Response Division’s Effectiveness in Responding to Individuals with Mental Health Crises and Meeting Its Goals
audits.plain_title: Is the city's non-police mental health crisis team reaching people?
audits.agency: New York City Mayor's Office of Community Mental Health
audits.what_they_audited: Auditors examined whether the Behavioral Health Emergency Assistance Response Division (B-HEARD), the pilot program that sends social workers and Emergency Medical Technicians (EMTs) instead of police officers to 911 mental health calls, is meeting its goals and effectively serving patients. The program is administered by the Mayor's Office of Community Mental Health (OCMH) and run jointly with the fire department's Emergency Medical Services, New York City Health + Hospitals and the police department.
audits.background: B-HEARD was established as a pilot in 2021 as a health-centered alternative to the traditional response to mental health crises, which sends New York City Police Department officers and an ambulance with two EMTs. Its goals include routing 911 mental health calls to a health-centered response, reducing unnecessary use of police resources, increasing connection to community-based care and reducing unnecessary hospital transports; its fiscal year 2024 budget was $35.9 million.

findings.plain: The pilot is limited in when it operates, where it operates and which calls qualify, so many people who might need a B-HEARD team instead get the traditional response of police officers and an ambulance.
findings.quote: The Behavioral Health Emergency Assistance Response Division (B-HEARD) pilot program is limited in its hours of operation, its geographic distribution, and in the types of calls considered eligible for a response.

findings.plain: Because the program only runs from 9am to 1am, more than 14,000 calls that qualified for a B-HEARD team between January 2022 and September 2024 got a traditional response simply because they came in overnight.
findings.quote: Over 14,000 calls determined to be eligible for a B-HEARD team did not receive one because the calls were received during the overnight hours, when the pilot does not operate.

findings.plain: Even during operating hours, about a third of qualifying calls got no B-HEARD response. OCMH does not track why, though officials said team unavailability is the most likely reason.
findings.quote: 13,042 (35%) of the 37,113 calls determined to be eligible for B-HEARD did not receive program services.

findings.plain: The program fields just 18 teams split across two shifts and covers only 31 of the city's 78 police precincts across four boroughs, with no coverage in Staten Island.
findings.quote: The B-HEARD program is currently active in 31 (40%) of the 78 precincts in the City.

findings.plain: Of the 96,291 mental health calls received in pilot areas during program hours over fiscal years 2022 to 2024, more than 60% were counted as ineligible, a figure that includes calls that were never triaged at all, for instance because no fire department call-taker was available.
findings.quote: Of these, 59,178 calls (over 60%) were considered “ineligible” for a B-HEARD response by OCMH.

findings.plain: The share of B-HEARD responses that included a mental health assessment, which teams are expected to conduct, fell from 55% in fiscal year 2022 to 25% in fiscal year 2024, and OCMH does not track the reasons assessments are not done.
findings.quote: During FY2022, only 55% of the calls that B-HEARD teams responded to resulted in a mental health assessment of the patient. This number decreased to 31% in FY2023 and 25% in FY2024

findings.plain: OCMH's data collection is too weak to tell whether the program is working. It does not track why calls are not triaged, why eligible calls get no B-HEARD response, how often police officers request a B-HEARD team or whether people receive treatment after the initial crisis intervention.
findings.quote: The auditors found that OCMH’s overall tracking of program and performance data is inadequate.

numbers.label: Mental health 911 calls in pilot areas, fiscal 2022-2024
Calls deemed eligible for a B-HEARD response
Eligible calls that got no B-HEARD response
Eligible calls received outside program hours
B-HEARD teams covering two shifts
Program budget for fiscal year 2024
Responses with a mental health assessment in fiscal 2024

recommendations: Formally assess the citywide need for B-HEARD mental health response teams.
Work with partner agencies to expand the program's reach and number of teams in line with established need, including covering the overnight hours.

Work with the fire department to explore additional ways, such as tuition assistance, livable wages or loan forgiveness, to recruit enough qualified EMS responders so all eligible calls are triaged and answered.

Work with partner agencies to develop performance metrics and collect the data needed to evaluate the program, including reasons calls are ineligible or untriaged, reasons eligible calls get no response, police responses caused by team unavailability and reasons assessments are not performed.
Work with the fire department to require EMS responders to consistently update the final call type on every call so eligible-call counts are accurate.
Continue developing ways to increase contact with and assessments of patients when B-HEARD teams respond.
Continue working with the New York State Office of Mental Health and Health Department to expand community-based care centers across all five boroughs.
audits.agency_response: OCMH agreed with three recommendations, partially agreed with three and disagreed with one, on updating final call types, calling it infeasible and outside its role. It also disputed any need for increased oversight or improved metrics and said many issues were outside its purview, positions the auditors strenuously disagreed with.

audits.title: Nineteenth Report for the Monitoring Period July 1, 2024 to December 31, 2024
audits.plain_title: Rikers shows momentum under new leadership but violence stays high
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The court-appointed independent monitor's 19th compliance assessment of the Department of Correction under the Nunez consent judgment and remedial orders, covering July through December 2024, including the department's use of force, its management of people with a propensity for violence, body-worn cameras and compliance with dozens of specific court order provisions.
audits.background: The report was filed nearly 10 years after the consent judgment took effect in fall 2015, days after the court's May 13, 2025 order creating a remediation manager to address the city's contempt. Five commissioners have led the agency in that time, at least 10 remedial orders have been issued and the monitor describes 2021 to 2023 as a period of extraordinary instability and danger in the jails.

findings.plain: The monitor found the department appears to be emerging from its crisis phase, with tangible momentum toward reform since Commissioner Maginley-Liddie's appointment in December 2023, though the road to sustainable reform remains very long.
findings.quote: As will be described throughout this report, the Department appears to be emerging from

findings.plain: Of the 39 court order provisions rated or updated in the report, the commissioner's team moved the department from non-compliance into partial compliance on 10, sustained progress on 15 already in partial or substantial compliance, made progress on seven others and left seven with no progress.
findings.quote: moved the Department out of Non-Compliance and into Partial Compliance

findings.plain: Key measures of violence and use of force remain far above where they stood when the consent judgment took effect: the systemwide use of force rate was 9.13 in 2024 versus 3.96 in 2016, and the fight rate was 9.95 versus 5.11.
findings.quote: substantially higher than those observed at the time the Consent Judgment went into effect

findings.plain: After ten years, the monitor sees signs that staff practice on use of force has started to change, but says it is too early to draw definitive conclusions and the department has made little progress in reducing how often staff use force.
findings.quote: certain signs that Staff practice has started to change

findings.plain: Excessive and unnecessary uses of force remain pervasive, and the risk of harm in the jails remains high for both incarcerated people and staff.
findings.quote: ...unnecessary uses of force are still pervasive

findings.plain: The commissioner's administration catalyzed improvements including restored collaboration with the monitor, stronger leaders, better searches and contraband recovery, an improved restrictive housing unit, faster staff discipline, upgraded body-worn cameras and steps against staff absenteeism.
findings.quote: ...administration has demonstrated greater acknowledgement and ownership of core problems and

audits.title: Twenty-Fourth Report of the Independent Monitor: Compliance Snapshot of NYPD’s Stop, Frisk, and Search Practices
audits.plain_title: NYPD stop and frisk compliance snapshot for 2024
audits.what_they_audited: A visual "compliance snapshot" of how well New York City Police Department (NYPD) stops, frisks and searches complied with the federal court's requirements in Floyd v. City of New York, Ligon v. City of New York and Davis v. City of New York, based on the monitor team's audits of stop reports and body-worn camera videos through 2024.
audits.background: The independent monitor oversees the NYPD's compliance with federal court orders in the Floyd, Ligon and Davis stop and frisk cases. The monitor's audits assess whether stops, frisks and searches complied with the Fourth Amendment, reviewing samples of 100 stop reports per month and 225 body-worn camera videos per quarter.

findings.plain: Compliance rose over the first three quarters of 2024. In the third quarter, the monitor's audits found 91% of reported stops, 79% of frisks and 78% of searches were lawful.
findings.quote: 91% of stops, 79% of frisks, and 78% of searches were assessed as lawful

findings.plain: Stops that officers initiated on their own observations were far less lawful than stops responding to 911 or 311 calls or witness information. For the first three quarters of 2024, self-initiated stops were lawful 79% of the time, with frisks at 60% and searches at 66%.
findings.quote: ...complainant information were lawful, and 79% of self-initiated stops were lawful.

findings.plain: Most NYPD commands fell short of even an 85% lawfulness rate for frisks and searches: in the third quarter of 2024 only 46% of commands cleared that bar for frisks and only 27% did for searches.
findings.quote: In other words, most NYPD commands did not achieve minimum...

findings.plain: Supervision was a critical gap. The monitor found 11% of stops, 26% of frisks and 26% of searches unlawful in the third quarter of 2024, while NYPD reviewing supervisors approved nearly everything, flagging only 3% of stops, 1% of frisks and 7% of searches. The NYPD's own Quality Assurance Section audits, by contrast, had improved and closely mirrored the monitor's findings.
findings.quote: ...approved close to 100% of all stops, frisks, and searches and barely identified any...

findings.plain: Officers often did not document stops. About 38% of stops identified in the monitor's audits over 2022 to 2024 went unreported, and in the fourth quarter of 2024 officers failed to complete stop reports for 30% of stops the audit identified.
findings.quote: approximately 38% of stops in the Monitor’s audits have gone...

findings.plain: Stops prompted by complainants or radio runs led to arrests far more often than self-initiated stops. In the fourth quarter of 2024 the arrest rate was 41% for complainant stops and 42% for radio run stops, versus 11% for self-initiated stops and just 7% for self-initiated stops for suspected weapon possession.
findings.quote: the arrest rate for RR stops was 42%; the arrest rate for all SI stops was 11%

findings.plain: Housing Bureau officers had lower compliance than the department overall: in the first half of 2024, 77% of their stops, 52% of frisks and 48% of searches were lawful, though trespass arrests showed high compliance (98% had an objective credible reason to approach and 99% had probable cause).
findings.quote: 77% of stops, 52% of frisks, and 48% of searches were assessed as lawful

audits.title: DOI's Investigation of Excessive Workers' Compensation Claims by City Department of Correction Employees
audits.plain_title: Correction employees' injury claims cost the city over $340 million
audits.agency: New York City Department of Correction
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) examined the volume and cost of workers' compensation claims filed by New York City Department of Correction (DOC) employees, after several city agencies including the City Law Department raised concerns about the claims.
audits.background: Under New York law employers must pay workers' compensation benefits when an employee is disabled by an on-the-job injury, and the city self-insures, meaning awards are directly funded by public money. The Law Department represents the city in proceedings before the state Workers' Compensation Board.

findings.plain: In fiscal year 2024 the city paid more than $340 million for workers' compensation claims by correction department employees, compared with just under $225 million for claims by employees of all other mayoral agencies combined.
findings.quote: it paid just under $225 million for claims by  employees of all other

findings.plain: Over fiscal years 2022 through 2024, the city's total spending on claims by correction employees passed the billion-dollar mark.
findings.quote: compensation claims by DOC employees exceeded $1 billion.

findings.plain: Between fiscal 2015 and fiscal 2024, workers' compensation expenses for correction employees grew about 337%, from roughly $78 million to roughly $341 million, while expenses for all other mayoral agencies combined grew only 65%.
findings.quote: expenses for DOC employees grew by approximately 337%

findings.plain: Correction employees led all mayoral agencies in claims filed, with 3,547 new claims in fiscal 2024. Many claims that drove the increase were for permanent partial disability, where employees can collect lump-sum Schedule Loss of Use awards while continuing to draw their usual wages.
findings.quote:
many

wages on top of significant payments

findings.plain: DOI and federal prosecutors announced charges against one current and two former correction officers for allegedly fraudulent claims. findings.quote:
the pattern of claims by

recommendations: The Law Department should appoint a Director of Claims Integrity to identify potentially fraudulent workers' compensation claims by city employees and serve as a liaison referring possible fraud to DOI.

audits.title: Audit Report on the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene’s Oversight of Doula Programs in Underserved Neighborhoods
audits.plain_title: Are the city's free doula programs improving birth outcomes?
audits.agency: New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene
audits.what_they_audited: Auditors assessed how the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH) runs the Citywide Doula Initiative (CDI), which provides free doula support to people in underserved neighborhoods, shelters and foster homes, and whether the program is increasing access to doula services and reducing negative birth outcomes for clients from March 2022 through June 2024.
audits.background: City laws require DOHMH to expand access to doula services and to provide them at no cost to residents of marginalized neighborhoods in all five boroughs. DOHMH contracted with seven vendors to provide CDI doula services, with $4,066,429.32 approved for services and training from March 2022 through June 2024, in a city where Black non-Hispanic women accounted for 17.7% of live births in 2021 but 39.7% of pregnancy-associated deaths.

findings.plain: The program is reaching its target areas. All 33 neighborhoods identified as underserved by the city's Taskforce on Racial Inclusion & Equity now have access to CDI doula services, and use of the services has grown quickly.
findings.quote: the number of CDI doula visits conducted during the second quarters of Calendar Years 2022 through 2024 has increased an average of 75% each year

findings.plain: Black and Hispanic women who used CDI doulas had better birth outcomes than Black and Hispanic women citywide, with lower rates of C-sections, low birth weight and pre-term births. CDI clients also breastfed exclusively at a 53% rate versus 40.4% citywide, and no pregnancy-associated deaths were reported among CDI clients during the audit period.
findings.quote: among both Black and Hispanic women, CDI clients fared better than those in the general population in all three categories of negative birth outcomes relating to C-sections, low birth weights, and pre-term births

findings.plain: Results were weaker for Asian American/Pacific Islander (AAPI) and White clients, though far fewer of them participated in the program, so there was much less data to go on.
findings.quote: Birthing outcomes of White CDI clients varied when compared to citywide birth outcome rates, while birthing outcomes of AAPI CDI clients were worse than citywide birth outcome rates.

findings.plain: Pregnant people living in homeless shelters are not getting doula services as reliably as other clients. About half of doulas surveyed said shelter clients were difficult or impossible to reach, with some shelters denying entry and others requiring caseworker approval that delays services.
findings.quote: Clients residing in shelters are not receiving doula services with the same level of consistency as CDI clients not residing in shelters, either because doulas are delayed waiting for case worker approvals or because some shelters outright deny doulas access to their clients.

findings.plain: There are not enough doulas who speak languages other than English. Clients requested services in another language 321 times, and while six of the seven vendors could serve clients in Spanish, fewer than half could cover other languages.
findings.quote: Vendors that responded to the survey reported a need for non-English-speaking doulas.

findings.plain: Some hospitals still get in doulas' way. In DOHMH's own survey, doulas reported being prevented from helping clients use the restroom, supporting mobility out of bed or staying with clients during delivery.
findings.quote: DOHMH’s assessment and the audit’s review of the Doula Assessment survey found that a significant portion of doulas were prevented from providing certain care.

findings.plain: DOHMH stores program data across multiple datasets instead of one comprehensive one, which makes it labor intensive to analyze whether the program is achieving its goals.
findings.quote: However, the agency does not maintain a single comprehensive dataset containing key data (e.g., doula services provided, clients served, birth outcomes) relating to the CDI.

recommendations: Make all reasonable efforts to collect or use available provisional citywide birth outcome data so CDI client rates can be compared with citywide rates sooner.
Consolidate data collection into more efficient reporting to determine how well doula services reduce negative birth outcomes and maternal mortality.
Increase the number of doulas who speak languages other than English.
Continue working with the Department of Homeless Services to increase doula access to clients in shelters.
Continue promoting doula-friendly policies in the Maternity Hospital Quality Improvement Network hospitals and expand the incorporation of doulas into hospital birthing teams.
Build client satisfaction surveys into data collection and evaluate satisfaction by vendor, analyzing differences in practice that may affect satisfaction.
Conduct additional studies of outcomes for AAPI and White women to understand why the program appears to help them less.
audits.agency_response: DOHMH agreed with six of the seven recommendations and disagreed with one, on studying outcomes for AAPI and White women, saying the program's focus is Black and Hispanic birth outcomes and the sample sizes for those groups were very small. The auditors responded that the worse outcomes for those clients should not be dismissed without closer consideration.

findings.plain: Tech has been adding jobs far faster than the rest of the city's economy since the pandemic began.

findings.plain: The sector added jobs steadily over the past decade across the five boroughs.

findings.plain: Demand for tech skills now runs through most of the city's job market, not just tech companies.

findings.plain: The number of funded start-ups in the city has more than doubled in a decade, spread across many industries.
findings.quote: the city was home to 8,750 funded tech start-ups, more than double the figure (3,772) from a decade ago

findings.plain: New York's tech workforce is more racially diverse than those in other major tech hubs.
findings.quote: Black and Hispanic New Yorkers make up 24.3 percent of New York’s tech sector workforce

findings.plain: The report identifies two threats to continued growth: housing costs that make it harder to attract and keep workers, and what interviewees described as a regulatory environment out of step with the sector's role.

audits.title: Audit of the New York City Department of Buildings’ Enforcement of Building Codes
audits.plain_title: How the buildings department enforces the building code
audits.agency: New York City Department of Buildings
audits.what_they_audited: Auditors examined whether the Department of Buildings (DOB) enforces building codes for one- and two-family properties in an equitable way, so that no communities are disproportionately impacted, covering calendar years 2022, 2023 and the first quarter of 2024. The audit was prompted by housing advocates' concerns that small property owners, particularly in communities of color, are hit hardest by violations and fines.
audits.background: DOB regulates more than 1,000,000 buildings and over 40,000 active construction sites, issuing summonses through the Office of Administrative Trials and Hearings (OATH) when properties violate the construction codes. If an immediately hazardous violation is not certified as corrected within 60 days, owners can be issued a Failure to Comply summons that repeats every 60 days, and owners who miss their hearings face default judgments with maximum penalties.

findings.plain: DOB's enforcement of existing one- and two-family homes is essentially driven by anonymous 311 complaints. The agency identified no other routine way of checking whether such properties comply with the code, so it cannot tell whether the most-penalized communities actually have the most violations or just the most complaints.
findings.quote: The audit found that the Department of Buildings (DOB) relies almost exclusively on 311 complaints for its enforcement actions, and that certain communities were disproportionately impacted by penalties that were assessed as a result.

findings.plain: The penalties fell hardest on lower-income areas. Black households were among the two largest demographic groups in seven of the 10 community districts with the most one- and two-family properties carrying $20,000 or more in accumulated penalties.
findings.quote: seven of the 10 community districts with the most one- and two-family properties with high accumulated penalties had median household incomes below the Citywide median

findings.plain: DOB issued 13,466 OATH violations with $38.3 million in fines against one- and two-family properties in 2022 and 2023, and most of the penalty dollars came from illegal conversions and from owners who missed their hearings.
findings.quote: Overall, default judgments accounted for 63% ($24.3 million out of $38.3 million) of the total penalties imposed during the audit scope for one- and two-family properties

findings.plain: Some homeowners were fined for failing to fix violations they legally could not fix yet, because the correction plans they had submitted were still awaiting DOB approval. Three more owners were fined within 60 days of getting plan approval, leaving little time to do the work.
findings.quote: In four cases, homeowners still had seven plans pending with DOB when they were issued eight FTC violations with fines totaling $17,500.

findings.plain: Plan reviews are getting much slower and vary widely by borough. In the first quarter of 2024 the citywide average from plan submission to approval for major alterations was 124 business days, ranging from an average of 100 business days in Staten Island to 175 in the Bronx, and penalties keep accruing until the violation is fixed.
findings.quote: the number of days taken by DOB for its plan reviews increased 80% Citywide, as the number of applications filed Citywide also increased by 106%

findings.plain: DOB has no time targets for completing plan reviews and, since April 2022, has stopped publicly reporting its plan review and approval times, tracking them internally only.
findings.quote: The audit found that DOB has not established time targets for plan reviews and permit approvals.

findings.plain: The Homeowner Relief Program, which gives eligible owners a chance to fix problems without a summons, appears to have had limited success: of 9,167 substantiated complaints handled under the program, only 19% were confirmed corrected and most were never re-inspected at all.
findings.quote: 5,504 (60%) remained open with no evidence of an attempted re-inspection by DOB

OATH violations issued to one- and two-family homes

recommendations: Re-evaluate the total reliance on complaints to drive code enforcement and consider additional approaches.
Consider ways to track the source of complaints and other remedies to make sure the 311 complaint system is not abused to target certain communities.
Change processes so Failure to Comply summonses are not issued while correction plans are still pending DOB review, or within 60 days of DOB approving a plan.
Establish education and engagement strategies in the communities most affected by illegal conversions, emphasizing the financial impact of violations, fines and penalties.
Work with OATH to educate the public about the financial consequences of defaulting on summonses.
Restore the practice of publicly reporting service levels, including plan approval times, on the agency's website tracker.
Identify why review times vary among the boroughs, work to reduce those variances and minimize review times, and set time targets for plan reviews.
Set key performance indicators for the Homeowner Relief Program to assess its effectiveness.
Formally survey participants in homeowner-assistance initiatives about their satisfaction and possible improvements.
audits.agency_response: DOB agreed with three recommendations, partially agreed with two and disagreed with four, including the calls to look beyond complaints, track complaint sources, hold off on Failure to Comply summonses while plans are pending and set plan review time targets. DOB also argued the finding of disproportionate impact on lower-income districts was unfounded; the auditors responded that DOB was conflating intent with impact.

audits.title: Oversight of Horizon and Crossroads Juvenile Centers
audits.plain_title: How the city runs its two juvenile detention centers
audits.agency: New York City Administration for Children's Services
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the New York City Administration for Children's Services (ACS) adequately operates the Horizon and Crossroads juvenile detention centers for court-placed youth, meeting federal, state and city health and safety standards and providing required services. The audit covered October 2018 through December 2023.
audits.background: ACS runs the city's two secure juvenile detention facilities, Horizon in the Bronx and Crossroads in Brooklyn, providing medical, mental health, case management and educational services to detained youth. Between October 2018 and March 2023, 3,643 youth were admitted to the two facilities, and police data show the number of people under 18 accused of major crimes increased sharply in the city from 2021 to 2024.

findings.plain: ACS did not adequately make sure intake and case management services happened on time. Only 53% of sampled youth got the required initial intake interview within 24 hours, and one youth did not get an interview until 76 days after admission.
findings.quote: Only 53% of the youth sampled received an initial intake interview within 24 hours, as required. One youth did not receive an interview until 76 days after being admitted to the facility.

findings.plain: Case managers often missed required check-ins: 94% of sampled youth did not get all their required daily face-to-face meetings with their case manager, some assessments were not completed and service records were incomplete or missing.
findings.quote: 94% of the youth sampled did not receive all their daily face-to-face meetings with their case manager, as required.

findings.plain: ACS under-reported incidents to the state Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS): 37% of 9,693 unique incidents recorded in ACS' own database were never reported to OCFS through the state's Juvenile Detention Automated System.
findings.quote: 37% of 9,693 unique incidents at the two detention facilities were not reported to OCFS through JDAS

findings.plain: Serious incidents were reported late. A youth setting a garbage can on fire was not reported for 24 hours though immediate reporting is required, 14 incidents including sexual abuse and assault were reported 1 to 22 days late, and a May 2020 escape attempt at Crossroads was not reported until 2 days later.
findings.quote: 14 incidents including sexual abuse, assault, harassment, employee misconduct, and contraband were required to be reported within 24 hours—but were reported from 1 to 22 days late.

findings.plain: Contraband prevention is falling short. Reported contraband incidents rose from 62 in 2019 to 706 in 2023, an increase of more than 1,038%, and auditors watched an ACS official pass through security at Horizon with two cell phones despite a policy barring employees from bringing personal phones inside.
findings.quote: The number of reported contraband incidents increased from 62 in 2019 to 706 in 2023—over a 1,038% increase.

findings.plain: School attendance oversight was inadequate: both facilities showed chronic absenteeism across all educational programs and ages, with 13-73% of days absent, even though classes are on site and ACS staff are responsible for walking students to class.
findings.quote: Both facilities exhibited chronic absenteeism levels across all educational programs and ages, ranging from 13-73% days absent.

audits.background: DOT is responsible for more than 6,300 miles of streets and highways and issues 150 different types of sidewalk and roadway construction permits. audits.title: How to Remove the New York City Mayor Over Misconduct
audits.plain_title: A proposed process for removing a mayor for misconduct
audits.what_they_audited: A report from Citizens Union proposing a process for removing a New York City mayor for misconduct, and comparing removal rules in other large American cities.
audits.background: State Public Officers Law lets the governor remove a mayor after giving the official a copy of the charges and a chance to be heard, and the only other route, under section 10 of the City Charter, covers a mayor's inability to serve rather than misconduct.

findings.plain: The report says New York City has no practical, clearly defined way to remove a mayor for misconduct, which sets it apart from other large cities.
findings.quote: It is one of the only large cities without such a system of accountability.

findings.plain: The governor's removal power is broad and has never been used.
findings.quote: This unilateral authority is so ill-defined that it has never been exercised

findings.plain: The City Charter's existing removal path is modeled on the 25th Amendment and is meant for incapacity, not wrongdoing.
findings.quote: this process is intended for cases of physical, mental, or medical incapacity rather than misconduct

findings.plain: Citizens Union rejects impeachment for New York City, arguing that a single-chamber City Council with an overwhelming Democratic majority would not provide enough scrutiny.
findings.quote: For these reasons, we do not support impeachment as a method for removing the mayor.

findings.plain: The report also rejects recall elections, which it says would require state action and would be vulnerable to well-funded petition drives.
findings.quote: State law does not provide for recall of officials and does not grant that power to localities

findings.plain: Recall is nonetheless the most common removal route in large American cities.
findings.quote: Of the 30 largest U.S. cities, 22 mayors can be recalled.

findings.plain: The report says giving the courts or a panel of other elected officials the final say would create its own problems, including conflicts of interest for officials who might succeed the mayor.
findings.quote: the political dynamics within New York City may introduce unwanted conflicts of interest to the decisions of such ad-hoc body

audits.title: Audit Report on the New York City Department of Education/School Construction Authority’s Asbestos Management Program
audits.plain_title: Are schools getting their required asbestos inspections?
audits.agency: New York City Department of Education and School Construction Authority
audits.what_they_audited: Auditors checked whether the Department of Education (DOE) and School Construction Authority (SCA) are inspecting every public school building for asbestos hazards every three years and every six months as the federal Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act (AHERA) requires, and whether asbestos found in inspections is documented and management plans are kept up as mandated.
audits.background: Asbestos fibers, once airborne and inhaled, can cause severe diseases including asbestosis, lung cancer and mesothelioma, and AHERA was enacted in 1986 to protect students, teachers and school staff from exposure. As of March 2024, about 1,431 of the roughly 1,700 New York City school buildings, about 80%, were identified as containing asbestos containing materials (ACM) and are subject to AHERA's inspection requirements.

findings.plain: DOE has been out of compliance with the federal asbestos law for decades. Since 1997, across nine three-year inspection cycles, DOE conducted an average of only 11% of the required triennial inspections, with one cycle at 0%.
findings.quote: The audit found that DOE is not in compliance with Asbestos Hazard Emergency Response Act (AHERA) regulations and has not been for many years.

findings.plain: In the most recent three-year cycle, from March 2021 to March 2024, just 18% of schools with known asbestos got the required triennial reinspection, leaving 1,175 buildings unassessed. DOE typically does 200 to 250 inspections every three years but needs about 480 per year to comply.
findings.quote: only 257 of the 1,431 buildings (18%) with identified ACM received the triennial inspection required by AHERA

findings.plain: The required twice-a-year surveillance inspections are also mostly not happening. From May 2023 to April 2024, only 22% of the required periodic inspections were completed, and compliance was similarly low in every borough.
findings.quote: a total of 620 of the required 2,862 periodic surveillance inspections were performed

findings.plain: DOE has no centralized system for tracking this work. It did not start tracking periodic inspections until March 2023, previously relying on outdated management plans and, in some schools, custodians who lacked the training AHERA requires.
findings.quote: DOE maintains no centralized recordkeeping system with reporting features to support compliance with AHERA.

findings.plain: Evidence of mandatory asbestos training was inadequate or missing for most of 2020 through 2023, and the required annual notifications to parents, teachers and employee organizations were sent only to DOE email addresses, so auditors could not verify all stakeholders were reached.
findings.quote: DOE did not maintain training records during most of the period from 2020 to 2023, and while complete records exist for 2024, DOE lacked training certificates for all custodians in the previous years

findings.plain: Poor coordination between DOE and SCA has left 57 school buildings with asbestos status listed as to be determined, and delays in certifying buildings as asbestos-free led to unnecessary spending. One Queens school got its certification 13 years after opening, after DOE had paid for inspections it may not have needed.
findings.quote: In April 2022, DOE spent about $31,000 on one triennial and one periodic inspection because the ACM status had not been determined for over 10 years.

audits.title: Expanding Concession Opportunities in NYC’s Parks
audits.plain_title: More park cafes and restaurants to pay for park upkeep
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future examining concessions in New York City parks and how the organization says a modest expansion could raise money for park maintenance.
audits.background: The report notes that the Department of Parks and Recreation absorbed a $20 million cut last year and met less than one-third of its $725 million in state-of-good repair needs, and that concessions are the agency's largest source of revenue.

findings.plain: Across more than 30,000 acres of parkland, only a handful of spaces are licensed to restaurants and cafes, and more than half of all park concessions are carts or food trucks.
findings.quote: the city licenses just 15 spaces to restaurants

findings.plain: Concessions revenue was flat for more than a decade and fell in inflation-adjusted terms, though it rose recently after renegotiated agreements and new surcharges.
findings.quote: flatlined around $40 million, declining 25 percent since 2012 after adjusting for inflation

findings.plain: Money from city-managed concessions goes to the general fund rather than back to parks, which the report says discourages the agency from pursuing new ones.
findings.quote: none of the revenue from concessions agreements with the agency flows back into the city’s public parks

findings.plain: A small number of parks run by nonprofit partners keep their concessions money, and together they earned more from concessions than the agency did citywide.
findings.quote: seven city parks operated by nonprofit partner organizations earned nearly $60 million from concessions in 2023

findings.plain: Many park buildings need repairs before a business can move in, and the cost of that work has deterred bidders.
findings.quote: The gap between what a prospective concessionaire is willing to invest and what the agency can afford to has become an obstacle

findings.plain: Terms vary park by park, which the people interviewed said makes planning difficult, alongside license lengths capped at 20 years and the city's ability to end a license at will.
findings.quote: there is no standardized process for concessions agreements

findings.plain: Large parts of the city have no park eateries at all, including much of the Bronx and Queens.
findings.quote: the NYC Parks website lists six eateries in parks there, three of which are limited to private events

recommendations: Promote culture change among judges through live and online training, bench cards and shared research on the city's release assessment, the role of race, the low risk that people with no prior arrest will miss court, and the legal purpose of bail.

audits.title: Eleventh Annual Report of DOI's Office of the Inspector General for the NYPD
audits.plain_title: Police watchdog's year in review: half its fixes adopted
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation's (DOI) Office of the Inspector General for the New York City Police Department (OIG-NYPD) issued its annual report, required by Local Law 70, reviewing each of its 23 investigative reports and one statement of findings issued between 2015 and December 31, 2024 and the status of 240 recommendations.
audits.background: Local Law 70 established OIG-NYPD as part of DOI to oversee the New York City Police Department (NYPD). The annual report tracks the office's investigations and how NYPD and the Civilian Complaint Review Board (CCRB) have responded to its recommendations; recommendations made in 2024, with responses due in 2025, are not assessed.

findings.plain: NYPD has fully implemented 120 of the 238 recommendations OIG-NYPD issued to it through 2024, about 50%, and accepted in principle or partially implemented 46 more, about 19%. Two recommendations to the CCRB have also been implemented.
findings.quote:

recommendations, or approximately 19%.

findings.plain: In its May 2024 Public Oversight of Surveillance Technology (POST) Act report, the office found NYPD issued no new Impact and Use Policies for five surveillance technologies introduced in 2023 and used grouping too expansively by folding the Digidog robot into an existing policy. Of seven recommendations, NYPD accepted five and rejected two.
findings.quote:
OIG -NYPD found that NYPD utilized grouping in an overly 
expansive manner by addressing Digidog within an existing IUP, rather than issuing an individual IUP.

findings.plain: The December 2024 POST Act report on drones found NYPD's unmanned aircraft policy did not describe all the capabilities of its drone fleet or accurately reflect operations in practice. NYPD accepted all ten recommendations.
findings.quote:
the UAS IUP did not describe all the capabilities of its drone fleet or provide 
a complete and accurate picture of NYPD UAS operations in practice.

findings.plain: The office's review of NYPD's Community Response Team found the quality-of-life unit had no mission statement, no unit-specific policies and procedures and striking gaps in data collection and analysis. NYPD accepted six of seven recommendations and rejected one.

audits.background: The investigation was prompted by March 2022 media reports on security lapses at NYCHA's Corsi Houses in East Harlem, where the front door did not lock. NYCHA contracted with FJC Security, doing business as Allied Universal Security Services, for guard services, and the city fire code requires round-the-clock fire guards in buildings with uncorrected fire safety deficiencies.

findings.plain: In DOI's surveillance of randomly selected senior buildings, 64 of 94 scheduled security guards, about 68%, were absent for all or part of their required shift. Fifty-four abandoned their post for an average of about two hours and five never showed for their entire eight-hour shift.

64 of the 94 scheduled security guards (approximately 68%) were absent for all or part of their

falsified their handwritten timesheets to indicate that they had worked 
their entire shift, jeopardizing the safety of NYCHA residents

findings.quote:
44 of the 63 Senior Buildings (approximately 70%) had CCTV 
cameras that were inoperable or unable to be viewed remotely.

audits.title: Twenty-Second Annual Report of the Commission
audits.plain_title: Police corruption watchdog: faster cases, weaker interviews
audits.what_they_audited: This is the annual monitoring report of the Commission to Combat Police Corruption (CCPC), not a financial audit. The Commission read the case files of a random sample of closed New York City Police Department (NYPD) Internal Affairs Bureau (IAB) investigations, 46 closed in 2022 and 35 closed in 2023, to judge whether they were fair, thorough, accurate and impartial, and it also reprints a summary of its March 2024 review of how the Department carried out the recommendations of the 2019 Independent Panel on the Disciplinary System.
audits.background: The Commission was created in 1995 by Mayoral Executive Order No. 18 to monitor how the NYPD gathers information, investigates allegations and sets policy to detect, control and deter corruption among its members. IAB is the bureau inside the Department that investigates allegations of corruption and serious misconduct against members of the service, and the Commission monitors it by attending briefings, steering committee meetings and case reviews and by reading closed case files.

findings.plain: Investigations moved faster than at any point the Commission has tracked. Cases reviewed in 2022 took 8.9 months on average, the shortest in eight years of reviews, and the 2023 average of 10.4 months fell to 8.6 months once a single 73-month case was set aside.
findings.quote:
In 2022 and 2023, the Commission observed the lowest average length of time IAB 
investigations were pending since we began tracking this metric.

findings.plain: The Commission's satisfaction rate fell in all seven areas it tracks in the 2023 sample, after mostly small declines in 2022. It attributes the drop partly to dropping failed drug tests from its sample and partly to turnover among IAB executives and group commanders.
findings.quote:
In 2023, our 
satisfaction rates decreased in all seven areas.

findings.plain: Interview quality remains the weakest part of IAB's work. The Commission found problems in 13 of the 46 cases reviewed in 2022 and 13 of the 35 reviewed in 2023, most often failure to ask follow-up questions and failure to cover all relevant issues, with questioning that at times seemed designed only to elicit a denial.
findings.quote:
we identified interview quality issues in 13 of the 46 cases we 
reviewed in 2022 and 13 of the 35 cases we reviewed in 2023

findings.plain: Investigators repeatedly failed to interview people who were available to them. The Commission flagged missed civilian or officer interviews in 12 cases from the 2022 sample and 13 cases from the 2023 sample, and in some property cases officers who had access to the missing property were never made subjects.
findings.quote:
The Commission noted deficiencies related to the failure to interview witnesses in 12 of 
the cases reviewed in 2022.

findings.plain: The Commission disagreed with more case outcomes than in any of the previous four years. It found three cases in the 2022 sample where the overall disposition was wrong, and in the 2023 sample it identified three cases where allegations closed as unsubstantiated should have been substantiated; IAB agreed with its assessment in two of those.
findings.quote:
We disagreed with more overall dispositions of investigations in this review than we have 
had in the prior four years.

findings.plain: Body-worn camera footage has been a clear benefit to IAB investigations, but officers who failed to record properly were rarely punished beyond a warning, even though the Department's own penalty guidelines call for the forfeiture of one to five days.
findings.quote:
it did not appear that penalties beyond 
warnings were given in a majority of these cases

findings.plain: Long stretches of inactivity persisted in some files even when cases closed on time, and supervisors' directions were not always carried out. Eight investigations in the 2023 sample sat for more than 30 days with no explained activity, and in six 2023 cases team leaders ordered steps that were never taken and never explained.
findings.quote:
there were eight investigations that we reviewed in 2023 
that had unexplained gaps of longer than 30 days

recommendations: Conduct investigations promptly and without lapses in activity, but do not sacrifice quality for speed; IAB has directed each group commander to name backup investigators who can take over when the primary investigator is unavailable.
Identify subject officers as early as possible, and in property cases treat every officer who had access to the missing property as a subject unless there is a specific reason to exclude them.

Interview civilian witnesses without delay and interview witness officers close in time to the incident absent a strategic reason; the assigned investigator should personally contact the complainant, and civilians should be shown body-worn camera footage that contradicts their account unless there is a strategic or privacy reason not to.
Document in the case file, preferably on the worksheet summarizing the interview, any reason for departing from best interview practices.

Train newly assigned investigators in interviewing techniques and give all investigators routine refresher courses; the current Department Advocate should put this training in place with the attorneys in that office.
Have supervisors who are skilled at interviewing help less experienced investigators, both in preparing for interviews and during the questioning.

Before conducting surveillance, have investigators discuss the objectives with supervisors and plan the surveillance for the times they are most likely to observe what they are looking for.

When summarizing recorded interviews, include only what can be heard on the audio, record anything said outside the recording on a separate worksheet or clearly mark it as before or after the recording, and have supervisors confirm the summaries are accurate and complete.

Search for relevant video as soon as the complaint comes in, have supervisors check within the first one to two weeks that a video canvass was done, and follow up quickly on cameras whose footage could not be accessed.

Promptly perform investigative steps directed in team leader or commanding officer reviews, document any reason a step was not taken, and admonish or discipline investigators who skip a step without a legitimate reason.

audits.auditor: Center for New York City Affairs
audits.title: New York City Needs Additional Funds to Maintain Child Care Assistance Program (CCAP) Vouchers in State Fiscal Year 2026 and Beyond
audits.plain_title: What it would cost to keep child care vouchers going
audits.what_they_audited: An issue brief from the Center for New York City Affairs giving an independent analysis of the Child Care Block Grant (CCBG) shortfall that the city's Administration for Children's Services (ACS) identified during the state budget process.
audits.background: The city is required to give Child Care Assistance Program (CCAP) vouchers to families on cash assistance, known in New York as Temporary Assistance (TA), and work requirements for those families that were paused during the pandemic are being reinstated.

findings.plain: Voucher use by families on cash assistance is projected to climb sharply once work requirements return.
findings.quote: The upper-bound estimate for TA monthly CCAP voucher need is 67,000 by the end of State FY2026

findings.plain: Because vouchers for cash assistance families are mandatory and vouchers for other low-income families are not, the brief says a shortfall would fall on the second group.
findings.quote: the City will be required to cut vouchers currently being used by 37,717 non-TA low-income families

findings.plain: The average value of a voucher has roughly doubled since 2019, which the brief attributes to state market rate increases and the collapse in legally exempt providers.
findings.quote: The current estimated average weekly CCAP voucher value is $301, compared to $154 in 2019.

findings.plain: The number of legally exempt providers, where cash assistance families most often used vouchers before the pandemic, fell steeply.
findings.quote: In 2018, there were 10,758 LE providers in the city caring for one or more children with a CCAP voucher.

findings.plain: Current funding covers the 2024 average level of voucher use but not the higher level reached in December 2024.
findings.quote: it is insufficient to continue funding CCAP voucher use (non-TA low-income and TA combined) at the level reached in December 2024 (88,911)

findings.plain: The brief's own cost estimate comes in somewhat below the amount ACS asked the state for.
findings.quote: We estimate that the City needs an additional $823 to $907 million through Federal FY2026

findings.plain: The brief says federal block grant funding is set by formula and rollover balances, so it will not rise to meet growing demand.
findings.quote: NYS should not expect to receive more TANF or CCDBG funding due to increased demand

numbers.label: Added funding the brief estimates the city needs
ACS's own additional funding request
Estimated average weekly voucher value
Average weekly voucher value in 2019
Non-mandated low-income vouchers at risk
Total vouchers in use in December 2024

recommendations: Fill the funding gap so the Child Care Assistance Program can keep operating at its current eligibility level, rather than cutting vouchers already issued to low-income families.

Have the state and city work together to develop non-federal revenue streams for the program, since federal block grants will not grow with demand, and revisit the estimate once work requirements have been in effect for a year.
Improve uptake of unfilled Department of Education contracted early childhood seats, particularly among cash assistance recipients, to offset projected voucher spending.

audits.title: Special Master Program Monitoring Report
audits.plain_title: Special education fixes stall: one obligation met in four months
audits.what_they_audited: A periodic monitoring report to the court, filed as a slide deck, on how far New York City Public Schools (NYCPS) has gotten in meeting the obligations imposed by the court's order of July 19, 2023 in L.V. v. D.O.E. It includes an independent assessment of the four technology systems the obligations depend on.
audits.background: When a special education hearing is held, an Impartial Hearing Officer can order that a service be provided or a payment be made on a student's behalf, and the school system then has 35 days to carry the order out unless the order says otherwise. NYCPS runs an Implementation Unit (IU) to authorize the payments and arrange the services. Obligation #39 of the 2023 order requires the special master to report to the court every 120 days on whether each obligation has been fulfilled, what is blocking the unfulfilled ones and what comes next.

findings.plain: As of March 7, 2025, 19 of the 51 tracked obligations had been fulfilled and 32 remained unfulfilled. Only one had been fulfilled since the November 2024 report, a recruiting and hiring strategy, and every remaining obligation was past due as of January 19, 2025.
findings.quote: have been fulfilled, while thirty-two (32) remain

findings.plain: Work on the Impartial Hearing Management System (IHMS), the system most of the obligations depend on, had nearly stopped while the project waited for funding for its second phase. Funding for the change request was approved on February 26, 2025, but the contract and comptroller steps remained.
findings.quote: OMB approved the funding for change request on 2/26/2025

findings.plain: The independent technology assessment estimated that even in a best case the remaining development and testing of the hearing system would not finish until the first quarter of 2027.
findings.quote: remaining development and testing will be the first quarter 2027.

findings.plain: SupportHub, the new customer support platform, went live on January 8, but the special master's survey of attorneys and parents who used it found no one rated it very helpful and about half reported it unhelpful or a bad experience.
findings.quote: and 0% found it very helpful. About 52% did

findings.plain: The school system had not carried out everything the judge ordered at the December 5, 2024 conference on public communications and process changes, and the special master attached a status report tracking the outstanding items.
findings.quote: report tracking these items. In short, NYCPS has not satisfied all of the directives

findings.plain: Polaris, the new custom-built invoicing tool, launched with 57 vendors in late December 2024 and processed 207 invoices in January, 98% of them within five days, though the special master's team had not yet reviewed technical documentation to verify the results.
findings.quote: from Polaris now and processed 207 invoices in January, (98% within 5 days).

findings.plain: Hiring was moving: the school system reported 100 of the 148 needed implementation positions filled with full-time or temporary staff. Meanwhile the independent auditor was so far behind on its quarterly compliance reports that the special master arranged for it to audit a single recent month of orders instead.
findings.quote: reports they have onboarded 100 staff (full-time and temp) out of 148 needed

audits.title: Audit Report on Controls over Payroll, Personnel, and Purchasing at the 14 Queens Community Boards
audits.plain_title: Payroll, leave and purchasing lapses at Queens community boards
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the 14 Queens community boards maintained adequate controls over their payroll, personnel and purchasing functions in compliance with applicable city rules, regulations and official guidance. The audit covered July 1, 2021 through March 15, 2023, with employee leave data extended to November 25, 2024.
audits.background: New York City is divided into 59 community districts, each served by a community board, a local advisory body created by the New York City Charter with up to 50 unsalaried volunteer members. Each board employs a district manager who runs the district office, and board operations are funded through the city budget.

findings.plain: Eleven of the 14 Queens community boards had at least one reportable problem, generally involving excess annual leave accruals and payroll and invoicing procedures. Boards 5, 8 and 9 had no reportable issues.
findings.quote: 11 of the 14 Community Boards in the borough had at least one problem

findings.plain: Seven district managers had annual leave balances above the two-year maximum for managers as of November 25, 2024. The excess was not converted to sick leave as required and waivers to carry it over were not consistently granted. One manager had accumulated over 1,600 hours of excess leave.
findings.quote: One District Manager accumulated over 1,600 hours in excess leave.

findings.plain: Those excess balances carry a real cost. Even with excess leave converted to sick leave, auditors estimated separation payouts for the seven district managers would run from over $27,000 to $66,000 each and total more than $293,000 across the borough's boards.
findings.quote: the total pay-out amounts for the District Managers would range today from over $27,000 to $66,000 each, and cumulatively total over $293,000

findings.plain: Half of the board chairpersons did not consistently approve their district managers' timesheets on time, if at all. Of 41 sampled timesheets, 17 (41%) did not comply with the approval procedure, and in 18 instances the Queens Borough President's Office approved timesheets without evidence of the chairperson's sign-off.
findings.quote: did not consistently approve their District Managers’ timesheets in a timely manner, if at all

findings.plain: Community Board 13 could not produce 11 vendor invoices covering 33% of its sampled payments, worth $12,649.24, so auditors could not confirm the goods or services were received or the payments were proper.
findings.quote: Community Board 13 did not provide auditors with 11 vendor invoices, amounting to 33% of the sampled payments and totaling $12,649.24

findings.plain: Community Boards 12 and 14 batched multiple invoices into single payments without recording every invoice number in the Financial Management System, and Board 12 paid one $826.82 invoice twice without clearly demonstrating it recouped the full double payment.
findings.quote: auditors found that Community Board 12 paid $826.82 for one invoice twice on the same payment

findings.plain: No procurement issues were found at 11 of the 14 boards, and sampled micro-purchases totaling $177,790.69 showed the boards are generally buying goods and services for legitimate business purposes.
findings.quote: the Community Boards are generally procuring goods and services for legitimate business purposes

numbers.label: Queens boards with at least one reportable problem
Excess leave accumulated by one district manager
Combined estimated leave payouts for seven managers
Sampled district manager timesheets out of compliance
Board 13 payments not backed by vendor invoices
Invoice Board 12 paid twice

recommendations: All Queens board chairpersons should encourage district managers and staff to use their annual leave, limit authorizations to carry over excess leave where practicable and make sure district managers' timesheets are approved on time and promptly sent to the Queens Borough President's Office.

All Queens boards should actively monitor leave accruals and require written authorization or conversion of excess annual leave to sick leave, obtain and verify vendor invoices before every payment and develop written policies for managing employee leave and purchasing.
Community Board 12 should make sure the $826.82 overpayment is fully recouped.
Community Boards 12, 13 and 14 should record each paid invoice number in the Financial Management System.
Community Board 13 should consider hiring support staff as needed to support the district office's operations.
audits.agency_response: Twelve of the 14 boards sent written responses between February 24 and 27, 2025; many did not directly address the recommendations but their comments implied a general sense of agreement. Community Boards 4 and 13 did not respond.

audits.title: Letter Re: Audit of the Financial and Operating Practices of the 3 Staten Island Community Boards
audits.plain_title: Leave warning as Staten Island community board audit is called off
audits.what_they_audited: This is a closure letter, not a full audit report. The Comptroller's office told Staten Island Community Board 2 that a planned audit of the financial and operating practices of the borough's three boards was terminated, and it flagged the district manager's excess annual leave balance.
audits.background: Recent changes to the New York City Charter allow the Comptroller to treat all community boards as a single combined agency, so auditing one board's operations in a four-year cycle now fulfills the mandate. Before the change, the office had to audit all 59 community boards every four years.

findings.plain: The planned audit of the three Staten Island community boards was terminated because charter changes let the Comptroller satisfy the audit mandate by examining a single board in each four-year cycle.
findings.quote: This decision was made based on recent changes to the New York City Charter which allows the Comptroller to treat all Community Boards as a single combined agency.

findings.plain: The district manager of Staten Island Community Board 2 had banked 843.25 hours of annual leave as of November 25, 2024, which is 493.25 hours (70.5 days) over the two-year maximum for managers.
findings.quote: an annual leave balance of 843.25 hours, as of November 25, 2024

findings.plain: Auditors estimated the payout on separation at $61,458.19 with a waiver to carry over the excess and $42,169.57 without one, as much as 41% of the manager's salary and 23% of the board's fiscal year 2025 personal services budget.
findings.quote: These amounts were determined to be $61,458.19 and $42,169.57, respectively.

findings.plain: Under the city personnel order, managers may only bank two years of annual leave unless the agency head grants a waiver; without one, excess leave converts to sick leave that pays out at one-third the balance. Either way, unmanaged accruals can strain a board's small budget.
findings.quote: a Community Board’s budget and fiscal health can be crippled if leave accruals are not effectively managed

Establish protocols for monitoring future leave accruals and ensure compliance with the personnel order's leave regulations.

audits.what_they_audited: This is a set of closure letters, not a full audit report. The Comptroller's office told Brooklyn community boards that a planned audit of the financial and operating practices of the borough's 18 boards was terminated, and it flagged excess annual leave balances for the district managers of Boards 6, 11, 12 and 17.
audits.background: Recent changes to the New York City Charter allow the Comptroller to treat all community boards as a single combined agency, so auditing one board's operations in a four-year cycle now fulfills the mandate. Before the change, the office had to audit all 59 community boards every four years.

findings.plain: The planned audit of the 18 Brooklyn community boards was terminated because charter changes let the Comptroller satisfy the audit mandate by examining a single board in each four-year cycle.
findings.quote: This decision was made based on recent changes to the New York City Charter, which allows the Comptroller to treat all Community Boards as a single combined agency.

findings.plain: The district manager of Brooklyn Community Board 6 had banked 840 hours of annual leave as of November 25, 2024, which is 560 hours (80 days) over the two-year maximum for managers. Auditors estimated the payout on separation at $26,824.80 with a waiver to carry over the excess and $13,412.40 without one.
findings.quote: an annual leave balance of 840 hours, as of November 25, 2024

findings.plain: The district manager of Brooklyn Community Board 11 had 592.5 hours of annual leave, 214.5 hours (30.6 days) over the limit, with an estimated payout of $57,456.54 with a waiver and $49,334.98 without one, as much as 40% of the manager's salary and 24% of the board's fiscal year 2025 personal services budget.
findings.quote: an annual leave balance of 592.5 hours, as of November 25, 2024

findings.plain: The district manager of Brooklyn Community Board 12 had 934.5 hours of annual leave, 584.5 hours (83.5 days) over the limit, with an estimated payout of $89,295.99 with a waiver and $65,883.55 without one, as much as 50% of the manager's salary and 33% of the board's fiscal year 2025 personal services budget.
findings.quote: an annual leave balance of 934.5 hours, as of November 25, 2024

findings.plain: The district manager of Brooklyn Community Board 17 had 747 hours of annual leave, 369 hours (52.7 days) over the limit, with an estimated payout of $47,060.92 with a waiver and $28,887.37 without one.
findings.quote: an annual leave balance of 747 hours, as of November 25, 2024

findings.plain: Under the city personnel order, managers may only bank two years of annual leave unless the agency head grants a waiver; without one, excess leave converts to sick leave that pays out at one-third the balance. Either way, unmanaged accruals can strain a board's small budget.
findings.quote: a Community Board’s budget and fiscal health can be crippled if leave accruals are not effectively managed

Limit authorizations to carry over excess annual leave where practicable.
Establish protocols for monitoring future leave accruals and ensure compliance with the personnel order's leave regulations.
