audits.title: Investigation Concerning New York City Police Department Security Details for City Elected Officials
audits.plain_title: Police security details for elected officials still lack clear rules
audits.what_they_audited: The Department of Investigation (DOI) investigated how the New York City Police Department (NYPD) runs security details for elected officials and reviewed the status of recommendations from DOI's 2021 report on the subject.
audits.background: DOI's 2021 report concluded that former mayor Bill de Blasio repeatedly misused his security detail for personal benefit in violation of the city's Conflicts of Interest Law, and identified flaws including a lack of rules, minimal officer training and recordkeeping violations. NYPD accepted most of those recommendations and in November 2022 issued written Protection Detail Guidelines.

findings.plain: NYPD has implemented or begun to implement some but not all of DOI's 2021 recommendations, and substantial gaps remain in its policies and procedures for elected officials' security details.
findings.quote:
finding substantial 
and continuing gaps in NYPD’s policies and procedures concerning security details for elected officials

findings.plain: The new Protection Detail Guidelines provide little useful substance for detail officers or protected officials, failing to define "official purposes" or the scope of permitted uses, even though the 2021 report called lack of guidance the root of nearly all the problems it found.
findings.quote:
The PDGs provide little useful information for either members of  
service assigned to security details, or the elected officials afforded protection.

findings.plain: Detectives assigned full time to an elected official's detail received minimal training, two or three total days of dignitary protection training, in some cases a decade or more before their current assignment, and had little or no knowledge of the governing policies.
findings.quote:
two or three total days of dignitary protection 
training, in some cases a decade or more prior to their current protection assignment.

findings.plain: NYPD's security detail training did not cover the ethical and legal restrictions that apply to details for city officials.
findings.quote:
its security detail training did not cover the 
ethical and legal restrictions applicable to security details.

findings.plain: NYPD still does not maintain records recommended in 2021, with officers testifying they keep no trip logs, tour summaries or other records that would establish where details went and what they did.
findings.quote:
they do not maintain trip logs, 
tour summaries, or other records that would establish detail usage, destinations, o r other 
duties undertaken by detail members.

numbers.label: Policy and procedure recommendations in this report
Year of DOI's earlier security detail report

recommendations: Further develop substantive guidance on proper security detail use, updating the Protection Detail Guidelines with executive protection best practices from outside experts and clear rules for officers and protectees reflecting the Conflicts of Interest Law.

Require and provide high-quality executive protection training, ideally from outside experts, to all personnel assigned to elected officials' security details, both inside and outside the Executive Protection Unit.
Maintain appropriate records for all security details, such as detailed memo books and car logs establishing the location and time of each stop and other duties undertaken by detail members.

Promptly review whether written security determinations exist for all elected officials currently assigned details, make and document determinations where they are missing and adjust assignments if needed.
Regularly update written security determinations for elected officials and adjust details to reflect changes in identified threats, given the need to use limited government resources efficiently.
audits.agency_response: NYPD said it could not fully implement the training recommendation as written because outside experts such as the United States Secret Service have limited availability, but planned to extend its Executive Protection Unit training to all detail members. NYPD rejected the recordkeeping recommendation, which DOI called a substantial deviation from the practices of other protective agencies.
audits.implementation_note: The report found NYPD has implemented or begun to implement some but not all of the recommendations in DOI's 2021 report; three of the five new recommendations reiterate and expand on 2021 recommendations not yet fully implemented.

audits.title: Audit Report on the Development and Implementation of the New York City Fire Department’s Fire Inspection Revenue and Enforcement System
audits.plain_title: The Fire Department's $18.4 million inspection software fell short
audits.what_they_audited: Whether the Fire Inspection Revenue and Enforcement System (FIRES), the software the Fire Department (FDNY) paid contractor GCOM Software about $18.4 million to build for scheduling inspections, processing violations and collecting fees, meets its goals and handles information reliably and securely.
audits.background: The Fire Department previously ran inspections, violations and billing on paper forms, phone calls, spreadsheets and a 30-year-old unsupported mainframe system. It contracted with GCOM in 2016 to build a replacement, paid Gartner another $5.5 million for quality assurance and project oversight and launched the new system in September 2021.

findings.plain: The department never made its contractor deliver key inspection and enforcement functions required by the contract, yet still gave the vendor positive performance ratings across seven evaluations.
findings.quote: FDNY gave GCOM ratings of satisfactory, good, or excellent, and did not hold GCOM accountable for its performance.

findings.plain: Automated inspection scheduling and routing was never fully built. Supervisors still juggle Outlook calendars and spreadsheets, the system automatically cancels inspections nobody finalizes within 45 days and a May 2024 report showed 49,834 inspections past due.
findings.quote: 49,834 inspections are past due

findings.plain: Enforcement work is still largely manual. Summonses are issued on paper and hand-delivered to court, and the department paid in full for a $190,500 electronic interface for hearing dispositions that was never implemented.
findings.quote: GCOM received full payment for this work, which was not performed.

findings.plain: The department could not show the system was properly tested before launch. The only test report provided said testing could not be completed because of significant defects, and there was no documented approval of final test results.
findings.quote: due to the unacceptable amount of defects, lack of confidence of the stakeholders and untested functionalities, it was decided that there will be another round of SIT and UAT

findings.plain: When the scope of work was cut, the department did not reduce the contract price. Instead $506,928.44 was shifted to vaguely defined enhancements without the price and cost analysis city rules require.
findings.quote: the $506,928.44 was reallocated to milestones 17–20

findings.plain: Users are unhappy. About a quarter of surveyed department staff and public users were dissatisfied overall, a third of staff said the system does not let them work easily and efficiently and inspectors reported frequent connectivity failures in the field, which auditors also observed.
findings.quote: approximately 25% of respondents were overall dissatisfied or very dissatisfied with FIRES

findings.plain: The system ran on an unsupported software version for two years after launch, missing vendor updates that included stronger password enforcement and multi-factor authentication and exposing sensitive data to greater risk.
findings.quote: FDNY did not update FIRES for two years and operated in an unsupported version of Accela

recommendations: Consult with legal counsel about available contract remedies for system functions that were paid for under the contract but never developed, tested or approved.

Consult with the fire prevention and fire operations bureaus on business needs, fully implement automated inspection scheduling and routing based on inspector availability and require all units to use it.
Add a feature that automatically alerts units when an inspection needs scheduling and disable the feature that cancels inspections not assigned within a set time.

Consult with the Bureau of Legal Affairs and implement functions and two-way interfaces to automate summons issuance and transmission, court date and inspector scheduling, hearing disposition updates and appeals.
Conduct refresher training for all system users.
Consider the survey results, solicit more feedback from internal and external users and promptly address concerns about ease of use, functionality, connectivity and customer service.
Ensure future system development and testing contract requirements are fully met and results are approved and documented before deployment.
Ensure department information systems continuously receive updates to improve functionality and optimize workflow.
audits.agency_response: The Fire Department agreed with four recommendations, partially agreed with one and disagreed with three, and it disputed the audit's findings on system testing and the security risk of running unsupported software.

audits.auditor: Advocates for Children of New York
audits.title: Ensuring All Students Learn to Read: Where We Go from Here
audits.plain_title: Three next steps for the city on teaching reading
audits.what_they_audited: A policy brief from Advocates for Children of New York, a legal and advocacy group that helps New York City families with school problems, arguing that literacy should stay a top priority for the next mayoral administration and setting out three things it says the city should do next.
audits.background: The brief traces the city's recent literacy efforts, from the Universal Literacy reading coach initiative launched under Mayor de Blasio in 2016-17, through universal screening for reading difficulties in 2021-22, to NYC Reads, which required 15 of the city's 32 community school districts to pick one of three pre-approved English Language Arts curricula in 2023-24 and expanded citywide in 2024-25.

findings.plain: Only about half of city students in grades three through eight read proficiently, and the rates are far lower for Black and Latinx students, students with disabilities and English Language Learners.
findings.quote: according to the 2024 New York State tests, only half of New York City students in grades 3–8—

findings.quote: individual schools in New York City long had free reign to choose their own English Language Arts

findings.plain: The group says the experience of other states and districts suggests that overhauling reading instruction takes years and sustained money, so the city's changes should not be judged or funded as a short-term effort.

findings.plain: Families of students with dyslexia or other reading difficulties often cannot get help within the public system, and the group says it frequently ends up suing for private school tuition or private tutoring instead.
findings.quote: often resort to suing for private school tuition or private tutoring for such

findings.plain: City literacy work so far has concentrated on core instruction in the early elementary grades, leaving adolescents who still lack foundational reading skills without intensive help.

recommendations: Make sure every student who needs extra help in reading gets one-on-one or small group intervention aimed at their individual needs, for example by hiring a corps of reading interventionists, using existing staff for evidence-based intervention or creating district-level intervention hubs.
Strengthen core instruction by giving educators ongoing training and at-the-elbow coaching in carrying out the new curricula and in using screening data to differentiate instruction.

audits.title: 15 Policy Ideas for NYC to Start 2025
audits.plain_title: Fifteen local policy ideas for the city to take up in 2025
audits.what_they_audited: A short compilation from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City based think tank, gathering 15 policy ideas the group wrote about during 2024 and putting them forward for city leaders at the start of 2025.
audits.background: The group frames the list around its expectation that New York will get less help from Washington, and argues city leaders will need locally driven solutions. The ideas cover the City University of New York, workforce training, parks, housing, small business and the arts.

findings.plain: Small unpaid bills keep students from coming back to finish a City University of New York degree.
findings.quote: these unpaid balances, even those as little as $250, are a major factor in preventing students from reenrolling in CUNY

findings.plain: The city has roughly 20,000 Black- and Latino-owned businesses, but few grow past the small stage, and they take in far less revenue on average than white-owned firms.
findings.quote: the city’s average minority-owned employer business generates less than half the revenue—45 percent—of the average white-owned employer business

findings.plain: Four-year graduation rates at CUNY's senior colleges remain low, and lower still for Black and Hispanic students, while the program shown to lift them reaches a small share of students.
findings.quote: today only 36 percent of full-time students at CUNY’s senior colleges graduate in four years

findings.plain: Parks concessions, the department's largest revenue source, have not grown in a decade and have lost ground to inflation.
findings.quote: concessions revenue has flatlined just above $42 million for more than a decade—and has declined 25 percent since 2012, after adjusting for inflation

findings.plain: The creative economy pays above the citywide median and employs more than 300,000 people, but Black New Yorkers hold a small share of those jobs.
findings.quote: Black workers hold fewer than 8 percent of the city’s advertising jobs, while comprising nearly 21 percent of the city’s total workforce

findings.plain: About a third of new city teachers come out of CUNY, but very few arrive prepared to teach computing concepts.
findings.quote: fewer than 5 percent of all new teachers are prepared to teach computational thinking

findings.plain: Nonprofits delivering city human services cannot fill their jobs, and immigrant training programs are turning away hundreds of applicants.
findings.quote: the average human services nonprofit has more than 15 percent of its positions vacant

recommendations: Create CUNY Fresh Start, a city and state partnership that wipes out unpaid balances of up to $1,000 so former students can re-enroll and finish their degrees.

Create a competitive Scale-Up Challenge Fund, modeled on Race to the Top, that awards flexible three-year city grants to nonprofit economic mobility programs with demonstrated results, judged by an independent panel.

Launch a New York City Minority Business Accelerator modeled on Cincinnati's, giving a selected group of established Black- and Latino-owned firms business strategy help, access to expansion capital and procurement commitments from large regional companies.

Add restaurants, cafes and other concessions in parks, keep the revenue with parks rather than the General Fund and split future concession revenue 80 percent to the host park and 20 percent to a fund for parks in less affluent neighborhoods.
Baseline funding for CUNY ACE in the fiscal 2025 budget and grow the program over two years so it reaches more senior college students.
Create an annual five-borough cultural festival, starting with the mayor picking a week on the calendar and convening cultural leaders to design it.

Run three challenge-based artificial intelligence procurement competitions with the Economic Development Corporation, each starting as a pilot and scaling to a citywide contract tied to performance milestones, focused on housing affordability, safer streets and social services.

Start a Creative Economy Talent Pipeline in the Mayor's Office of Talent and Workforce Development, modeled on the Tech Talent Pipeline, to open creative industry careers to underrepresented New Yorkers.
Invest in decarbonizing CUNY's roughly 300 buildings and put CUNY students to work on the upgrades as training for green economy careers.
Expand CUNY's Computing Integrated Teacher Education program so it reaches all 11,000 aspiring teachers enrolled at the university each year.

Make it easier for nonprofits and community groups to help maintain and fund parks, with the mayor directing the Law Department and agency lawyers to speed up agreements and a handbook for community groups to follow.

Create a Pathways to Human Services Initiative that expands the Human Services Career Advancement Scholarship at CUNY by 1,000 people, designs a CUNY human services fellowship and launches a training accelerator with stipends for on-the-job training.
Commit to at least a dozen more projects over five years that rebuild an aging branch library with affordable housing above it, following the Sunset Park and Inwood examples.
Create CUNY Flex, a wraparound support program modeled on CUNY ASAP but built for part-time and returning adult students, who make up most adult learners.

Increase funding for adult literacy programs serving immigrants and write future requests for proposals so they support joint English language and job training programs run by CUNY, the public libraries and nonprofits.

audits.title: Enacting a Ticket Surcharge to Strengthen New York City’s Parks
audits.plain_title: A ticket surcharge to pay for park maintenance
audits.what_they_audited: A report from the Center for an Urban Future, a New York City based think tank, working out how much money a surcharge on tickets to concerts, sporting events and Broadway shows could raise for park maintenance and what legal steps enacting one would take. It follows the group's 2024 report on ways to fund parks.
audits.background: The Parks Department cares for more than 30,000 acres, nearly 2,000 parks and 1,000 playgrounds. All revenue the department collects from ground leases and concessions goes into the city's General Fund under a system created by the 1975 state Financial Emergency Act, so the department has no dedicated revenue of its own.

findings.plain: The Parks Department's budget was cut while its repair backlog stayed large, and it is covering only a fraction of what it needs to keep facilities in good shape.
findings.quote: the city’s Parks Department (NYC Parks) absorbed a $20 million budget cut, and today the agency is meeting less than a third of its $725 million in state-of-good repair needs

findings.plain: New Yorkers and visitors bought about 33 million tickets to city events in 2023, worth roughly $3.8 billion, which is the base the group used for its estimates.
findings.quote: The Center for an Urban Future estimates that such a surcharge would generate anywhere from $15 million to $190 million annually

findings.plain: Even the smallest version of the fee would raise a meaningful sum, at about $1.20 on the average city ticket.
findings.quote: would generate over $38 million in recurring annual revenue

findings.plain: Three stadiums sit on city parkland, but the rent they pay goes into the General Fund rather than to parks.
findings.quote: each stadium pays a ground lease to NYC Parks, but those dollars flow back to the city’s General Fund

findings.plain: Parks draw tourists but capture none of the tourist spending they generate, unlike hotels through the occupancy tax.
findings.quote: New York City’s parks generate about $17.9 billion in tourism spending annually, but do not benefit directly from that impact

findings.plain: Other cities already do this. Columbus, Ohio put a 5 percent fee on ticketed events in 2018 to support cultural institutions, and Denver and Atlanta use ticket revenue for parks and public assets.
findings.quote: In 2023, the 5 percent fee generated $10.7 million

findings.plain: New York State has repeatedly created standalone entities that hold dedicated revenue outside the regular budget, including the Battery Park City Authority and the Hudson River Park Trust.
findings.quote: In 1998, the state passed a law to form the Hudson River Park Trust

recommendations: Have the City Council pass a home rule resolution asking Albany to let the city collect a parks improvement surcharge on event tickets.
Have the state pass legislation authorizing the city to enact the surcharge, which the report says avoids any question of state preemption.

Have the City Council then pass a local law creating the surcharge and putting the Department of Finance in charge of collecting it, with the report favoring a 3 percent rate, exempting tickets under $30 and exempting events such as SummerStage and Celebrate Brooklyn that already raise money for parks.
Have the state create a Parks Improvement Trust that receives the surcharge money and passes it through to the Parks Department, so the revenue does not land in the General Fund.
Write flexibility into the legislation so the surcharge can be adjusted over time as inflation erodes its value.

Release Trust money only if the city keeps its own parks funding at or above a set baseline, such as the fiscal 2025 level, and give the Trust representation from the City Council, labor unions and community organizations rather than the mayoral administration alone.
Have the City Council require the Parks Department to publish an annual report showing how the surcharge money was spent and whether it reached under-resourced neighborhoods.
